question:
A multinational company with hundreds of AWS accounts has gradually adopted AWS Organizations with all features enabled.

    The company has also configured some Organizational Units (OUs) to meet its business objectives. The company has some IAM roles that must be configured in each new AWS account that is created. Additionally, security policy requires that AWS CloudTrail be enabled on all AWS accounts. The company is looking for an automated solution that can:

- Add required IAM roles
- Configure CloudTrail
- Automatically apply it to all new accounts
- Delete resources/settings when an account leaves the organization
- Without manual intervention

What should a DevOps engineer do to meet these requirements with the lowest operational overhead?

options.A: From your AWS Organizations management account, create an AWS CloudFormation StackSet to enable AWS Config and deploy centralized IAM roles. Configure the StackSet to deploy automatically when you create an account through AWS Organizations.
options.B: Run automation across multiple accounts using AWS Systems Manager Automation. Create an AWS resource group from the management account (or from a centralized account) and name it exactly the same for all accounts and OUs, adding the account ID or OU as a prefix according to the naming standard. Include the CloudTrail configuration and the IAM role that needs to be created.
options.C: From your AWS Organizations management account, create an Amazon EventBridge rule that fires when the AWS Account Creation API is run. Configure an AWS Lambda function to: enable CloudTrail logging, attach the required IAM roles to the account
options.D: From the AWS Organizations management account, enable AWS CloudTrail logs for all member accounts. Similarly, create an IAM role and share it between accounts and OUs in the AWS organization.

explanation:
From your AWS Organizations management account, create an AWS CloudFormation StackSet to enable AWS Config and deploy your centralized AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles. Configure the StackSet to deploy automatically when an account is created through AWS Organizations.

You can centrally orchestrate any service supported by AWS CloudFormation across multiple AWS accounts and Regions. For example, you can display:

- centralized IAM roles
- Amazon EC2 instances
- AWS Lambda functions

across multiple regions and accounts within your organization. CloudFormation StackSets simplify setting up permissions between accounts and enable the automatic creation and deletion of resources when accounts are added or removed from your organization. To get started, you can enable data sharing between CloudFormation and Organizations from the StackSets console. Once this is done, you can use StackSets from your AWS Organizations master account to deploy stacks to:

- all accounts of the organization, or
- specific organizational units (OUs).

With these StackSets a new permissions model called Service-managed permissions is available.

When you choose Service-managed permissions, StackSets automatically configures the IAM permissions necessary to deploy the stack to accounts in your organization. In addition to configuring permissions, CloudFormation StackSets allows you to automatically create or delete stacks when a new account joins or leaves your organization. This means that:

- you do not need to manually connect to each new account to deploy common infrastructure
- you also do not need to manually delete infrastructure when an account is removed from the organization

When an account leaves the organization, the stack is removed from StackSets management.

However, you can choose if you want to:

- delete the resources, or
- maintain existing resources

that were being managed by that stack. Finally, you can choose whether you want to deploy a stack to:

- the entire organization, or
- one or more Organizational Units (OU).

You can also configure deployment options such as:

- how many accounts will be deployed in parallel
- how many failures are tolerated before stopping the entire deployment

Incorrect options (translated)

Wrong option

Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that fires when the account creation API runs, and configure a Lambda function to enable CloudTrail and attach IAM roles.

❌ This option uses too many services, unnecessarily increasing the complexity and cost of the solution.

Wrong option

Run automation across multiple accounts using AWS Systems Manager Automation and create a resource group in the management account with standardized names.

❌ Although AWS Systems Manager can automate tasks across multiple accounts, the other details described are not relevant to the intended use case.When you run automation across multiple accounts and regions, you must target resources using tags or the name of a resource group.

That resource group must:

- exist in each account
- exist in each region
- have exactly the same name

The automation will fail on resources that do not have the specified tag or do not belong to the specified resource group.

Wrong option

Enable CloudTrail from the management account for all accounts and create a shared IAM role between all accounts.

❌ Although it is possible to enable organizational CloudTrail, its goal is to centralize event logging.

Additionally, creating an IAM role in the management account and sharing it with all accounts requires manual work, so it does not meet the automation requirement of the use case.

question:
A CloudFormation stack consists of the following AWS resources:

- an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket
- an Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud instance (Amazon EC2)
- an Amazon EBS volume

Due to a high-impact security issue, the DevOps team has been asked to rename the AWS CloudFormation stack.

However, resources created by the stack cannot be deleted for business reasons.

What steps would you take to rename the CloudFormation stack without deleting the created resources?

options.A: TO). Launch a new CloudFormation stack that deploys all the resources in the stack. Launch another CloudFormation stack that deploys all resources in the stack under a new name. In the second CloudFormation stack, use the DependsOn attribute to create a resource dependency with the first stack. Eliminate both stacks while maintaining resources.
options.B: B) Launch a CloudFormation stack that deploys all the resources in the stack. Add a Retain attribute to the DeletionPolicy for each of these resources. Delete the original stack. Create a new stack with a different name and import the resources that were retained from the original stack. Remove the Retain attribute from the stack to return to the original template.
options.C:
C) Use the CloudFormation registry to create custom hooks for all resources in the CloudFormation stack. Then delete the original CloudFormation stack and create a new one with the updated name.

Using the hooks created above, import the resources back into the newly created stack.
options.D: D) Launch a CloudFormation stack that deploys all the resources in the stack. Add a Retain attribute to the S3 bucket and EC2 instance deletion policy. Add a Snapshot attribute to the Amazon EBS volume deletion policy. Delete the original stack. Create a new stack with a different name and import the resources that were retained from the original stack. Remove the Retain and Snapshot attributes from the stack to return to the original template.

explanation:
Correct option

Launch a CloudFormation stack that deploys all the resources in the stack.
Add a Retain attribute to the DeletionPolicy for each of these resources.

Delete the original stack.

Create a new stack with a different name and import the resources that were retained from the original stack.

Remove the Retain attribute from the stack to return to the original template.

Explanation

With the DeletionPolicy attribute, you can preserve and, in some cases, backup a resource when its stack is deleted.

You must specify a DeletionPolicy attribute for each resource whose behavior you want to control.

If a resource does not have a DeletionPolicy attribute, AWS CloudFormation deletes the resource by default.

To keep a resource when the stack is removed, you must specify:

DeletionPolicy: Retain

for that resource.

You can use Retain with any type of resource.

For resources that support snapshots, such as AWS::EC2::Volume, you can specify:

DeletionPolicy: Snapshot

to have CloudFormation create a snapshot before deleting the resource.

Steps to be followed

1. Launch a CloudFormation stack that deploys the necessary resources.
2. Add the Retain attribute to the removal policy for all resources deployed by the stack.
3. Delete the stack and verify that the resources are maintained.
4. Create a new stack and import the resources that were retained from the original stack. This new stack is created with a different name.
5. Remove the Retain attribute from the stack to return to the original template.

Incorrect options

Wrong option

Add Retain to the S3 bucket and EC2 instance, and Snapshot to the EBS volume.

This is incorrect because the Snapshot attribute deletes the resource after the snapshot is created.
Therefore, the original resource is not preserved, which does not meet the problem requirement.

Wrong option

Use CloudFormation Registry to create custom hooks.

A hook is executable custom logic that inspects resources before they are provisioned.

Hooks can parse the resources that CloudFormation is about to create.
If they detect resources that do not comply with the organization's policies, they can stop the provisioning process.

However, hooks are useless for this use case, so this option is incorrect.

Wrong option

Create two stacks and use DependsOn.

This option only works as a distractor, since it does not solve the problem of renaming the stack while maintaining resources.

Sources

AWS CloudFormation – DeletionPolicy[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-attribute-deletionpolicy.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-attribute-deletionpolicy.html)

AWS Blog – Renaming a CloudFormation Stack While Keeping Resources[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/keep-your-aws-resources-when-you-rename-an-aws-cloudformation-stack/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/keep-your-aws-resources-when-you-rename-an-aws-cloudformation-stack/)AWS CloudFormation Hooks Documentation[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudformation-cli/latest/userguide/hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cloudformation-cli/latest/userguide/hooks.html)

question:
A company wants to impose regulations to prevent frequent logins by DevOps engineers to Amazon EC2 instances. Additionally, there is the additional condition that an immediate notification must be sent to the security team if any login occurs.

What solution would you suggest to meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure the Amazon CloudWatch Agent on each Amazon EC2 instance with the configuration to send all logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create a CloudWatch metric filter to detect user logins. Use Amazon SNS to notify the security team when a login is detected.
options.B: Configure AWS CloudTrail to trace AWS API calls and log them to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Subscribe CloudWatch Logs to Amazon Kinesis. Configure an AWS Lambda function as a consumer of the Kinesis stream to process logs and detect logins. Use Amazon SNS to send notifications to the security team when a sign-in event is detected.
options.C: Configure the Amazon Inspector Agent on each EC2 instance to send all logs to CloudWatch Logs. Create a CloudWatch metric filter to detect user logins. Use Amazon SNS to notify the security team when a login is detected.
options.D: Configure the Amazon CloudWatch Agent on each EC2 instance to send all logs to CloudWatch Logs. Create a CloudWatch subscription filter to detect user logins. Use Amazon SNS to notify the security team when a login is detected.

explanation:
Correct option

Configure the Amazon CloudWatch Agent on each Amazon EC2 instance with the configuration to send all logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

Create a CloudWatch metric filter to detect user logins.

Use Amazon SNS to notify the security team when a login is detected.

Explanation

The Amazon CloudWatch Agent can be installed on EC2 instances to collect and send log data to CloudWatch Logs.

By configuring a metric filter within CloudWatch Logs, you can search for specific patterns, such as user login events.

If a login is found in the log data, Amazon SNS is used to send an immediate notification to the security team.

You can use CloudWatch Logs to monitor applications and systems using log data in near real-time.

For example, CloudWatch Logs can track the number of errors that occur in your application logs and send you a notification when the error rate exceeds a threshold you have defined.

The CloudWatch Logs Agent sends log data every five seconds by default, and this behavior can be configured by the user.

You can monitor log events as they are sent to CloudWatch Logs by creating Metric Filters.

Metric Filters convert log data into Amazon CloudWatch metrics, which can be used to:

- generate graphs
- create alarms

Source:[https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/faqs/)

Incorrect options

Wrong option

Configure the CloudWatch Agent on each EC2 instance to send logs to CloudWatch Logs, create a subscription filter to detect logins, and use SNS for notifications.

Subscriptions are used to get a real-time stream of log events from CloudWatch Logs and send them to other services such as:

-Amazon Kinesis
-Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose
- AWS Lambda

for custom processing, analysis or uploading to other systems.

A subscription filter defines:

- the filter pattern
- the destination to which matching events will be sent

However, to convert log data into CloudWatch metrics for creating charts or alarms, you must use Metric Filters, not Subscription Filters.

Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Wrong option

Configure AWS CloudTrail to log AWS API calls and send them to CloudWatch Logs, then process them with Kinesis and Lambda.

AWS CloudTrail records calls to the AWS API, including sign-in events.

However, CloudTrail typically delivers logs with an average delay of approximately 5 minutes after the API call, and this time is not guaranteed.

Therefore, it does not meet the immediate notification requirement, and this option is incorrect.

Wrong option

Configure the Amazon Inspector Agent to send logs to CloudWatch Logs and detect logins.

Amazon Inspector is a vulnerability management service that continuously scans AWS workloads for:

- software vulnerabilities
- unintended network exposure

Inspector can analyze:- EC2 instances
- container images in Amazon ECR
- AWS Lambda functions

But it cannot be used to detect user login events in real time.

Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Sources

Amazon CloudWatch FAQs[https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/faqs/)

CloudWatch Features[https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/features/#CloudWatch_Logs](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudwatch/features/#CloudWatch_Logs)

AWS CloudTrail Documentation[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/how-cloudtrail-works.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/how-cloudtrail-works.html)

question:
An e-commerce company is deploying its core application on Amazon EC2 instances.

The DevOps team needs a solution to query both the application logs and the API activity of the AWS account.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer – Professional, what solution would you recommend to meet these requirements?

options.A: Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon Athena to query both sets of logs.
options.B: Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to CloudWatch Logs. Use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query both sets of logs.
options.C: Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Amazon S3. Use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances to Amazon S3. Use Amazon Athena to query both sets of logs.
options.D: Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Kinesis Data Streams. Use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances to Kinesis Data Streams. Send both streams to Kinesis Data Analytics to run queries in near real time.

explanation:
CORRECT CHOICE

Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to CloudWatch Logs.
Use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances to Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
Use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query both sets of logs.

EXPLANATION

CloudTrail is enabled by default for your AWS account. You can use Event history in the CloudTrail console to view, search, download, archive, analyze, and respond to account activity across your entire AWS infrastructure. This includes activity carried out through:

- AWS Management Console
- AWS Command Line Interface (CLI)
- AWS SDKs and APIs

To keep a running record of events in your AWS account, you can create a trail. A trail allows CloudTrail to deliver log files to an Amazon S3 bucket.

By default, when you create a trail in the console:

- the trail applies to all AWS regions
- logs events from all regions within the AWS partition
- deliver the log files to the Amazon S3 bucket you specify

Additionally, you can configure other AWS services to analyze or act on event data collected in CloudTrail logs.

You can also configure CloudTrail with CloudWatch Logs to monitor trail API logs and receive notifications when specific activity occurs.

When you configure your trail to send events to CloudWatch Logs, CloudTrail sends only the events that match the trail's configuration.

For example, if you configure your trail to log only data events, the trail will send only data events to the CloudWatch Logs log group.

CloudTrail supports sending the following types of events to CloudWatch Logs:

- data events
- Insights events
- management events

You can collect metrics and logs from:

- Amazon EC2 instances
- on-premises servers

using the CloudWatch agent.

Metrics collected by the CloudWatch agent can be stored and viewed in CloudWatch, just like any other CloudWatch metrics.

The default namespace for metrics collected by the CloudWatch agent is:

CWAgent

However, you can specify a different namespace when configuring the agent.

Logs collected by the CloudWatch unified agent are processed and stored in Amazon CloudWatch Logs.

For this use case, you can have AWS CloudTrail and Amazon CloudWatch Agent send their respective logs to CloudWatch Logs. You can then use CloudWatch Logs Insights to query both sets of logs.

WRONG OPTIONS

Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Amazon S3, use the CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 to Amazon S3, and use Amazon Athena to query both sets of logs.

It is not possible to use Amazon CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 instances directly to Amazon S3, so this option is incorrect.Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Kinesis Data Streams and use the CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 to Kinesis Data Streams, then direct both streams to Kinesis Data Analytics to run queries in near real-time.

It is not possible to deliver CloudTrail API logs directly to Kinesis Data Streams.
It is also not possible to send logs from EC2 to Kinesis Data Streams using CloudWatch Agent.
Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Configure AWS CloudTrail to deliver API logs to Amazon S3, use the CloudWatch Agent to send logs from EC2 to CloudWatch Logs, and use Amazon Athena to query both sets of logs.

It is not possible to use Amazon Athena to query logs that are in CloudWatch Logs, so this option is incorrect.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-getting-started.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-getting-started.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/send-cloudtrail-events-to-cloudwatch-logs.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/send-cloudtrail-events-to-cloudwatch-logs.html)

question:
A web application is hosted on Amazon EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB).

While using CodeDeploy Blue/Green deployment to deploy a new version, the deployment failed during the AllowTraffic lifecycle event.

The DevOps team found no errors in the deployment logs.

Which of the following would you identify as the root cause of the deployment failure?

options.A: A scale-in event or any other termination event, during a deployment in progress, causes the instance to be detached from the Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and the instance to fail in the AllowTraffic lifecycle event.
options.B: Incorrectly configured health checks in the Application Load Balancer (ALB) are responsible for this issue.
options.C:
The cause of the failure could be a script from the last successful deployment that never runs correctly.

Create a new deployment and specify that ApplicationStop, BeforeBlockTraffic, and AfterBlockTraffic failures should be ignored.
options.D: If an instance is terminated between lifecycle events or before the first step of the lifecycle event begins, then the AllowTraffic event fails without generating logs.

explanation:
CORRECT CHOICE

An incorrect configuration of the health checks in the Application Load Balancer (ALB) is responsible for this problem.

In some cases, a Blue/Green deployment fails during the AllowTraffic lifecycle event, but the deployment logs do not indicate the cause of the failure.

This failure is generally due to poorly configured health checks in Elastic Load Balancing, either for:

-Classic Load Balancer
- Application Load Balancer
- Network Load Balancer

that are used to manage deployment group traffic.

To resolve the issue, errors in the load balancer health check configuration must be reviewed and corrected.

WRONG OPTIONS

The cause of the failure could be a script from the last successful deployment that never runs correctly. Create a new deployment and specify that ApplicationStop, BeforeBlockTraffic, and AfterBlockTraffic failures should be ignored.

During a deployment, the CodeDeploy agent runs the scripts specified for ApplicationStop, BeforeBlockTraffic, and AfterBlockTraffic in the AppSpec file of the last successful deployment.

(All other scripts are run from the AppSpec of the current deployment.)

If any of these scripts contain an error and do not run correctly, the deployment may fail.

This type of failure generates logs, and does not specifically fail the AllowTraffic event.

If an instance is terminated between lifecycle events or before the first step of the lifecycle event begins, then the AllowTraffic event fails without generating logs.

This statement is incorrect.

Deployments do not fail for up to one hour when an instance is terminated during a deployment.

A scale-in event or any termination event during a deployment in progress causes the instance to be disassociated from the Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group and the instance to fail in the AllowTraffic event.

During a deployment in progress, a scale-in event or any termination event causes the instance to be disassociated from the Auto Scaling Group (ASG) and then terminated.

Because the deployment cannot be completed, the deployment fails.

However, this error is specific to Auto Scaling Groups (ASG) and is not related to the issue described in the question.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-deployments.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-deployments.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-ec2-instances.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/troubleshooting-ec2-instances.html)

question: A company uses a serverless application architecture to process thousands of requests using AWS Lambda with Amazon DynamoDB as the database. An Amazon API Gateway REST API is used to invoke an AWS Lambda function that loads a large amount of data from the Amazon DynamoDB database. This results in cold start latencies of 7 to 10 seconds. DynamoDB tables have already been configured with DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) to reduce latency. However, customers continue to report application latency, especially during peak hours. The app receives maximum traffic between 2 PM and 5 PM every day and then gradually reduces, reporting minimum traffic after 8 PM. How should a DevOps engineer configure the AWS Lambda function to reduce its latency at all times?

options.A:
Configure the AWS Lambda function to use provisioned concurrency.

Configure Application Auto Scaling on the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency values ​​of 1 (minimum) and 100 (maximum) respectively.
options.B:
Configure the Lambda function runtime to use up to 10,240 MB of ephemeral storage.

This transient cache of data between invocations can be accessed from the Lambda function code through the /tmp space.
options.C:
Configure the AWS Lambda function to use reserved concurrency.

Configure Application Auto Scaling on the Lambda function with reserved concurrency as half of the Lambda function instances invoked during peak traffic hours.
options.D:
Use Lambda function layers for parallel processing of Lambda runtime requests.

Deploy the Lambda function as a .zip file to use the Lambda layer functionality.

explanation:
CORRECT CHOICE

Configure the AWS Lambda function to use provisioned concurrency.

Configure Application Auto Scaling on the Lambda function with provisioned concurrency values ​​of 1 (minimum) and 100 (maximum) respectively.

EXPLANATION

For a Lambda function, concurrency is the number of ongoing requests your function is handling at the same time.

Provisioned concurrency is the number of pre-initialized runtimes you want to assign to your function.

These runtimes are prepared to respond immediately to incoming function requests.

Setting up provisioned concurrency incurs charges to your AWS account.

ESTIMATION OF THE NECESSARY PROVISIONED CONCURRENCY

If your function is already receiving traffic, you can easily view its concurrency metrics using CloudWatch metrics.

In particular, the metric:

ConcurrentExecutions

shows the number of concurrent invocations for each function in your account.

When you work with provisioned concurrency, AWS Lambda recommends including an additional 10% buffer over the concurrency that your function normally needs.

For example:

If your function typically peaks at 200 concurrent requests, you should configure:

220 provisioned concurrency

(200 concurrent requests + 10% = 220 provisioned concurrency)

You can mitigate cold start issues by configuring the optimal amount of provisioned concurrency for the Lambda function.

LATENCY OPTIMIZATION WITH PROVISIONED CONCURRENCY

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html)

ACCURATE ESTIMATION OF PROVISIONED CONCURRENCY

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html)

WRONG OPTIONS

Configure the AWS Lambda function to use Reserved concurrency.

Configure Application Auto Scaling on the Lambda function with reserved concurrency as half of the instances invoked during peak hours.

Reserved concurrency is the maximum number of concurrent instances you want to assign to your function.

When a function has reserved concurrency, no other function can use that concurrency.

Reserved concurrency is best suited for use cases where traffic is constant and predictable throughout the day.

Configure the Lambda function runtime to use up to 10,240 MB of ephemeral storage.

This transient cache of data between invocations can be accessed from the Lambda function code through the /tmp space.

For data intensive applications such as:

- machine learning inference
- financial calculations

Clients often need to read and write large amounts of data to ephemeral storage.

The Lambda runtime provides an ephemeral file system accessible via /tmp, which is persisted for the life of the runtime and can serve as a temporary cache between invocations.

This option acts only as a distractor.Use Lambda layers for parallel processing of Lambda runtime requests.

Deploy the Lambda function as a .zip file to use the Lambda layer functionality.

A Lambda layer is a .zip file that may contain additional code or data.

A layer can contain:

- bookstores
- a custom runtime
- data
- configuration files

Layers promote code sharing and separation of responsibilities, allowing you to iterate faster on business logic.

This option is not relevant for the given use case.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#calculating-concurrency](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/lambda-concurrency.html#calculating-concurrency)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/provisioned-concurrency.html)

[https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/03/aws-lambda-configure-ephemeral-storage/](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2022/03/aws-lambda-configure-ephemeral-storage/)

question:
Amazon S3 buckets are widely used by a media company to store image files, documents, and other business-specific data. The company has mandated enabling logging for all Amazon S3 buckets. The audit team publishes reports of all AWS resources that do not meet the company's security standards. Until recently, the security team would take the audit list of non-compliant S3 buckets and manually execute remediation actions for each resource. This process is not only time-consuming but also leaves non-compliant resources vulnerable for a long period. What combination of steps should a DevOps Engineer take to meet these requirements using an automated solution?

(Select two)

options.A:
Configure AWS Config Auto Remediation for the AWS Config s3-bucket-logging-enabled rule.

From the list of remediation actions choose AWS Lambda to implement a custom function that enables S3 logging for the S3 bucket ID received as a parameter.
options.B:
The AutomationAssumeRole in the remediation action parameters must be able to be assumed by SSM.

The user must have pass-role permissions for that role when you create the remediation action in AWS Config.
options.C:
While configuring the remediation action, pass the resource ID of the non-compliant resources to the remediation action.

This configuration is required for auto-remediation to work.
options.D:
Configure AWS Config Auto Remediation for the AWS Config s3-bucket-logging-enabled rule.

From the list of remediation actions choose AWS-ConfigureS3BucketLogging.
options.E:
Configure AWS Config Auto Remediation for the AWS Config s3-logging-enabled rule.

Create your own custom remediation action using AWS Systems Manager Automation documents to enable logging to the S3 bucket.

explanation:
AWS Config Auto Remediation enables you to automatically remediate non-compliant resources evaluated by AWS Config rules. You can associate remediation actions with AWS Config rules and configure them to run automatically without manual intervention.

AWS Config allows:

- Choose a remediation action from a predefined list.
- Create custom remediation actions using AWS Systems Manager Automation documents.
- Retry self-remediation if the resource remains non-compliant after the first attempt.

For this case:

1. You must have AWS Config enabled on the account.
2. The AutomationAssumeRole parameter must be assumed by AWS Systems Manager (SSM).
3. The user configuring remediation must have iam:PassRole permissions.
4. That role must have the necessary permissions to run the SSM automation document.

The s3-bucket-logging-enabled rule already has a remediation action managed by AWS:

AWS-ConfigureS3BucketLogging

Therefore, there is no need to create custom code.

WRONG OPTIONS

A. Although you can use AWS Lambda for custom remediation, it is not necessary in this case because AWS Config already has a predefined action to enable S3 logging.

C. The Resource ID parameter can be used to pass the ID of the non-compliant resource to the remediation action.

However, it is not required for Auto Remediation to work.

E. The correct AWS Config rule is:

s3-bucket-logging-enabled

Not s3-logging-enabled, so this option is incorrect.

SOURCE

AWS Config Auto Remediation for S3 Compliance

question: A support team wants to be notified using an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when an AWS Glue Job fails after a retry. As a DevOps Engineer, how would you implement this requirement?

options.A: Configure Amazon EventBridge events for AWS Glue. Configure an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when the Glue job fails after a retry.
options.B: Review the AWS Personal Health Dashboard for failed AWS Glue jobs. Schedule an AWS Lambda function to collect the failed event from the service health dashboard and trigger an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) notification when a retry fails.
options.C: Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) cannot retry failures; Use Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with dead-letter queues to retry failed Glue jobs.
options.D: Configure Amazon EventBridge events for AWS Glue. Define an AWS Lambda function as an EventBridge target. The Lambda function will have the logic to process the events and filter the Glue job retry event. Publish a message to Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) if such an event is detected.

explanation:
The correct solution is to use Amazon EventBridge to capture AWS Glue events, send those events to AWS Lambda, and have Lambda specifically filter the event when a Glue Job fails after a retry. If that event is detected, the function publishes a message to Amazon SNS to notify the support team.

Architecture:

1. AWS Glue generates job status events.
2. Amazon EventBridge captures those events.
3. AWS Lambda processes the event and checks if it corresponds to job retry failure.
4. If it matches, Lambda publishes a message to Amazon SNS.
5. SNS sends the notification to the support team.

This is necessary because EventBridge alone cannot filter with enough logic to specifically detect the failure after the retry, so Lambda implements that filtering logic.

Steps:

1. Create an SNS Topic.
2. Create a Lambda function that:
    - receive events from EventBridge
    - check the retry failure event
    - post a message on SNS.
3. Create an EventBridge rule for AWS Glue that invokes the Lambda.

Reference:[https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/glue-job-fail-retry-lambda-sns-alerts](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/glue-job-fail-retry-lambda-sns-alerts)

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

Configure EventBridge for AWS Glue and directly send an SNS notification when the Glue job fails on a retry.

Why it seems correct: EventBridge can send events directly to SNS.

Why it is incorrect: The requirement is to notify only when the job fails after a retry.
EventBridge does not have enough logic to filter this specific scenario, so Lambda is needed to process the event and apply the filtering logic.

b.

Review AWS Personal Health Dashboard and use Lambda to detect failures.

Why it seems correct: The Personal Health Dashboard can generate events related to AWS services.

Why it's incorrect: The AWS Personal Health Dashboard only provides notifications about AWS infrastructure or maintenance events, not about Glue-specific job failures.
Therefore it is not relevant for this use case.

c.

SNS cannot retry failures, use SQS DLQ to retry Glue jobs.

Why it seems correct: Dead-Letter Queues (DLQs) are commonly used to handle failures and retries.

Why it is incorrect: The requirement is not to retry the job, but to notify when the retry fails.
Therefore, SQS DLQ does not solve the problem.

SOURCE

AWS re:Post[https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/glue-job-fail-retry-lambda-sns-alerts](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/glue-job-fail-retry-lambda-sns-alerts)

question:
An AWS Config cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check managed rule is defined to detect drift in AWS CloudFormation resources. The DevOps team faces two problems:
a) How to detect drifts of custom resources (custom resources) from CloudFormation.
b) The stack status appears as IN_SYNC in the CloudFormation console, but the following error appears in the drift detection:
"While AWS CloudFormation failed to detect drift, defaulting to NON_COMPLIANT. Re-evaluate the rule and try again. If the problem persists contact AWS CloudFormation support"
As a DevOps Engineer, what steps should you combine to solve the mentioned problems?
(Select two)

options.A: You receive the error when the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role for the required parameter cloudformationRoleArn does not have sufficient service permissions.
options.B: The AWS Config rule depends on the availability of the CloudFormation API DetectStackDrift action. AWS Config sets the rule state to NON_COMPLIANT when throttling occurs.
options.C: AWS CloudFormation does not support drift detection for custom resources.
options.D: This error is a false positive and can be ignored in this scenario.
options.E: AWS CloudFormation only determines drift for property values ​​that are explicitly defined. Explicitly define property values ​​for your custom resource so that they are included in drift detection.

explanation:
The AWS Config managed rule cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check checks whether the actual configuration of a CloudFormation stack differs from the expected configuration defined in the template.

A stack is considered:

- COMPLIANT → when drift status is IN_SYNC
- NON_COMPLIANT → when the status is DRIFTED

AWS CloudFormation Drift Detection enables you to detect unmanaged changes to stack resources. This allows corrective actions to be taken to re-synchronize the resources with the CloudFormation template.

For the problem scenario there are two key points:

1️⃣ DetectStackDrift API Dependency

The AWS Config rule depends on the DetectStackDrift action of the CloudFormation API.

If throttling or “Rate Exceeded” occurs, AWS Config automatically marks the rule as NON_COMPLIANT, generating the observed error.

2️⃣ Limitation with Custom Resources

Currently AWS CloudFormation does NOT support drift detection for custom resources.

Drift detection only works with resource types supported by CloudFormation.

Therefore:

- It is not possible to detect drift in custom resources
- This explains the behavior observed in the scenario.

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

You receive the error when the IAM role for cloudformationRoleArn does not have sufficient permissions.

Why it appears correct: Permission errors are common when running CloudFormation operations.

Why it is incorrect: A permissions error would generate a different message, for example:

"Your stack drift detection operation for the specific stack has failed. Check your existing AWS CloudFormation role permissions and add the missing permissions."

The error shown is not an IAM issue.

d.

This error is a false positive and can be ignored.

Why it appears correct: Sometimes AWS Config may incorrectly mark resources as NON_COMPLIANT.

Why it is incorrect: The error has a clear technical cause:

- DetectStackDrift throttling
- lack of support for custom resources

Therefore it should not be ignored.

e.

CloudFormation only detects drift for explicitly defined properties.

Why it seems correct: It is true that CloudFormation detects drift only for properties explicitly defined in the template or parameters.

Why it is incorrect: Although this is true, it does not apply to custom resources, because these resources are not supported for drift detection.

SOURCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudformation-stack-drift-detection-check.html)

[https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/config-cloudformation-drift-detection](https://repost.aws/knowledge-center/config-cloudformation-drift-detection)

question:
An e-commerce company has a serverless application that consists of CloudFront, API Gateway, and Lambda functions. The company has hired you to improve the current deployment process, which creates a new version of the Lambda function and then runs an AWS CLI script to perform the deployment. If the new version fails, another CLI script is run to deploy the previous working version of the Lambda function.

The company has requested to reduce the time needed to deploy new versions of Lambda functions and also reduce the time needed to detect and rollback when errors are identified.

What solution would you suggest for this use case?

options.A: Use the Serverless Application Model (SAM) and take advantage of SAM's built-in traffic shifting functionality to deploy the new version of Lambda using CodeDeploy, and use pre-traffic and post-traffic testing functions to verify the code. Rollback if CloudWatch alarms are triggered.
options.B: Configure and deploy nested CloudFormation stacks with CloudFront distribution and API Gateway in the parent stack. Create and deploy a child stack that contains the Lambda functions. To manage changes in Lambda, create a CloudFormation change set and deploy it. If the Lambda function fails, revert the change set to the previous version.
options.C: Configure and deploy nested CloudFormation stacks with CloudFront distribution and API Gateway in the parent stack. Create and deploy a child stack that contains the Lambda functions. For changes in Lambda, create a CloudFormation change set and deploy it. Use pre-traffic and post-traffic test functions of the change set to verify the deployment. Rollback if CloudWatch alarms are triggered.
options.D: Configure and deploy a CloudFormation stack that contains a new API Gateway endpoint that points to the new version of Lambda. Test the updated CloudFront origin that points to this new API Gateway endpoint and, if errors are detected, revert the CloudFront origin to the previous API Gateway endpoint that was working correctly.

explanation:
The best solution is to use AWS Serverless Application Model (SAM) together with AWS CodeDeploy to implement secure AWS Lambda deployments using traffic shifting.

AWS SAM is an open-source framework for building serverless applications. It allows you to define resources such as Lambda, API Gateway and DynamoDB with a simplified syntax in YAML. During deployment, SAM transforms the template into CloudFormation, which ultimately provisions the resources.

For this use case, SAM includes native integration with CodeDeploy for incremental Lambda deployments, allowing:

- Publish a new version of Lambda without sending traffic immediately
- Run a PreTraffic test to validate the new version
- Shift traffic gradually towards the new version (traffic shifting)
- Run PostTraffic validations
- Automatic rollback if CloudWatch alarms are triggered

This allows:

- Reduce time to detect errors
- Reduce rollback time
- Avoid sending 100% of traffic immediately to a new version

Deployment flow:

1. SAM deploys a new version of Lambda
2. CodeDeploy runs the PreTraffic test
3. If the test is successful, CodeDeploy moves traffic gradually
4. CloudWatch monitors errors
5. If an alarm is activated → automatic rollback

Reference:

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/implementing-safe-aws-lambda-deployments-with-aws-codedeploy/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/implementing-safe-aws-lambda-deployments-with-aws-codedeploy/)

WRONG OPTIONS

b.

Use nested CloudFormation stacks and change sets.

Why it seems correct: CloudFormation change sets allow you to review changes before deploying them.

Why it is incorrect: Change sets do not help detect errors quickly, because the failure is only detected after the deployment is executed.
There is no traffic shifting or automatic validations.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html)

c.

Use change sets with pre-traffic and post-traffic tests.

Why it seems correct: The terms pre-traffic and post-traffic are common in CodeDeploy deployments.

Why it is incorrect:
CloudFormation change sets do NOT have pre-traffic or post-traffic functions. This is a feature of CodeDeploy for Lambda, not CloudFormation.

d.

Create a new API Gateway endpoint and change the CloudFront origin.

Why it seems correct: It could allow you to test a new version before redirecting traffic.

Why it is incorrect: It does not reduce the time to detect errors or automate rollback.
Changing endpoints requires manual operation and infrastructure changes, which increases operational overhead.

SOURCES

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/implementing-safe-aws-lambda-deployments-with-aws-codedeploy/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/implementing-safe-aws-lambda-deployments-with-aws-codedeploy/)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/serverless-application-model/latest/developerguide/automating-updates-to-serverless-apps.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/serverless-application-model/latest/developerguide/automating-updates-to-serverless-apps.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-changesets.html)

question:
A production environment has Amazon EC2 instances configured to log all application/system logs using the CloudWatch Logs agent, which is configured on all instances.

The company recently introduced a security policy that requires terminating any production EC2 instance that is manually accessed by a non-administrator user in less than one hour.

All production instances are configured with Auto Scaling Groups.

As a DevOps Engineer, how would you automate this process?

options.A: Configure an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that is triggered by login event data and invokes an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda function to add a decommission tag to the EC2 instance that generated the login event. Schedule an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke the Lambda function every hour and terminate all EC2 instances with the decommission tag.
options.B: Create an Amazon CloudWatch alarm that is triggered by the login event data. Create an alarm action that notifies system administrators with a message using Amazon Simple Notification Service (SNS). System administrators will manually terminate the instance.
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Logs subscription to an AWS Step Function that coordinates with AWS Lambda and Amazon EventBridge to create an automated serverless solution. Configure a Lambda function to add a decommission tag to the EC2 instance that produced the login event. Create an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke a second Lambda function every hour, which will terminate all instances with that tag.
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Logs subscription to send login event data from EC2 instances to an AWS Lambda function. Configure the Lambda to add a decommission tag to the EC2 instance that generated the login event. Schedule an Amazon EventBridge rule to invoke another Lambda function every hour that will terminate all EC2 instances with the decommission tag.

explanation:
The correct solution is to use a CloudWatch Logs subscription to send login events to an AWS Lambda function.

CloudWatch Logs Subscriptions allow you to receive a real-time stream of log events and send them to other services such as:

- AWS Lambda
-Amazon Kinesis
- Kinesis Data Firehose

In this case:

1️⃣ The login logs generated in the EC2 instances are sent to CloudWatch Logs through the CloudWatch Logs agent.

2️⃣ A CloudWatch Logs subscription sends those events to Lambda.

3️⃣ The Lambda analyzes the login event and adds a label:

decommission=true

to the EC2 instance that generated the unauthorized access.

4️⃣ A scheduled Amazon EventBridge rule is configured (for example every hour).

5️⃣ This rule executes another Lambda function that:

- looks for EC2 instances with the decommission tag
- terminates such instances automatically

This ticks all the boxes:

✔ Complete automation

✔ Reaction based on real-time logs

✔ Completion within an hour

✔ Compatible with Auto Scaling Groups (instances will be replaced automatically)

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

Use a CloudWatch Alarm to invoke Lambda.

Why it seems correct: CloudWatch can react to metrics or events.

Why it's incorrect: CloudWatch Alarms cannot invoke Lambda directly as an alarm action.
SNS would be needed as an intermediary.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html)

b.

Send a notification to administrators using SNS.

Why it seems correct: SNS is commonly used for operational alerts.

Why it is incorrect: The requirement calls for complete automation.
This option requires manual termination of instances.

c.

Use CloudWatch Logs + Step Functions + Lambda + EventBridge.

Why it seems correct: Step Functions can orchestrate serverless workflows.

Why it is incorrect: It is unnecessarily complex (overkill) for this case.
A simple Lambda triggered by CloudWatch Logs subscription is sufficient.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html)

SOURCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/Subscriptions.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-create-rule-schedule.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/eventbridge/latest/userguide/eb-create-rule-schedule.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/AlarmThatSendsEmail.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/welcome.html)

question:
A data analytics company wants to move all of its customers who are in regulated and security-sensitive industries, such as financial services and healthcare, to the AWS Cloud, as it offers out-of-the-box security capabilities provided by AWS.

The DevOps team is developing a framework to validate the adoption of AWS best practices and industry-recognized compliance standards.

The AWS Management Console is the preferred method for internal teams to provision resources.

What strategies would you adopt to meet these business requirements to continually evaluate, audit, and monitor AWS resource configurations?

(Select two)

options.A: Use the CloudWatch Logs agent to collect all AWS SDK logs. Search log data using a predefined set of filter patterns that match mutating API calls. Use CloudWatch alarms to send notifications on SNS when unintended changes are made. Archive the logs by exporting them in batch to Amazon S3 and analyze them with Amazon Athena.
options.B: Use AWS Config rules to audit changes to AWS resources and monitor configuration compliance by running rule evaluations at a frequency you choose. Develop custom AWS Config rules to establish a test-driven development approach by triggering evaluation when any resource within the scope of the rule changes its configuration.
options.C: Use CloudTrail integration with SNS to automatically report unauthorized API activities. Ensure that CloudTrail is enabled for all available AWS accounts and services. Use Lambda functions to automatically roll back unauthorized changes to AWS resources.
options.D: Enable CloudTrail trails and configure CloudTrail events to review and monitor management activities for all AWS accounts by logging these activities in CloudWatch Logs using a KMS key. Ensure that CloudTrail is enabled for all available AWS accounts and services.
options.E: Use EventBridge events to leverage near real-time capabilities to monitor system event patterns and trigger Lambda functions to automatically roll back unauthorized changes to AWS resources. Send notifications through SNS topics to improve incident response time.

explanation:
To continually evaluate, audit, and monitor resource configurations on AWS, the key services are AWS Config and AWS CloudTrail.

1️⃣ AWS Config – Configuration Compliance Assessment

AWS Config allows you to continually evaluate, audit, and review configurations of AWS resources.

With AWS Config Rules you can define expected configurations (compliance policies).

AWS Config detects when a resource violates those rules and marks it as NON_COMPLIANT.

Key capabilities:

- Record resource configuration history
- Detect configuration changes
- Evaluate compliance against rules
- Use managed rules or custom rules

Types of rule evaluation:

Configuration Change Trigger

- Runs when a resource configuration changes
- Ideal for continuous compliance

Periodic Trigger

- Evaluation at intervals (for example every 24 hours)

This allows the implementation of automated compliance frameworks.

Reference:

[https://aws.amazon.com/config/](https://aws.amazon.com/config/)

2️⃣ AWS CloudTrail – Activity Audit

AWS CloudTrail records all actions taken in an AWS account, including:

- AWS Management Console
- AWS CLI
- AWS SDK
- Other AWS services

Each action generates a CloudTrail event, which allows:

- Audit
- Governance
- Compliance
- Activity analysis

Events can be sent to:

- CloudWatch Logs
-Amazon S3

In this case, it is recommended to send the events to KMS-protected CloudWatch Logs for centralized auditing.

CloudTrail logs:

- Management Events → control operations (create resources, modify policies, etc.)
- Data Events → data operations (S3 object access, Lambda invocation, etc.)

Management events are stored free of charge for 90 days in the event history.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html)

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

Use the CloudWatch Logs agent to collect logs from the AWS SDK.

Why it seems correct: CloudWatch Logs allows you to analyze logs and detect changes using filters.

Why it is incorrect: The scenario indicates that resources are provisioned from the AWS Management Console, not necessarily from SDKs or API calls.
Additionally, AWS Config and CloudTrail are designed specifically for auditing and compliance.

c.

Use CloudTrail + SNS + Lambda to revert unauthorized changes.

Why it seems correct: It allows you to detect activities and react automatically.

Why it's incorrect: The requirement is to evaluate, audit, and monitor configurations, not automatically roll back changes.

e.

Use EventBridge + Lambda to revert unauthorized changes.

Why it seems correct: EventBridge can react to events in near real time.

Why it's incorrect: Again, the requirement is auditing and monitoring, not automatic remediation.

SOURCES

[https://aws.amazon.com/config/](https://aws.amazon.com/config/)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/evaluate-config_manage-rules.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/evaluate-config_manage-rules.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html#cloudtrail-concepts-management-events](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-concepts.html#cloudtrail-concepts-management-events)

question:
A DevOps Engineer is working on multiple applications that need to be configured for Application Auto Scaling, however, there are some application restrictions that need to be considered:
a) A serverless application is built on AWS Lambda with the following traffic pattern: traffic starts to increase on Wednesday, peaks on Thursday, and starts to decrease on Friday.
b) Another critical application runs on Spot Fleet. Fleet CPU utilization should stay around 50% when application load changes.
What solutions would allow these requirements to be met?
(Select two)

options.A: Use a Scheduled Auto Scaling policy and create a scheduled action with AWS Lambda as a scalable target. Specify the minimum and maximum capacity according to the requirements. You can use AWS CLI, SDKs, or CloudFormation to configure scheduled scaling.
options.B: Create an Amazon CloudWatch metric to track an average CPU utilization of 50% for the Spot Fleet. Create a tracking auto-scaling policy with a CloudWatch alarm based on the metric created from the AWS console.
options.C: Use a Scheduled Auto Scaling policy and create a scheduled action with Spot instances as a scalable target. Specify the minimum and maximum capacity according to the requirements.
options.D: Create a target tracking auto scaling policy that targets an average CPU utilization of 50% for an application running in Spot Fleet. You can create and manage the tracking policy using the AWS CLI, SDKs, or CloudFormation.
options.E: Create an Amazon CloudWatch metric to track AWS Lambda function utilization. Configure a step scaling policy by setting the upper limit, lower limit, and threshold values ​​for the Lambda function.

explanation:
The scenario has two different types of auto scaling, so two different strategies are needed:

1️⃣ AWS Lambda – Predictable traffic (Wednesday → Friday)

Traffic follows a predictable weekly pattern, so the best solution is Scheduled Scaling.

Scheduled Scaling allows you to define scaling actions at specific times, for example:

- Increase capacity Wednesday
- Maintain capacity Thursday
- Reduce capacity Friday

With Application Auto Scaling you can define:

- Scalable target → Lambda function
- Min capacity
- Max capacity
- Schedule (cron or rate)

This allows capacity to be prepared before traffic peaks.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html)

2️⃣ Spot Fleet – CPU target 50%

When the requirement is to keep a metric close to a specific value, the best option is Target Tracking Auto Scaling.

In this case:

- Metric → Average CPU Utilization
- Target → 50%

Application Auto Scaling:

- scale out when CPU > 50%
- scale in when CPU < 50%

This maintains sufficient capacity without over-provisioning resources.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-target-tracking.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-target-tracking.html)

WRONG OPTIONS

b.

Create CloudWatch metric and manual alarm for Target Tracking.

Why it seems correct: Target tracking uses CloudWatch metrics.

Why it's incorrect: When you use Target Tracking, Application Auto Scaling automatically creates and manages CloudWatch alarms.
You should not create them manually.

c.

Scheduled scaling for Spot Instances.

Why it seems correct: Scheduled scaling works with many services.

Why it is incorrect: The requirement is to keep CPU at 50% dynamically, not scale at fixed schedules.
This requires Target Tracking, not scheduled scaling.

e.

Step scaling for Lambda.

Why it seems correct: Step scaling uses metrics and thresholds.

Why it is incorrect:
Step scaling is not supported with AWS Lambda in Application Auto Scaling.

Unsupported services include:

-Lambda
- DynamoDB
- Amazon MSK
-Amazon Keyspaces
- Neptune
- ElastiCache

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-step-scaling-policies.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-step-scaling-policies.html)

SOURCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-target-tracking.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-target-tracking.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-scheduled-scaling.html)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-step-scaling-policies.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/application/userguide/application-auto-scaling-step-scaling-policies.html)

question:
An application runs on a set of Amazon EC2 instances configured with an Auto Scaling Group (ASG). Both Spot and On-Demand instances are used depending on the ASG configuration. Overall, the ASG appears to be working as expected. However, the DevOps team has identified some issues:
a) During a scale-in activity, the ASG has terminated an instance in the Availability Zone (AZ) that already had fewer instances than the other AZ.
b) In some cases, the ASG has exceeded the specified maximum capacity of the group.
What reasons can explain this behavior?
(Select two)

options.A: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling may temporarily exceed the specified maximum capacity of the group by up to 10% (or at least one instance, whichever is greater) during a rebalancing activity.
options.B: When an Auto Scaling group with a mixed instances policy scales-in, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling first identifies which instance type (Spot or On-Demand) should be terminated. This may temporarily cause an imbalance between the AZs.
options.C: You can specify only one Lambda function in the termination policies of an Auto Scaling group. If more than one Lambda function is configured, the ASG will behave ambiguously.
options.D: The instance launched with the oldest launch template or launch configuration is terminated first. This can temporarily cause an unbalanced group.
options.E: With the default termination policy, instances that are closest to the next billing time are terminated first. This may temporarily cause an imbalance in the distribution of instances between AZs.

explanation:
The observed behavior is explained by two internal features of Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling.

1️⃣ Rebalancing may temporarily exceed the ASG maximum

During rebalancing activities, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling may temporarily exceed the group's max capacity.

The system can exceed the maximum by:

- 10% of group size
- or at least 1 instance (whichever is greater)

This occurs because Auto Scaling first launches new instances before terminating old ones to avoid impacting application availability or performance.

Example:

Max capacity = 10

During rebalancing → can temporarily reach 11 instances

Once the rebalancing is complete, the group returns to its normal size.

2️⃣ Mixed Instances Policy can cause temporary imbalance

When an Auto Scaling Group uses a Mixed Instances Policy (Spot + On-Demand) and a scale-in occurs, the process is:

1. ASG first decides what type of instance to terminate
    -Spot
    - On-Demand
2. Then apply the termination policies within each AZ

This process may temporarily generate an imbalance between Availability Zones, because the initial decision is based on instance type, not AZ balance.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policies.html#default-termination-policy-mixed-instances-groups] (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policies.html#default-termination-policy-mixed-instances-groups)

WRONG OPTIONS

c.

Only one Lambda function can be configured in termination policies.

Why it seems correct: ASG allows custom termination policies.

Why it is incorrect: Multiple Lambda functions cannot be configured, and it is not related to the problem described.

d.

The instance with the oldest launch template is terminated first.

Why it seems correct: There is a policy related to launch template / launch configuration.

Why it is incorrect:
Auto Scaling first attempts to balance the AZs, regardless of the termination policy.
Therefore, this criterion would not cause the observed imbalance.

e.

Instances close to the next billing time are terminated.

Why it seems correct: In the past AWS optimized costs per billing hour.

Why it's incorrect: The Default Termination Policy uses multiple criteria, not just the billing cycle.
Furthermore, the balance between AZs takes priority.

SOURCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policies.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/ec2-auto-scaling-termination-policies.html)

question:
As a best security practice, a company has decided to back up all of its Amazon Elastic Block Store (Amazon EBS) volumes every week. To implement this change, developers must label all EBS volumes with a custom label. This tag indicates the backup frequency (for example: weekly) and an automated solution reads that tag to schedule backups for each volume.

However, a recent audit found that some EBS volumes were not backed up because they did not have the required custom label.

As a DevOps Engineer, what solution would you choose to ensure that all EBS volumes in the account are labeled backup?

options.A: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to an EBS CreateVolume event in AWS CloudTrail Logs. Configure a custom AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to apply the custom tag with the default weekly value. Specify this runbook as the destination of the EventBridge rule.
options.B: Configure AWS Config in the AWS account. Use a managed rule for the EC2::Instance resource type that returns a compliance failure if the custom label is not applied to EBS volumes attached to the instance. Configure a remediation action that uses AWS Systems Manager Automation to apply the backup frequency label to all non-compliant volumes.
options.C: Create an Amazon EventBridge rule that responds to an EBS VolumeBackup check event from AWS Trusted Advisor. Configure a custom AWS Systems Manager Automation runbook to apply the custom tag with the default weekly value. Specify this runbook as the destination of the EventBridge rule.
options.D: Configure AWS Config in the AWS account. Use a managed rule for the EC2::Volume resource type that returns a compliance failure if the custom label is not applied to the EBS volume. Configure a remediation action that uses AWS Systems Manager Automation to apply the backup frequency label to all non-compliant volumes.

explanation:
The best solution is to use AWS Config to continually audit resources and detect if EBS volumes do not have the required label for backup.

AWS Config allows:

- Evaluate resource configurations
- Detect non-compliant resources
- Apply automatic remediation

For this case:

1️⃣ Configure AWS Config in the account

2️⃣ Use the required-tags managed rule

This rule allows you to verify if resources have the mandatory labels defined by the company.

In this case:

- Resource Type → AWS::EC2::Volume
- Tag required → backup-frequency

3️⃣ If a volume does not have the label, AWS Config marks it as:

NON_COMPLIANT

4️⃣ Configure Auto Remediation

Using AWS Systems Manager Automation Runbooks, you can:

- automatically apply the label
- set the default value → weekly

Architecture:

EBS Volume

↓

AWS Config rule (required-tags)

↓

NON_COMPLIANT

↓

SSM Automation Runbook

↓

Apply backup tag automatically

This ensures continued compliance, even if someone deletes the label after the volume is created.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/required-tags.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/required-tags.html)

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

Use EventBridge with CreateVolume event

Why it seems correct: It can detect when a volume is created.

Why it is incorrect: It only detects the creation of the volume.
If someone removes the label later, the system will not detect the nonconformity.

AWS Config allows for continuous evaluation, not just initial events.

b.

AWS Config with Resource Type EC2::Instance

Why it seems correct: EC2 instances can have EBS volumes.

Why it is incorrect: The resource that needs to be audited is the EBS Volume, not the EC2 instance.

The correct type is:

AWS::EC2::Volume

c.

Trusted Advisor + EventBridge

Why it seems correct: Trusted Advisor reviews best practices.

Why it is incorrect: Trusted Advisor does not allow automatic remediation or tag enforcement.

It only provides recommendations.

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/remediate-noncompliant-aws-config-rules-with-aws-systems-manager-automation-runbooks/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/remediate-noncompliant-aws-config-rules-with-aws-systems-manager-automation-runbooks/)

question:
A company uses multiple AWS accounts to isolate and manage business applications. This multi-account environment consists of an AWS Transit Gateway that routes all outbound traffic from one network account. A firewall appliance inspects all traffic before it is forwarded to an Internet gateway.

The firewall is configured to send logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs for all generated events.

Recently, the security team has indicated possible resource leaks. As a DevOps Engineer, you have been asked to configure an alert to the security team if the firewall generates a Critical severity event.

How should the DevOps Engineer configure this requirement?

options.A: Create a metric filter in Amazon CloudWatch filtering the logs to match the term Critical. Publish a custom metric for the finding. Use CloudWatch Lambda Insights to filter Critical events and send a notification using Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS). Subscribe the security team's email to the SNS topic.
options.B: Create a metric filter in Amazon CloudWatch filtering the logs to match the term Critical. Configure a metric stream to Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose with AWS Lambda as the destination. Process the stream with Lambda and send a notification to Amazon SNS if a critical event is detected. Subscribe the security team's email to the SNS topic.
options.C: Create a Transit Gateway Flow Log to capture all information sent by the firewall. Publish the logs to Amazon CloudWatch Logs. Create a metric filter in CloudWatch filtering the logs to match the term Critical. Publish a custom metric and configure a CloudWatch alarm to send a notification to Amazon SNS. Subscribe the security team's email to the SNS topic.
options.D: Create a metric filter in Amazon CloudWatch filtering the logs to match the term Critical in the logs. Publish a custom metric for the finding and configure a CloudWatch alarm to publish a notification to an Amazon SNS topic. Subscribe the security team's email to the SNS topic.

explanation:
The correct solution uses CloudWatch Logs Metric Filters + CloudWatch Alarms + Amazon SNS, which is the standard pattern in AWS for generating log-based alerts.

Solution flow

1️⃣ The firewall appliance sends logs to CloudWatch Logs.

2️⃣ A CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter is created that searches for the term:

Critical

in log events.

3️⃣ This filter converts detected events into a custom CloudWatch metric.

4️⃣ A CloudWatch Alarm is created on that metric.

5️⃣ When the metric exceeds the threshold (for example ≥1 event), the alarm executes an action:

➡ Post a notification to an Amazon SNS Topic

6️⃣ The security team subscribes to the SNS Topic (email, Slack, etc.).

Architecture:

Firewall Logs

↓

CloudWatch Logs

↓

Metric Filter ("Critical")

↓

Custom CloudWatch Metric

↓

CloudWatch Alarm

↓

SNS Topic

↓

Security Team Email

This approach is:

- Simple
- AWS native
- Near real-time
- No additional infrastructure

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch_architecture.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch_architecture.html)

WRONG OPTIONS

A.

Use CloudWatch Lambda Insights.

Why it seems correct: CloudWatch has integrations with Lambda.

Why it is incorrect:
Lambda Insights is for monitoring Lambda functions, not for analyzing firewall logs.

b.

Use Metric Streams + Kinesis Data Firehose + Lambda.

Why it seems correct: It allows metrics to be processed in real time.

Why it is incorrect:

- Metric Streams does not support Kinesis Data Firehose as a destination
- It is unnecessarily complex for a simple alert.

c.

Use Transit Gateway Flow Logs.

Why it seems correct: Flow Logs record network traffic.

Why it is incorrect: The requirement is to analyze firewall logs, not Transit Gateway IP traffic.
