question:
A financial services company is using a security-hardened AMI due to strict regulatory compliance requirements. The enterprise should be able to verify AMI vulnerabilities every day based on newly disclosed vulnerabilities through the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) program. Currently, all instances are launched using an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) leveraging the latest security hardened AMI.

As a DevOps Engineer, how can you implement this while minimizing cost and disruption to the application?

options.A: Create a CloudWatch event with a daily schedule. Invoke a Lambda function that will start an AWS Inspector execution directly from the AMI reference in the API call. AWS Inspector will automatically launch an instance and terminate it upon completion of the evaluation
options.B: Create a CloudWatch event with a daily schedule, with the target being a Lambda function. Tag all instances in your ASG with CheckVulnerabilities: True. The Lambda function should start an evaluation in AWS Inspector pointing to all instances that have the tag
options.C: Create a CloudWatch event with a daily schedule, with the target being a Step Function. The Step Function must launch an EC2 instance from the AMI and tag it with CheckVulnerabilities: True. The Step Function then launches an AMI evaluation template using AWS Inspector and the tag above. Terminate the instance later
options.D: Create a CloudWatch event with a daily schedule. Make the target of the rule AWS Inspector and pass some extra data into the rule using the ID of the AMI to inspect. AWS Inspector will automatically launch an instance and terminate it upon completion of the evaluation

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch event with a daily schedule, with the target being a Step Function. The Step Function must launch an EC2 instance from the AMI and tag it with CheckVulnerabilities: True. The Step Function then launches an AMI evaluation template using AWS Inspector and the tag above. Terminate the instance later

AWS Step Functions is a fully managed service that makes it easy to coordinate distributed application components and microservices using visual workflows.

A golden AMI is an AMI that contains the latest security patches, software, configuration, and software agents that you need to install for logging, security maintenance, and performance monitoring. A security best practice is to perform routine vulnerability assessments of your golden AMIs to identify whether newly found vulnerabilities apply to them. If you identify a vulnerability, you can update your golden AMIs with the appropriate security patches, test the AMIs, and deploy the patched AMIs to your environment.

You can create an EC2 instance from the golden AMI and then run an Amazon Inspector security assessment on the created instance. Amazon Inspector performs security assessments of Amazon EC2 instances using AWS-managed rules packages, such as the Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs) package.

Using CloudWatch with CodeDeploy, you can monitor metrics for Amazon EC2 instances or Auto Scaling groups managed by CodeDeploy and then invoke an action if the metric you're tracking crosses a certain threshold over a defined period. You can monitor metrics such as CPU utilization of instances. If the alarm is triggered, CloudWatch initiates actions such as sending a notification to Amazon Simple Notification Service, stopping a CodeDeploy deployment, or changing the state of an instance (for example, restart, terminate, recover). You can also automatically rollback a deployment when it fails or when a CloudWatch alarm is triggered.

For the given case, the CodeDeploy deployment must be associated with a CloudWatch Alarm for automatic rollbacks.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/monitoring-create-alarms.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/monitoring-create-alarms.html)

A deployment configuration is a set of rules and success and failure conditions that CodeDeploy uses during a deployment. When you deploy to an AWS Lambda compute platform, your deployment settings specify how traffic is switched to new versions of the Lambda function in your application.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html)

For canary deployments, traffic is changed in two increments. You can choose from predefined canary options that specify the percentage of traffic sent to the updated version of your Lambda function in the first increment and the interval, in minutes, before the rest of the traffic is switched in the second increment.

A canary deployment of LambdaCanary10Percent10Minutes means that traffic is 10% to the new function for 10 minutes, and then all traffic is switched to the new version after the time has elapsed.

question:
The engineering team at a multinational retail company is deploying their core web application to an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) using CodeDeploy. The team has chosen a rolling update strategy so that instances are updated in small batches within the ASG. At the end of the deployment, the ASG has five instances running. It looks like three instances are running the new version of the app, while the other two are running the old version. CodeDeploy is reporting a successful deployment.

As a DevOps Engineer, what is the most likely reason you would attribute to this problem?

options.A: A CloudWatch alarm was triggered during deployment
options.B: Auto scaling group launch settings have not been updated
options.C: Two new instances were created during deployment due to an Auto Scaling scale out event
options.D: Two instances have an IAM permissions issue and cannot download the new code review from S3

explanation:
Correct option:

Two new instances were created during deployment due to an Auto Scaling scale out event

If an Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling scale-up event occurs while a deployment is in progress, new instances will be updated with the revision of the application that was most recently deployed, not the revision of the application that is currently being deployed. If the deployment is successful, the old instances and the new instances created during scaling will be running different versions of the application.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/integrations-aws-auto-scaling.html#integrations-aws-auto-scaling-behaviors](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/integrations-aws-auto-scaling.html#integrations-aws-auto-scaling-behaviors)

To resolve this issue after it occurs, you can redeploy the new application revision to the affected deployment groups.

To avoid this issue, AWS recommends suspending Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling scale-up processes while deployments are in progress (only the CodeDeployDefault.OneAtATime deployment configuration supports this functionality). You can do this through a setting in the common_functions.sh script that is used for load balancing with CodeDeploy. If HANDLE_PROCS=true, the following Auto Scaling events are automatically suspended during the deployment process:

AZRebalance

AlarmNotification

ScheduledActions

ReplaceUnhealthy

Incorrect options:

Two instances have an IAM permissions issue and cannot download the new code revision from S3 - An IAM permissions issue would cause the overall deployment status to be failed, but CodeDeploy reports the status as successful. This option is just a distraction.

The auto scaling group launch settings have not been updated - The launch settings would affect all instances the same and not just 2 instances. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

A CloudWatch alarm has been triggered during deployment - This is another distracting option. A CloudWatch alarm does not affect the version of the application deployed to the instances.

Reference:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/integrations-aws-auto-scaling.html#integrations-aws-auto-scaling-behaviors](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/integrations-aws-auto-scaling.html#integrations-aws-auto-scaling-behaviors)

question:
The DevOps team at a financial services company is deploying the core application in highly available mode using Elastic Beanstalk, which has created an ASG and an ALB. The team has also specified a .ebextensions file to create an associated DynamoDB table. As a DevOps Engineer on the team, you want to perform an application update but need to ensure that the DNS name does not change and that no new resources are created. The application must remain available during the update.

Which of the following options would you suggest to meet the given requirements?

options.A: Use a rolling update with 20% at a time
options.B: Use immutable
options.C: Use a blue/green deployment and swap CNAMEs
options.D: Use in-place

explanation:
Correct option:

Use a rolling update with 20% at a time

AWS Elastic Beanstalk provides several options for how deployments are processed, including deployment policies (All at once, Rolling, Rolling with additional batch, Immutable, and Traffic splitting) and options that allow you to configure batch size and health check behavior during deployments. By default, your environment uses all-at-once deployments. If you created the environment with the EB CLI and it is a scalable environment (you did not specify the --single option), use rolling deployments.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.deploy-existing-version.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.deploy-existing-version.html)

Deployment method properties comparison: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.deploy-existing-version.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.deploy-existing-version.html)

With rolling deployments, Elastic Beanstalk divides the EC2 instances in the environment into batches (for this case, we use a batch of 20% of the instances) and deploys the new version of the application one batch at a time. Leave the rest of the instances running the previous version of the application. During a rolling deployment, some instances serve requests with the old version, while instances in completed batches serve requests with the new version. Therefore, for this case, we must use a rolling update, which will maintain the ASG,instances and allow the application to continue serving traffic.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.rolling-version-deploy.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/using-features.rolling-version-deploy.html)

Incorrect options:

Use a blue/green deployment and swap CNAMEs - In a blue/green deployment, you deploy the new version to a separate environment and then swap the CNAMEs of both environments to redirect traffic to the new version instantly. A blue/green deployment would create a new load balancer and a new ASG, so it does not meet the requirements of the case.

Use immutable - Immutable deployments launch a complete set of new instances running the new version of the application in a separate Auto Scaling group, alongside the instances with the old version. Therefore, this option does not meet the requirements.

Use in-place - Although it does not create new resources, the application would become unavailable since all instances are updated at the same time.

question:
A healthcare technology company provides a Software as a Service (SaaS) solution to hospitals across the United States to use the company's proprietary system to integrate their clinical documentation and coding workflows. The company's DevOps team wants to enable a CI/CD pipeline that allows secure deployments to production and the ability to work on new functionalities in the product roadmap.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer, what solution would you recommend for the given use case?

options.A: Create a CodeCommit repository and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new feature that is implemented, create a new branch and create pull requests to merge to master. Set an IAM policy in the developer group to prevent direct pushes to master
options.B: Create a CodeCommit repository and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new feature that is implemented, create a new branch and create pull requests to merge to master. Set a repository access policy to prevent direct pushes to master
options.C: Create the master repository in CodeCommit and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new functionality that is implemented, create a new CodeCommit repository and create pull requests to merge to the main repository. Set an IAM policy in the developer group to prevent direct pushes to the main repository
options.D: Create a CodeCommit repository and create a branch for each feature. Create a CI/CD pipeline for each branch, and the last step of the pipeline should be to merge to master. Set an IAM policy in the developer group to prevent direct pushes to master

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CodeCommit repository and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new feature that is implemented, create a new branch and create pull requests to merge to master. Set an IAM policy in the developer group to prevent direct pushes to master

CodeCommit is a secure, highly scalable, and managed source control service that makes code collaboration easy. A CI/CD pipeline helps you automate steps in the software delivery process, such as initiating automatic builds and then deploying to Amazon EC2 instances. You can use AWS CodePipeline, a service that builds, tests, and deploys your code whenever there is a code change, based on the release models you define to orchestrate each step of the process.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/projects/set-up-ci-cd-pipeline/](https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/projects/set-up-ci-cd-pipeline/)

It is a best practice to work with branches in your git repository to build functionality, as that is the expected use of branches. You should not create separate repositories for each functionality. To protect the master branch you need to set a Deny policy in the IAM group to which the developers belong.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html)

Incorrect options:

Create the master repository in CodeCommit and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new functionality that is implemented, create a new CodeCommit repository and create pull requests to merge to the main repository. Set an IAM policy in the developer group to prevent direct pushes to the main repository - You should not create a separate repository for each feature, so this option is incorrect.

Create a CodeCommit repository and configure the CI/CD pipeline to deploy the master branch. For each new feature that is implemented, create a new branch and create pull requests to merge to master. Set a repository access policy to prevent direct pushes to master - This option is a distraction since there is no such thing as a repository access policy.

Create a CodeCommit repository and create a branch for each feature. Create a CI/CD pipeline for each branch, and the last step of the pipeline should be to merge to master. question:
An Internet of Things (IoT) solutions company has decided to publish each application as a Docker container and use classic ECS (on EC2) as the container orchestration system and ECR as the Docker registry. Part of implementing a monitoring pipeline is ensuring that all application logs can be stored in CloudWatch Logs.

The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to provide the simplest possible instructions to achieve this goal. What are these instructions?

options.A: Create ECS task definitions that include the awslogs driver. Set an IAM task role on the task definition with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs
options.B: Create ECS task definitions for your applications, with a mapping from the /var/log directory to the local file system of the EC2 instance. Install the CloudWatch Agent on the EC2 instance using user-data and monitor the /var/log/containers directory. Create an EC2 instance role with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs
options.C: Create ECS task definitions that include the awslogs driver. Set an IAM instance role on the EC2 instance with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs
options.D: Create ECS task definitions for your applications, with a sidecar container containing the CloudWatch Agent monitoring the /var/log/containers directory. Map the application's /var/log directory to the sidecar file system. Set an IAM task role on the task definition with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs

explanation:
Correct option:

Create ECS task definitions that include the awslogs driver. Set an IAM instance role on the EC2 instance with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs

Several solutions can work here, but the simplest possible is sought. The important thing to remember is that ECS task definitions can include the awslogs driver and write to CloudWatch Logs natively. However, the EC2 instance is the one that actually writes to CloudWatch, so you must have an IAM Instance Role with the appropriate permissions to write to CloudWatch. Your ECS container instances also require logs:CreateLogStream and logs:PutLogEvents permissions on the IAM role with which you launch the instances.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/using_awslogs.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/using_awslogs.html)

Incorrect options:

Create ECS task definitions that include the awslogs driver. Set an IAM task role in the task definition with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs - As mentioned above, permissions must be granted to the IAM Instance Role and not the IAM task role to write to CloudWatch logs.

Create ECS task definitions for your applications, with a mapping from the /var/log directory to the local file system of the EC2 instance. Install the CloudWatch Agent on the EC2 instance using user-data and monitor the /var/log/containers directory. Create an EC2 instance role with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs - This is a more complex and indirect approach to sending container logs to CloudWatch Logs, so it is not the best option for this case.

Create ECS task definitions for your applications, with a sidecar container containing the CloudWatch Agent monitoring the /var/log/containers directory. Map the application's /var/log directory to the sidecar file system. Set an IAM task role in the task definition with the necessary permissions to write to CloudWatch logs - Using sidecars is a valid pattern, but in this case it is a more complex solution than necessary. Additionally, permissions must be assigned to the IAM Instance Role, not the task role.

question:
A graphic design company is experimenting with new functionality for an API and the goal is to pass the "color" field in the JSON payload to enable this functionality. The new Lambda function should treat "color": "none" as a request from an old client. The company wants to handle only one Lambda function in the backend while supporting both old and new clients. The API Gateway API is currently deployed at stage v1. Clients include Android applications that may take time to update. The technical requirements indicate that the solution must support legacy clients for years.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional, which of the following options would you recommend as the best for this case?

options.A: Enable API Gateway v1 caching and remove the Lambda v1 function. Deploy an API Gateway v2 backed by a new Lambda v2 function. Add a stage variable in API Gateway to enable the default "color": "none"
options.B: Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it. Use API Gateway mapping docs to add a default "color": "none" value to the JSON of the request passed in the API Gateway stage
options.C: Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it as a separate v2 function. Create a new API Gateway stage and deploy it as v2. API Gateway stage v1 points to Lambda function v1 and stage v2 points to Lambda function v2. Implement redirection from Lambda v1 to Lambda v2 when the request does not have the "color" field
options.D: Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it. Create a new API Gateway stage and deploy it as v2. They both use the same Lambda function as a backend for the v1 and v2 stages. Add a static mapping on route v1 to add "color": "none" in requests

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it. Create a new API Gateway stage and deploy it as v2. They both use the same Lambda function as a backend for the v1 and v2 stages. Add a static mapping on route v1 to add "color": "none" in requests

Amazon API Gateway is an AWS service for creating, publishing, maintaining, monitoring, and securing REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale. API Gateway handles tasks such as traffic management, authorization and access control, API monitoring and versioning. It acts as the gateway for applications to access data, business logic, or functionality from backend services such as EC2, AWS Lambda, or other web services.

For this case, API Gateway mapping templates must be used. API Gateway allows you to use mapping templates to transform the payload from the method request to the corresponding integration request, as well as the response. In this scenario, an API v2 must be deployed alongside the API v1 using the same Lambda function. Older clients will consume v1, where the template mapping will add the "color": "none" field. New clients will consume v2 by sending the field explicitly.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-override-request-response-parameters.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/apigateway-override-request-response-parameters.html)

Incorrect options:

Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it as a separate v2 function. Create a new API Gateway stage and deploy it as v2. Stage v1 points to Lambda v1 and stage v2 to Lambda v2. Implement redirection from Lambda v1 to Lambda v2 when the request does not have the "color" field - This would involve maintaining two Lambda functions, which goes against the requirement of having a single function.

Create a new version of the Lambda function and release it. Use API Gateway mapping docs to add a default value "color": "none" to the request JSON - Mapping templates do not support setting dynamic defaults, only static values ​​in the correct context.

Enable API Gateway v1 caching and remove the Lambda v1 function. Deploy an API Gateway v2 backed by a new Lambda v2 function. Add a stage variable in API Gateway to enable the default "color": "none" - Caching does not solve this case and is a distraction.

question:
A retail company is storing users' information along with their purchase history in a DynamoDB table and has also enabled DynamoDB Streams. Three use cases have been implemented for this table: a Lambda function reads the stream to send emails for new user subscriptions, another Lambda function sends an email after a user makes their first purchase, and finally a third Lambda function gives users discounts every 10 purchases. When there is a high volume of data in the DynamoDB table, the Lambda functions are experiencing throttling issues. You plan to add future Lambda functions to read from that stream, so you need to update the existing solution.

As a DevOps Engineer, which of the following options would you recommend?

options.A: Create a new Lambda function that reads from the stream and passes the payload to SNS. Make the other three and future Lambda functions read directly from the SNS topic
options.B: Increase the RCUs in your DynamoDB table to avoid throttling problems
options.C: Increase the memory of the Lambda function so that they have more vCPU allocation and process data faster by making fewer requests to DynamoDB
options.D: Create a DynamoDB DAX cluster to cache reads

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a new Lambda function that reads from the stream and passes the payload to SNS. Make the other three and future Lambda functions read directly from the SNS topic

DynamoDB Streams captures a time-ordered sequence of item-level modifications to a DynamoDB table and stores this information in a log for up to 24 hours. Applications can access this log and see the items as they were before and after being modified, almost in real time. A DynamoDB stream is an ordered flow of information about changes to items in a table.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html)

DynamoDB is integrated with AWS Lambda so you can create triggers that automatically react to events in DynamoDB Streams. When you enable a stream on a table, you can associate the stream's ARN with a Lambda function. AWS Lambda polls the stream and invokes your function when it detects new records.

No more than two processes should read from the same stream shard at the same time. Having more than two readers per shard can cause throttling. Therefore, you need to use a fan-out pattern, with SNS being a suitable option to distribute events to multiple consumers.

Incorrect options:

Increase the RCUs in your DynamoDB table to avoid throttling problems - DynamoDB Streams work asynchronously, so the RCUs do not affect the throttling problem in the stream.

Create a DynamoDB DAX cluster to cache reads - DAX enhances reads over the table, not the stream.

Increase the memory of the Lambda function so that they have a larger vCPU and process faster - The problem is not processing, but rather too many consumers reading from the same shard.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.Lambda.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/Streams.Lambda.html)

question:
A Silicon Valley-based startup runs a news discovery web application and uses CodeDeploy to deploy the application to a set of 20 EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer. The ALB is integrated with CodeDeploy. The DevOps team wants the rollout to be gradual and to automatically rollback in case of unusually high peak CPU utilization on EC2 instances while traffic is being served.

How can you implement this?

options.A: In the ValidateService hook in appspec.yml, measure CPU utilization for 5 minutes. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures. If the hook fails, CodeDeploy will rollback
options.B: Create a CloudWatch metric for the maximum CPU utilization of your EC2 instances. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch metrics
options.C: Create a CloudWatch metric for the maximum CPU utilization of your EC2 instances. Create a CloudWatch alarm on that metric. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch alarm
options.D: Create a CloudWatch metric for the maximum CPU utilization of your Application Load Balancer. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch metrics

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch metric for the maximum CPU utilization of your EC2 instances. Create a CloudWatch alarm on that metric. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch alarm

You can automatically monitor and react to changes in your AWS CodeDeploy deployments using Amazon CloudWatch alarms. With CloudWatch, you can monitor metrics for EC2 instances or Auto Scaling groups managed by CodeDeploy and take action if a metric exceeds a threshold over a defined period. For example, you can monitor CPU utilization. If the alarm is triggered, CloudWatch can stop deployment, send notifications, or change the state of instances. You can also configure automatic rollback when an alarm is activated.

CodeDeploy will redeploy the last known stable version when the rollback occurs.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/monitoring-create-alarms.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/monitoring-create-alarms.html)

Configure advanced options for a deployment group: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-groups-configure-advanced-options.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-groups-configure-advanced-options.html)

Incorrect options:

In the ValidateService hook in appspec.yml, measure CPU utilization for 5 minutes. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on failures - When using ValidateService with ALB, the traffic is not fully flowing yet, so you would not see any real CPU load.

Create a CloudWatch metric for the maximum CPU utilization of your EC2 instances. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch metrics - CodeDeploy only supports automatic rollback via alarms, not metrics directly.

Create a CloudWatch metric for the Application Load Balancer's maximum CPU utilization. Create a deployment in CodeDeploy with rollback enabled, integrated with CloudWatch metrics - You should monitor EC2 CPUs, not ALB, and again, alarms are required, not metrics.

References:

question:
As a DevOps Engineer at a data analytics company, you are deploying a web application on EC2 using an Auto Scaling Group. The data is stored in RDS MySQL Multi-AZ, and there is a caching layer using ElastiCache. Setting up the app takes time and currently needs more than 20 minutes to start. 10 of those minutes are spent installing and configuring the web application, and another 10 minutes warming up the instance's local cache.

What can be done to improve the performance of this setup?

options.A: Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script
options.B: Migrate from ElastiCache to DynamoDB. Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script
options.C: Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script. Use AWS Lambda to configure the instance's local cache at startup
options.D: Create an AMI that contains the web application and a copy of the local data cache. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script

A golden AMI is a standardized AMI with consistent configuration, security patches, and hardening. It may also contain approved agents for logging, security, and monitoring. In this case, you can include the web application within the AMI to avoid the installation and configuration time at each boot.

Once you create a golden AMI for a product (for example, an OS base AMI or an application-specific AMI), you can validate and approve it for deployment in different environments.

About the golden AMI pipeline: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/awsmarketplace/announcing-the-golden-ami-pipeline/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/awsmarketplace/announcing-the-golden-ami-pipeline/)

Incorrect options:

Create an AMI that contains the web application and a copy of the local data cache. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script - The local cache is dynamic and changes over time, so it is not feasible to include it in the AMI.

Migrate from ElastiCache to DynamoDB. Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script - DynamoDB is not a direct replacement for ElastiCache for this case, as it is not an equivalent caching solution.

Create an AMI that contains the web application. Configure the dynamic part at runtime using an EC2 User Data script. Use AWS Lambda to configure the instance's local cache at boot - It is not possible to use Lambda to configure an instance's local cache at boot that way, and the cache is still dynamic.

Reference:

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/awsmarketplace/announcing-the-golden-ami-pipeline/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/awsmarketplace/announcing-the-golden-ami-pipeline/)

question:
The technology team at a leading bank is using software with a license rate that is billed based on the number of CPU sockets being used. The team wants to ensure they are using the most appropriate EC2 release mode and create a compliance dashboard that highlights any violations of this decision. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

Which of the following solutions would you recommend as the best option?

options.A: Launch the EC2 instances on Dedicated Hosts and create a tag for the application. Implement a custom AWS Config rule backed by a Lambda function that checks the application tag and ensures that the instance is launched in the correct mode
options.B: Launch the EC2 instances in Reserved Instances and create a tag for the application. Implement an AWS Service Catalog rule backed by a Lambda function to track that the application is always launched on an EC2 instance with the correct mode
options.C: Launch the EC2 instances in Reserved Instances and create a tag for the application. Implement a custom AWS Config rule backed by a Lambda function that checks the application tag and ensures that the instance is launched in the correct mode
options.D: Launch the EC2 instances on Dedicated Hosts and create a tag for the application. Implement an AWS Service Catalog rule backed by a Lambda function to track that the application is always launched on an EC2 instance with the correct mode

explanation:

Launch the EC2 instances on Dedicated Hosts and create a tag for the application. Implement a custom AWS Config rule backed by a Lambda function that checks the application tag and ensures that the instance is launched in the correct mode

An Amazon EC2 Dedicated Host is a physical server with EC2 instance capacity completely dedicated for your use. When you use your own licenses on Dedicated Hosts, you can properly manage CPU socket-based licensing.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/dedicated-hosts/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/dedicated-hosts/faqs/)

To access CPU sockets for licensing purposes, you need to use Dedicated Hosts. Reserved Instances are primarily for cost optimization, not for socket license control.

AWS Config provides detailed visibility into your account resources, including their configuration, relationships, and changes over time. An AWS Config rule defines desired configurations and can mark resources as non-compliant if they do not comply with those rules. You can support these rules with Lambda for custom logic and generate compliance dashboards.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/how-does-config-work.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/how-does-config-work.html)

Launching EC2 instances on Dedicated Hosts and using AWS Service Catalog - Service Catalog is not the right tool for continuous compliance monitoring.

Launch EC2 instances in Reserved Instances - Does not allow controlling licensing by CPU sockets.

Combine Reserved Instances with Service Catalog - Wrong for both reasons above.

question:
The DevOps team at an auditing firm has deployed its main application on Elastic Beanstalk that processes invoices uploaded by clients in CSV format. Invoices can be quite large, with up to 10MB and 1,000,000 records in total. The processing is CPU intensive which is slowing down the application. Clients are sent an email when processing is complete, using a cron job. The auditing firm has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

What do you recommend for the application to ensure good performance and meet scalability requirements?

options.A: Create a separate Beanstalk environment that is a worker environment and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are uploaded to S3 and a reference to them is sent to SQS by the web tier. The worker tier processes these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file will send the emails
options.B: Create a separate Beanstalk tier within the same environment that is a worker configuration and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are sent directly to SQS after being compressed by the web tier. The workers process these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file in the web tier will send the emails
options.C: Create a separate Beanstalk environment that is a worker environment and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are uploaded to S3 and a reference to them is sent to SQS by the web tier. The worker tier processes these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file in the web tier will send the emails
options.D: Create a separate Beanstalk tier within the same environment that is a worker configuration and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are sent directly to SQS after being compressed by the web tier. The workers process these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file will send the emails

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a separate Beanstalk environment that is a worker environment and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are uploaded to S3 and a reference to them is sent to SQS by the web tier. The worker tier processes these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file will send the emails

With Elastic Beanstalk, you can quickly deploy and manage applications in the AWS cloud without having to learn about the infrastructure that runs them. You simply upload your application, and Elastic Beanstalk automatically handles details like capacity provisioning, load balancing, scaling, and application health monitoring.

AWS Elastic Beanstalk allows you to manage all the resources that run your application as environments. An environment is a collection of AWS resources that run an application version. When you launch an Elastic Beanstalk environment, you need to choose an environment tier. An application that serves HTTP requests runs in a web server environment tier. A backend environment that fetches tasks from an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue runs in a worker environment tier.

Elastic Beanstalk Concepts: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts.html)

When you create a web server environment, Beanstalk provisions the resources required to run your application. AWS resources created for this type of environment include an elastic load balancer, an Auto Scaling group, and one or more Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts-webserver.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts-webserver.html)

AWS resources created for a worker environment tier include an ASG, one or more Amazon EC2 instances, and an IAM role. For the worker environment tier, Beanstalk also creates and provisions an SQS queue if you don't already have one. When you launch a worker environment, Beanstalk installs the necessary support files for the programming language of your choice and a daemon on each EC2 instance of the ASG. The daemon reads messages from an SQS queue. The daemon sends the data of each message it reads to the web application running in the worker environment for processing.

For the given case, the worker tier is used to asynchronously process invoices from an SQS queue. The SQS size limit is 256KB and therefore files must be uploaded to S3 and a reference to them must be sent to SQS by the web tier. Finally, the cron.yml file must be defined in the worker tier. Using this strategy we have decoupled the render tier from the web tier, and CPU usage will decrease as a result. The worker tier will also be able to easily scale in case many invoices are uploaded.

Elastic Beanstalk Worker environment: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts-worker.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/concepts-worker.html)

Incorrect options:Create a separate Beanstalk tier within the same environment that is a worker configuration and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are sent directly to SQS after being compressed by the web tier. The workers process these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file will send the emails - As mentioned before, the worker tier must be a separate environment from the web tier, so this option is incorrect.

Create a separate Beanstalk environment that is a worker environment and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are uploaded to S3 and a reference to them is sent to SQS by the web tier. The worker tier processes these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file in the web tier will send the emails - The cron.yml file must be defined in the worker tier, it is not supported by the web tier, so this option is incorrect.

Create a separate Beanstalk tier within the same environment that is a worker configuration and processes invoices through an SQS queue. Invoices are sent directly to SQS after being compressed by the web tier. The workers process these files. A cron job defined using the cron.yml file in the web tier will send the emails - The worker tier must be a separate environment from the web tier, so this option is incorrect.

question:
The DevOps team at a geohazard monitoring agency maintains an app that provides near real-time notifications to Android and iOS devices during earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and tsunamis. The team has created a CodePipeline pipeline, consisting of CodeCommit and CodeBuild, and the application is deployed on Elastic Beanstalk. The team wants to enable Blue/Green deployments for Beanstalk through CodePipeline.

As a DevOps Engineer, how would you implement a solution for this requirement?

options.A: Have CodePipeline deploy to a new Beanstalk environment. After that stage action, create another stage action to invoke a Custom Job using AWS Lambda, which will make the API call to swap the CNAME of the environments
options.B: Have CodePipeline deploy to the current Beanstalk environment using a rolling with additional batch strategy. Add a CodeDeploy action afterwards to enable Blue/Green
options.C: Have CodePipeline deploy to a new Beanstalk environment. After that stage action, create another stage action to invoke a CloudFormation template that will perform the CNAME swap
options.D: Have CodePipeline deploy to the current Beanstalk environment using an immutable strategy. Add a CodeStar action afterwards to enable Blue/Green configured via template.yml

explanation:
Correct option:

Have CodePipeline deploy to a new Beanstalk environment. After that stage action, create another stage action to invoke a Custom Job using AWS Lambda, which will make the API call to swap the CNAME of the environments

Elastic Beanstalk allows you to quickly deploy and manage applications on AWS. For Blue/Green deployments in Beanstalk, two identical environments are required: one (blue) in production and another (green) as a temporary environment for deployment.

The CI/CD pipeline creates a clone (green) environment, deploys the new version there and then performs a CNAME exchange to redirect traffic to the new environment. Once validated, the old environment can be deleted.

To automate the CNAME swap within CodePipeline, a custom action is required, typically using a Lambda function that invokes the corresponding API, since CloudFormation does not directly support this operation.

Incorrect options:

Deploy to current environment with rolling or immutable - Does not comply with Blue/Green, as a separate environment is not used.

Use CodeDeploy or CodeStar to enable Blue/Green in Beanstalk - Not applicable in this context; CodeStar is not a pipeline action and CodeDeploy does not handle Blue/Green in Beanstalk that way.

Use CloudFormation for CNAME swap - Not possible, as CloudFormation does not support that operation directly.

[https://aws-quickstart.s3.amazonaws.com/quickstart-codepipeline-bluegreen-deployment/doc/blue-green-deployments-to-aws-elastic-beanstalk-on-the-aws-cloud.pdf] (https://aws-quickstart.s3.amazonaws.com/quickstart-codepipeline-bluegreen-deployment/doc/blue-green-deployments-to-aws-elastic-beanstalk-on-the-aws-cloud.pdf)

question:
The DevOps team at a yoga-inspired clothing company wants to set up development environments to test new features. The team wants to be notified when a CodePipeline pipeline fails and sent to the company's #devops Slack channel. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this case.

Which of the following options would you suggest? (Select two)

options.A: The target of the rule must be a Lambda function that invokes a third-party Slack webhook
options.B: The objective of the rule should be a “Slack send”. Provide channel name and webhook URL
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event rule with the source corresponding to { "source": [ "aws.codepipeline" ], "detail-type": [ "CodePipeline Pipeline Execution State Change" ], "detail": { "state": [ "FAILED" ] } }
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule with the source corresponding to { "source": [ "aws.codepipeline" ], "detail-type": [ "CodePipeline Action Execution State Change" ], "detail": { "state": [ "FAILED" ] } }
options.E: Create a CloudWatch Event rule with the source corresponding to { "source": [ "aws.codepipeline" ], "detail-type": [ "CodePipeline Stage Execution State Change" ], "detail": { "state": [ "FAILED" ] } }

explanation:
Correct options:

The target of the rule must be a Lambda function that invokes a third-party Slack webhook

CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) rules do not support sending directly to Slack as a destination. Therefore, you need a Lambda function that consumes the event and calls the Slack webhook.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule with the source corresponding to

{

"source": [

"aws.codepipeline"

],

"detail-type": [

"CodePipeline Pipeline Execution State Change"

],

"detail": {

"state": [

"FAILED"

]

}

}

AWS CodePipeline emits state events that can be captured by CloudWatch Events/EventBridge. To detect failures of the entire pipeline, you must use the event type **Pipeline Execution State Change** and filter by FAILED state.

Incorrect options:

The target of the rule must be a “Slack send” - There is no native support for Slack as a target in CloudWatch Events.

CodePipeline Action Execution State Change - This detects failures at the action level, not the entire pipeline.

CodePipeline Stage Execution State Change - This detects failures at the stage level, not the entire pipeline.

[https://aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/faqs/)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/detect-state-changes-cloudwatch-events.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/detect-state-changes-cloudwatch-events.html)

question:
As part of your CodePipeline, you are running multiple test suites. Two are packaged as Docker containers and run directly in CodeBuild, while another runs as a Lambda function executing Python code. All test suites are based on HTTP requests and are determined to be network dependent, not CPU dependent. Currently, CodePipeline takes a long time to execute as these actions occur one after another. The company plans to add more tests. The entire pipeline is managed by CloudFormation.

As a DevOps Engineer, which of the following options would you recommend to improve the completion time of your pipeline?

options.A: Migrate all test suites to Jenkins and use the ECS plugin
options.B: Enable CloudFormation StackSets to run actions in parallel
options.C: Change the runOrder of your actions so that they have the same value
options.D: Increase the number of vCPUs assigned to CodeBuild builds and the RAM assigned to your Lambda function

explanation:
Correct option:

Change the runOrder of your actions so that they have the same value

AWS CodePipeline allows you to define actions within stages and control their execution using the runOrder parameter. If multiple actions have the same runOrder value, they are executed in parallel within the same stage.

Since the tests are network-bound (not CPU-bound), the problem is not compute capacity but sequential execution. Running them in parallel significantly reduces the total pipeline time.

Incorrect options:

Increase vCPU or memory - Does not significantly improve performance because the bottleneck is the network, not the compute.

CloudFormation StackSets - Not used to parallelize actions within CodePipeline.

Migrate to Jenkins - Does not solve sequential execution problem.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/reference-pipeline-structure.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/reference-pipeline-structure.html)

question:
A global financial services company manages over 100 accounts using AWS Organizations, and several accounts and regions were recently found to not have AWS CloudTrail enabled. You also want to be able to track compliance with CloudTrail enablement using a dashboard and be automatically alerted in case of problems. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

How would you implement a solution for this case?

options.A: Create a CloudFormation template to enable CloudTrail. Create a StackSet and deploy it to all accounts and regions under the AWS organization. Create another CloudFormation StackSet to enable AWS Config and create a Config rule to track whether CloudTrail is enabled. Create an AWS Config aggregator for a centralized account to track compliance. Create a CloudWatch Event to generate events when compliance is breached and subscribe to a Lambda function that will send notifications
options.B: Create a CloudFormation template to enable CloudTrail. Create a StackSet and deploy it to all accounts and regions under the AWS organization. Create another StackSet to enable AWS Config and create a Config rule to track whether CloudTrail is enabled. Create an AWS Config aggregator for a centralized account to track compliance. Create an SQS topic for notifications and subscribe a Lambda function
options.C: Create a CloudFormation template to enable CloudTrail. Create a StackSet and deploy it to all accounts and regions under the AWS organization. Create a CloudFormation template in a centralized account to enable AWS Config and create a Config rule. Create an AWS Config aggregator. Create an SNS topic for notifications
options.D: Create a CloudFormation template to enable CloudTrail. Create a StackSet and deploy it to all accounts and regions under the AWS organization. Create a CloudFormation template in a centralized account to enable AWS Config and create a Config rule. Create an AWS Config aggregator. Create a CloudWatch Event for notifications

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudFormation template to enable CloudTrail. Create a StackSet and deploy it to all accounts and regions under the AWS organization. Create another CloudFormation StackSet to enable AWS Config and create a Config rule to track whether CloudTrail is enabled. Create an AWS Config aggregator for a centralized account to track compliance. Create a CloudWatch Event to generate events when compliance is breached and subscribe to a Lambda function that will send notifications

To solve the problem you need three key things:

1. Enable CloudTrail on all accounts and regions → StackSets
2. Monitor compliance → AWS Config + rule + aggregator
3. Automatically alert → EventBridge (CloudWatch Events) + Lambda

StackSets allows configurations to be deployed to multiple accounts/regions.

AWS Config allows you to evaluate compliance and the aggregator centralizes the view.

CloudWatch Events/EventBridge allows you to react to compliance changes.

Incorrect options:

Using SQS topic → does not exist (SQS uses queues, not topics)

Enable AWS Config only on central account → incorrect, must be on all accounts

Using SNS without proper integration with Config events → incomplete for compliance-based automation

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/what-is-cfnstacksets.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/what-is-cfnstacksets.html)

question:
As a Lead DevOps Engineer at a retail company, you have a Spring Boot web application running in an Auto Scaling group and behind an Application Load Balancer. You must collect the logs before an instance is terminated so you can analyze them later. It is also necessary to collect the access logs. Analysis of these logs should be done at the lowest possible cost and only needs to be run occasionally.

Which of the following options would you suggest to implement the MOST cost-effective solution for this requirement? (Select three)

options.A: Analyze logs using an EMR cluster
options.B: Analyze logs using AWS Athena
options.C: Enable Access Logs at the Target Group level
options.D: Enable Access Logs at the Application Load Balancer level
options.E: Create a Lifecycle Hook in the Auto Scaling Group for the termination action. Create a CloudWatch Event rule for that hook and invoke a Lambda function. The Lambda function must use an SSM Run Command to extract the application logs and store them in S3
options.F: Create a Lifecycle Hook in the Auto Scaling Group for the termination action. Create a CloudWatch Event rule for that hook and invoke a Lambda function. The Lambda function must use an SSM Run Command to install the CloudWatch Logs Agent and send the logs to S3

explanation:
Correct options:

Analyze logs using AWS Athena

Athena allows you to query data directly in S3 using SQL, without infrastructure. It is serverless and very economical for occasional analysis.

Enable Access Logs at the Application Load Balancer level

Access logs are enabled in the ALB, not in the target group, and are stored in S3 for later analysis.

Create a Lifecycle Hook in the Auto Scaling Group for the termination action…

Lifecycle hooks allow you to pause the termination of instances to execute custom actions. Here it is used to extract logs before the instance disappears, using SSM and saving them to S3.

Incorrect options:

EMR - Expensive and non-serverless, not suitable for occasional analysis.

Access logs in Target Group - This configuration does not exist, only in the ALB.

Install CloudWatch Logs Agent on termination - This agent is for continuous streaming, not for spot extraction before termination.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html)

question:
The DevOps team at an analytics company is deploying an Apache Kafka cluster that contains 6 instances and is distributed across 3 Availability Zones (AZs). Apache Kafka is a stateful application and needs to store its data on EBS volumes. Therefore, each instance must have self-healing capability and always attach the correct EBS volume.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional, which of the following solutions would you suggest for this requirement?

options.A: Create 6 EC2 instances using CloudFormation with EBS volumes. Define the attachments in the template. If the EC2 instance is terminated, it will be automatically recreated by CloudFormation with the correct EBS
options.B: Create 6 EC2 instances using CloudFormation with EBS volumes. Define the attachments in the template. If the EC2 instance is terminated, run a drift detection in CloudFormation and then do remediation
options.C: Create an Auto Scaling Group in CloudFormation with min/max/desired capacity of 6 instances distributed across 3 AZs, and 6 EBS volumes. Use user data to have instances grab any available volumes in your AZ
options.D: Create a CloudFormation template with a min/max capacity ASG of 1 and an EBS volume. Label the ASG and EBS volume. Create a User Data script that attaches the correct EBS volume on boot. Use a CloudFormation master template and reference this nested template 6 times

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudFormation template with a min/max capacity ASG of 1 and an EBS volume. Label the ASG and EBS volume. Create a User Data script that attaches the correct EBS volume on boot. Use a CloudFormation master template and reference this nested template 6 times

The key to the problem is that Kafka is stateful and each node must maintain its specific volume. Self-healing is also required.

The correct solution is to detach each node into its own size 1 ASG (one per broker), ensuring that if the instance dies, the ASG recreates it in the same AZ and the boot script reattaches the correct EBS volume (identified by tags).

CloudFormation nested stacks are used to repeat this pattern 6 times.

Incorrect options:

Simple EC2 instances with CloudFormation - Do not have automatic self-healing.

Drift detection - Only detects changes, does not automatically correct them.

ASG of 6 instances sharing volumes - Risk of misalignment between instances and volumes, especially on AZ failures.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/quickref-autoscaling.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/quickref-autoscaling.html)

question:
Your company has adopted CodeCommit and forces developers to create new branches and pull requests before merging to master. The development team reviews the pull requests and wants the CI/CD system to automatically build the Pull Request to provide a testing badge with pass/fail status.

How can you implement Pull Request validation using CodeBuild efficiently?

options.A: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that reacts to the creation and updates of Pull Requests in the repository. The target must be a Lambda function that invokes CodeBuild and waits for the result to update the Pull Request
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that reacts to the creation and updates of Pull Requests in the repository. The target must be CodeBuild. Create a second CloudWatch Event rule to detect success or failure of the build and as a target invoke a Lambda that updates the Pull Request with the result
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event rule scheduled every 5 minutes that invokes Lambda to review Pull Requests and run CodeBuild. Then another rule to update the result
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule scheduled every 5 minutes that invokes Lambda, runs CodeBuild, and waits for the result to update the Pull Request

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that reacts to the creation and updates of Pull Requests in the repository. The target must be CodeBuild. Create a second CloudWatch Event rule to detect success or failure of the build and as a target invoke a Lambda that updates the Pull Request with the result

The efficient solution is completely event-driven:

1. Pull Request event → fires CodeBuild
2. Build result event → fires Lambda to update the PR

This avoids polling and prevents Lambda from waiting (which is expensive and limited by timeout).

Incorrect options:

Lambda waiting for CodeBuild - May exceed timeout (15 min) and generates unnecessary cost.

Scheduled execution (polling) - Inefficient compared to real-time events.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html)

question:
Your application is deployed on Elastic Beanstalk and you manage the stack configuration using a CloudFormation template. A new AMI is created every week containing the latest security patches. You've deployed more than 100 applications using CloudFormation and Beanstalk, and you want to ensure that the AMI used by EC2 instances is updated every week. There is no standardization or naming conventions between templates.

As a DevOps Engineer, how would you implement a solution for this requirement?

options.A: Store the ID of the Golden AMI in an SSM Parameter Store parameter. Create a CloudFormation parameter of type String and pass it to the Beanstalk configuration. Create a weekly CloudWatch Event rule that invokes a Lambda that gets the parameter and updates the stacks with UpdateStack
options.B: Store the ID of the Golden AMI in an SSM Parameter Store parameter. Create a CloudFormation parameter that points to SSM and pass it to Beanstalk. Create a weekly CloudWatch Event rule that invokes a Lambda that does UpdateStack on all stacks
options.C: Store the Golden AMI ID in an S3 object and use a CloudFormation parameter pointing to that object. Use Lambda to refresh stacks
options.D: Store the ID of the Golden AMI in S3 and modify mappings in each template using Lambda

explanation:
Correct option:

Store the ID of the Golden AMI in an SSM Parameter Store parameter. Create a CloudFormation parameter that points to SSM and pass it to Beanstalk. Create a weekly CloudWatch Event rule that invokes a Lambda that does UpdateStack on all stacks

SSM Parameter Store allows you to centralize the AMI value.

CloudFormation can directly reference SSM parameters, so you don't need additional logic to manually pass values.

Every time the parameter is updated in SSM, just run an UpdateStack and CloudFormation will automatically take the new value.

Since there is no standardization in templates, this solution avoids modifying each one.

Incorrect options:

Pass value manually from Lambda (String) - Does not scale well without standardization.

Use S3 as parameter source - CloudFormation does not support fetching parameters directly from S3.

Modify templates dynamically - Very complex, fragile and difficult to maintain.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-ssm-parameter.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-ssm-parameter.html)

question:
A healthcare company has strong regulatory requirements and it has recently been detected that some EBS volumes have not been encrypted. Compliance needs to be monitored and audited over time and alert appropriate teams when unencrypted EBS volumes are detected.

How should a DevOps Engineer implement an alert for unencrypted EBS volumes with the least administrative effort?

options.A: Create a Lambda function triggered by CloudWatch Events that monitors new EBS volumes and sends notifications to SNS
options.B: Create an AWS Config managed rule that verifies encryption of EBS volumes and connect it directly to SNS
options.C: Create a custom AWS Config rule to review EC2 instances and their volumes, and connect to SNS
options.D: Create an AWS Config managed rule that verifies encryption of EBS volumes and use CloudWatch Events for alerts

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an AWS Config managed rule that verifies encryption of EBS volumes and use CloudWatch Events for alerts

AWS Config offers managed rules such as **encrypted-volumes**, which allow you to automatically evaluate whether EBS volumes are encryption compliant.

This covers two key needs:

- Continuous audit (compliance history)
- Automatic evaluation without code (lower overhead)

For specific non-compliance alerts, CloudWatch/EventBridge events are used that react to compliance status changes and send notifications (for example via SNS or Lambda).

Incorrect options:

Lambda + CloudWatch Events - Does not provide historical auditing or continuous compliance.

AWS Config + Direct SNS - SNS in Config sends all events, does not allow easy filtering by a specific rule.

AWS Config custom rule - Unnecessary, a managed rule already exists.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/encrypted-volumes.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/encrypted-volumes.html)

question:
The DevOps team at a multinational financial services company manages hundreds of accounts through AWS Organizations. As part of security compliance requirements, the team must force the use of a hardened AMI on each account. When creating a new AMI, the team wants to ensure that new EC2 instances cannot be launched from the old AMI. Additionally, the team also wants to track and audit AMI usage compliance across all accounts.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional, what do you recommend? (Select two)

options.A: Create an AWS Automation document to create the AMI and deploy it to all accounts using CloudFormation StackSets
options.B: Create a custom AWS Config rule across all accounts using CloudFormation StackSets and report results with an AWS Config aggregator
options.C: Create an AWS Automation document to create the AMI in a central account and copy it to other accounts
options.D: Create an AWS Automation document to create the AMI in a central account and share it with other accounts. When there is a new AMI, stop sharing the old one and share the new one
options.E: Create a Lambda function on all accounts to verify AMIs and send events to SNS

explanation:
Correct options:

Create an AWS Automation document to create the AMI in a central account and share it with other accounts. When there is a new AMI, stop sharing the old one and share the new one

This guarantees centralized control. By sharing the AMI instead of copying it, proliferation is avoided and the old one can be easily overridden.

Create a custom AWS Config rule across all accounts using CloudFormation StackSets and report results with an AWS Config aggregator

AWS Config allows you to audit compliance over time. The aggregator centralizes visibility across multiple accounts.

Incorrect options:

Copy AMIs to each account - You lose central control and make enforcement difficult.

Create AMIs in each account - Does not scale and breaks consistency.

Lambda + SNS - Does not provide historical auditing or formal compliance.

question:
A retail company is implementing a CodePipeline pipeline in which each push to the CodeCommit master branch is deployed to development, staging, and production environments based on EC2 instances.

For production, traffic must first be deployed to a few instances to collect metrics before manual approval to deploy to the rest.

How would you implement this solution?

options.A: Create 3 deployment groups (dev, staging, full production) and use Canary deployment in CodeDeploy with manual approval
options.B: Create 4 deployment groups (dev, staging, canary in production and full production). Create a single CodePipeline and add a manual approval after the canary
options.C: Create 4 deployment groups and pipelines separated by environment
options.D: Create 3 separate deployment groups and pipelines with Canary deployment

explanation:
Correct option:

Create 4 deployment groups:

- Development
- Staging
- Canary (production subset)
- Complete production

Then chain them together into a single CodePipeline and introduce a manual approval step after the canary deployment.

This allows:

- Validate in few instances
- Make manual decision before impacting all production
- Maintain centralized control in a single pipeline

Also, for EC2 (CodeDeploy EC2/On-Prem), there is no automatic canary like in Lambda/ECS, so you have to model it manually with separate deployment groups.

Incorrect options:

Using native Canary in CodeDeploy EC2 → Does not exist (Lambda/ECS only)

Separate pipelines → You lose control of the flow and cannot correctly insert the approval gate

3 deployment groups → Does not separate canary from full production

question:
A social media company is running its main application through an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) that has 15 EC2 instances distributed across 3 Availability Zones (AZs). During off-peak time, the group's average CPU utilization is at 15%. During peak hours, it goes up to 45%, and these spikes occur predictably during business hours. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

How can you improve instance utilization by reducing cost and maintaining application availability?

options.A: Use a CloudFormation UpdatePolicy to define how the Auto Scaling Group should behave during peak and off-peak times. Ensure ASG invokes CloudFormation using SNS notification relay
options.B: Create a Lambda function that terminates 9 instances at the end of business hours. Create a second Lambda function that creates instances when peak time begins. Schedule both functions using CloudWatch Events
options.C: Create a scaling policy that tracks CPU utilization with a target of 75%. Create a scheduled action that increases the minimum number of instances to 6 during peak times and a second scheduled action that reduces the minimum number of instances to 3 during off-peak times
options.D: Create a scaling policy that tracks CPU utilization with a target of 75%. Create a scheduled action that invokes a Lambda function that will terminate 9 instances after peak times

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a scaling policy that tracks CPU utilization with a target of 75%. Create a scheduled action that increases the minimum number of instances to 6 during peak times and a second scheduled action that reduces the minimum number of instances to 3 during off-peak times

With target tracking scaling policies, you choose a scaling metric and set a target value. Auto Scaling creates and manages the necessary alarms and adjusts capacity to keep the metric close to the configured goal.

In this case, since the spikes occur in a predictable way, the best solution is to combine:

- dynamic scaling with target tracking
- scheduled actions to adjust the minimum capacity according to the schedule

This way you reduce off-peak costs and maintain availability during peak hours.

Incorrect options:

Using Lambda to terminate instances - If the instances belong to an ASG, the group will recreate them if you don't change desired/min/max, so this doesn't properly solve the problem.

Use CloudFormation UpdatePolicy - Not for scheduling recurring ASG operational changes.

Invoke Lambda to terminate instances after the spike - Same issue: ASG will recreate them if the desired capacity doesn't change.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html)

question:
As a DevOps Engineer at an e-commerce company, you have deployed a web application in an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) behind an Application Load Balancer (ALB). The application uses RDS Multi-AZ as a backend and has had problems connecting to the database. The application health check currently returns unhealthy if the application cannot connect to the database. The integration of health checks between ALB and ASG is enabled, so the ASG continues to terminate instances right after they finish booting.

You need to be able to isolate an instance for troubleshooting for an indefinite amount of time. How should you proceed?

options.A: Create an Auto Scaling lifecycle hook for termination. Troubleshoot while the instance is in Terminating:Wait state
options.B: Suspend the Launch process
options.C: Enable termination protection for EC2
options.D: Put an instance on Standby right after it has booted

explanation:
Correct option:

Put an instance on Standby right after it has booted

When an instance is in Standby state within an Auto Scaling Group, it still belongs to the group, but it stops receiving traffic and can be maintained or analyzed without actively participating in the service.

This fits with the requirement to isolate an instance indefinitely for troubleshooting.

Incorrect options:

Create a termination lifecycle hook - It can help, but it has a timeout and is not good for an indefinite amount of time.

Suspend Launch - Only prevents new launches, it does not resolve the isolation of an already created instance.

Enable termination protection in EC2 - Does not prevent the ASG from terminating instances due to health checks or group policies.

question:
A 3D modeling company wants to deploy applications on Elastic Beanstalk with support for multiple programming languages ​​using predictable and standardized deployment strategies. Some languages ​​are supported (Node.js, Java, Golang), but others like Rust are not. You have been hired to design the most efficient solution.

Which of the following options would you recommend?

options.A: Run OpsWorks on top of Elastic Beanstalk to add support
options.B: Deploy to Elastic Beanstalk using Multi-Docker configuration. Package each application as a Docker container in ECR
options.C: Package each application as a standalone AMI with runtime included
options.D: Create a custom platform for each unsupported language

explanation:
Correct option:

Deploy to Elastic Beanstalk using a Multi-Docker configuration. Package each application as a Docker container in ECR

Docker allows you to completely encapsulate the runtime, dependencies and application, eliminating the limitation of languages supported by Beanstalk.

With Multi-container Docker (Dockerrun.aws.json):

You can standardize deployments
Support any language (including Rust)
Use ECR as registry
Maintain consistency in CI/CD

Incorrect options:

OpsWorks - Does not resolve runtime compatibility in Beanstalk.

Per-application AMI – Difficult to maintain and does not standardize deployment.

Custom platform by language - High operational cost and complexity.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/create_deploy_docker_ecs.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/create_deploy_docker_ecs.html)

question:
An e-commerce company has deployed a Spring application in Elastic Beanstalk on the Java platform. As a DevOps Engineer, you are referencing an RDS PostgreSQL database using an environment variable for the application to use to store its data. You are using a library to perform a database migration in case of schema changes. When deploying updates to Beanstalk, you have seen that the migration fails because all EC2 instances running the new version try to run the migration on the RDS database.

How can you correct this problem?

options.A: Create a .ebextensions/db-migration.config file in your repository and define a container_commands block. Place the migration command there and use the attribute leader_only: true
options.B: Create a .ebextensions/db-migration.config file in your repository and define a container_commands block. Place the migration command there and use the lock_mode: true attribute
options.C: Create a .ebextensions/db-migration.config file in your repository and define a commands block. Place the migration command there and use the attribute leader_only: true
options.D: Create a .ebextensions/db-migration.config file in your repository and define a commands block. Place the migration command there and use the lock_mode: true attribute

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a .ebextensions/db-migration.config file in your repository and define a container_commands block. Place the migration command there and use the attribute leader_only: true

In Elastic Beanstalk, .ebextensions files allow you to customize your environment and run commands during deployment.

The important difference is:

commands: runs on all instances and does not support leader_only
container_commands: runs after preparing the application and does support leader_only

Since you need the migration to run only once, you must put it in container_commands with leader_only: true.

Incorrect options:

Use commands with leader_only - Incorrect, because commands does not support that attribute.

Use lock_mode: true - That attribute does not exist in this context.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/customize-containers-ec2.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/customize-containers-ec2.html)

[https://stackoverflow.com/questions/35788499/what-is-difference-between-commands-and-container-commands-in-elasticbean-talk/40096352#40096352] (https://stackoverflow.com/questions/35788499/what-is-difference-between-commands-and-container-commands-in-elasticbean-talk/40096352#40096352)
