question:
An educational technology company has created a pay-as-you-go API using API Gateway. This API is available at http://edtech.com/api/v1. The website's static files have been uploaded to S3 and now support a new API path http://edtech.com/api/v1/new-feature, if available. Your team has decided to first send a small amount of traffic to that route and test if the metrics look correct. Your API Gateway routes are backed by AWS Lambda.

As a DevOps engineer, what steps should you take to enable these tests?

options.A: Create a new API Gateway Stage. Enable Canary deployments in stage v1. Deploy the new stage to stage v1 and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary stage. Monitor metrics data using CloudWatch
options.B: Create a new Lambda function alias. Enable Canary deployments in the Lambda alias. Deploy the new API to the Lambda alias and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary version of Lambda. Enable new route redirection for AWS Lambda and monitor metrics data using Amazon ES
options.C: Create a new API Gateway Stage. Enable Canary deployments in stage v1. Deploy the new stage to stage v1 and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary stage. Monitor metrics data using Amazon ES
options.D: Create a new Lambda function alias. Enable Canary deployments in the Lambda alias. Deploy the new API to the Lambda alias and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary version of Lambda. Enable new route redirection for AWS Lambda and monitor metrics data using CloudWatch

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a new API Gateway Stage. Enable Canary deployments in stage v1. Deploy the new stage to stage v1 and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary stage. Monitor metrics data using CloudWatch

Amazon API Gateway is an AWS service for creating, publishing, maintaining, monitoring, and securing REST, HTTP, and WebSocket APIs at any scale. API Gateway handles tasks such as traffic management, authorization and access control, monitoring and API version management. API Gateway acts as a “gateway” for applications to access data, business logic, or functionality from your backend services, such as workloads running on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), code running on AWS Lambda, any web applications, or real-time communication applications.

How API Gateway works:

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/)

Simply creating and developing an API in API Gateway does not automatically make it callable by your users. To make it callable, you must deploy your API to a stage. A stage is a named reference to a deployment, which is a snapshot of the API. You can configure stage settings to enable caching, customize request throttling, configure logging, define stage variables, or attach a release canary for testing. In a canary release deployment, the total API traffic is randomly separated into a production release and a canary release with a preconfigured ratio. Updated API features are only visible for the canary release. The canary release receives a small percentage of the API traffic and the production release receives the rest.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/canary-release.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/canary-release.html)

For the given use case, you must deploy the API to a new stage called v1, enable canary deployment on this v1 stage, and assign a small amount of traffic to this canary stage.

Incorrect options:

Create a new API Gateway Stage. Enable Canary deployments in stage v1. Deploy the new stage to stage v1 and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary stage. Monitor metrics data using Amazon ES - API Gateway and AWS Lambda have direct integration with CloudWatch and NOT with Amazon ES. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Create a new Lambda function alias. Enable Canary deployments in the Lambda alias. Deploy the new API to the Lambda alias and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary version of Lambda. Enable new route redirection for AWS Lambda and monitor metrics data using CloudWatch - When a new API route is deployed, you must create a new API Gateway stage and NOT a Lambda alias. Lambda aliases are only used to update the behavior of an existing route. Remember that a route in API Gateway maps to an AWS Lambda function (or other service).Create a new Lambda function alias. Enable Canary deployments in the Lambda alias. Deploy the new API to the Lambda alias and assign a small amount of traffic to the canary version of Lambda. Enable new route redirection for AWS Lambda and monitor metrics data using Amazon ES - When a new API route is deployed, you must create a new API Gateway stage and NOT a Lambda alias. Additionally, API Gateway and AWS Lambda have direct integration with CloudWatch and NOT with Amazon ES.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/canary-release.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/canary-release.html)

question:
You are working as a DevOps engineer in an e-commerce company and have a Node.js application deployed on Elastic Beanstalk. You would like to track error rates and specifically need to make sure, by looking at the application logs, that you don't have more than 100 errors in a 5 minute interval. In case you are receiving too many errors, you would like to be alerted via email.

Which of the following options represents the most efficient solution in your opinion?

options.A: Implement custom logic in your Node.js application to track the number of errors it has received in the last 5 minutes. In case the number exceeds the threshold, use the SetAlarmState API to trigger a CloudWatch alarm. Make CloudWatch alarm use SNS as destination. Create an email subscription on SNS
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter with a target being a CloudWatch alarm. Make CloudWatch alarm use SNS as destination. Create an email subscription on SNS
options.C: Use Elastic Beanstalk health metrics to monitor application health and track error rates. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the metric and use SNS as a destination. Create an email subscription on SNS
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter and assign a CloudWatch metric. Create a CloudWatch alarm linked to the metric and use SNS as a destination. Create an email subscription on SNS

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter and assign a CloudWatch metric. Create a CloudWatch alarm linked to the metric and use SNS as a destination. Create an email subscription on SNS

You can search and filter log data by creating one or more metric filters. Metric filters define the terms and patterns to look for in log data as it is sent to CloudWatch Logs. CloudWatch Logs uses these metric filters to convert log data into numerical CloudWatch metrics that you can graph or set an alarm on. Filters do not filter data retroactively. Filters only publish metric data points for events that occur after the filter was created.

You can use metric filters to search and match terms, phrases, or values ​​in your log events. When a metric filter finds one of the terms, phrases, or values ​​in your log events, you can increment the value of a CloudWatch metric. For example, you can create a metric filter to find and count the occurrence of the word ERROR in your log events.

CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter Concepts: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html)

For the given use case, you can have Beanstalk send the logs to CloudWatch Logs, and then create a metric filter. This will create a metric for us (and not an alarm), and on top of that metric, you can create a CloudWatch alarm. This alarm will send a notification to SNS, which in turn will send emails.

Incorrect options:

Create a CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter with a target being a CloudWatch alarm. Make CloudWatch alarm use SNS as destination. Create an email subscription in SNS - You cannot directly set a CloudWatch alarm as the destination of a CloudWatch Logs Metric Filter. First you need to create a metric filter which can then be used to create a CloudWatch metric that will eventually be used in a CloudWatch alarm.

Use Elastic Beanstalk health metrics to monitor application health and track error rates. Create a CloudWatch alarm on the metric and use SNS as a destination. Create an email subscription in SNS - Elastic Beanstalk health metrics do not track errors sent to a log file, so they do not meet the use case requirements. Additionally, a CloudWatch alarm cannot be used directly on Elastic Beanstalk health metrics.Implement custom logic in your Node.js application to track the number of errors it has received in the last 5 minutes. In case the number exceeds the threshold, use the SetAlarmState API to trigger a CloudWatch alarm. Make CloudWatch alarm use SNS as destination. Create an email subscription in SNS - Implementing custom logic in your Node.js application may seem like a good idea, but you must remember that your application may be distributed across multiple servers with Beanstalk, so it will not be possible to track the "100 errors" across all instances using this methodology.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/MonitoringLogData.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/FilterAndPatternSyntax.html)

question:
A global healthcare company has an EFS file system being used on eu-west-1. The company wants to plan a disaster recovery strategy and back up that EFS file system to ap-southeast-2. You must have a live copy of the data so that applications can be redeployed to ap-southeast-2 with minimal RPO and RTO. The VPCs in each region are not peered to each other.

How should a DevOps engineer implement a solution for this use case?

options.A: Create an EC2 managed replication cluster with Auto Scaling on eu-west-1. Scale according to a custom metric that you would publish with the application representing the delay in file reads. Replicate the data to Amazon S3 on ap-southeast-2. Create another replication cluster on ap-southeast-2 that reads from Amazon S3 and copies files to a standby EFS cluster
options.B: Create an EC2 managed replication cluster with Auto Scaling on eu-west-1. Scale according to a custom metric that you would publish with the application representing the delay in file reads. Create a standby EFS cluster on ap-southeast-2 and mount it on the same EC2 cluster. Let the replication software perform EFS-to-EFS replication
options.C: Create an hourly CloudWatch Event rule that triggers an AWS Batch cluster on eu-west-1 to perform incremental replication. Replicate data to Amazon S3 in another region. Create a Lambda function in ap-southeast-2 for PUT events in Amazon S3 that triggers an SSM Run command to copy the files from S3 to EFS
options.D: Create an hourly CloudWatch Event rule that triggers an AWS Batch cluster on eu-west-1 to perform incremental replication. Replicate data to Amazon S3 in another region. Create an EC2 replication cluster on ap-southeast-2 that reads from Amazon S3 and copies files to a standby EFS cluster

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an EC2 managed replication cluster with Auto Scaling on eu-west-1. Scale according to a custom metric that you would publish with the application representing the delay in file reads. Replicate the data to Amazon S3 on ap-southeast-2. Create another replication cluster on ap-southeast-2 that reads from Amazon S3 and copies files to a standby EFS cluster

Metrics are the fundamental concept in CloudWatch. A metric represents a set of time-ordered data points that are published to CloudWatch. Think of a metric as a variable to monitor, and data points represent the values ​​of that variable over time. You can use these metrics to verify that your system is working as expected.

Using custom metrics for your Auto Scaling groups and instances: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html)

RPO and RTO explained: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/recovery-time-objective-rto-and-recovery-point-objective-rpo.html] (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/recovery-time-objective-rto-and-recovery-point-objective-rpo.html)

For the given use case, we need to create a custom metric via the application that captures the delay in file reads and then use it to scale the ASG managing the EC2 instances to replicate the source EFS cluster to S3. Use another ASG to copy data from S3 to EFS in the destination region. Here we want a minimum RPO, so we need continuous replication, and a minimum RTO, so we want an active EFS system ready to use. Please note that because the RPO and RTO are low, the cost of the solution will be very high.

Additional note (FYI) the AWS DataSync service (not covered in the exam) can achieve EFS to EFS replication in a much more native way.

Note: With this solution, as files are copied to S3, Linux file permissions will not be replicated.

Incorrect options:

Create an EC2 managed replication cluster with Auto Scaling on eu-west-1. Scale according to a custom metric that you would publish with the application representing the delay in file reads. Create a standby EFS cluster on ap-southeast-2 and mount it on the same EC2 cluster. Let the replication software perform EFS-to-EFS replication - Since VPCs are not peered, it is not possible to mount EFS from two different regions on the same EC2 cluster. We need to use S3 as an intermediary for replication.

Create an hourly CloudWatch Event rule that triggers an AWS Batch cluster on eu-west-1 to perform incremental replication. Replicate data to Amazon S3 in another region. Create an EC2 replication cluster on ap-southeast-2 that reads from Amazon S3 and copies files to a standby EFS clusterCreate an hourly CloudWatch Event rule that triggers an AWS Batch cluster on eu-west-1 to perform incremental replication. Replicate data to Amazon S3 in another region. Create a Lambda function in ap-southeast-2 for PUT events in Amazon S3 that triggers an SSM Run command to copy the files from S3 to EFS - Since the goal is to have an active copy in EFS, both options are ruled out since there is a one hour delay.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/recovery-time-objective-rto-and-recovery-point-objective-rpo.html] (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/reliability-pillar/recovery-time-objective-rto-and-recovery-point-objective-rpo.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/as-scaling-target-tracking.html)

question:
The DevOps team at a leading bitcoin wallet and exchange services company is trying to deploy a CloudFormation template that contains a Lambda function, an S3 bucket, an IAM role, and a DynamoDB table from CodePipeline, but the team is getting an InsufficientCapabilitiesException.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional, which of the following options would you suggest to address this issue?

options.A: Fix CloudFormation template as there is a circular dependency and CloudFormation does not have that capability
options.B: Update the CodePipeline IAM role so that it has permissions to create all resources mentioned in the CloudFormation template
options.C: Increase the service limits for your S3 bucket since you have reached the limit
options.D: Enable IAM capability in CodePipeline configuration for CloudFormation deployment action

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable IAM capability in CodePipeline configuration for CloudFormation deployment action

With AWS CloudFormation and CodePipeline, you can use continuous delivery to automatically build and test changes to your CloudFormation templates before promoting them to production stacks. For example, you can create a workflow that automatically builds a test stack when you push an updated template to a code repository. After CloudFormation builds the test stack, you can test it and then decide whether to promote the changes to a production stack. Use CodePipeline to build a continuous delivery pipeline by creating a pipeline for CloudFormation stacks. CodePipeline has native integration with CloudFormation, so you can specify CloudFormation-specific actions, such as creating, updating, or deleting a stack within a pipeline.

You can use IAM with AWS CloudFormation to control what users can do with CloudFormation, such as whether they can view stack templates, create stacks, or delete stacks.

For the given use case, InsufficientCapabilitiesException means that the CloudFormation stack is trying to create an IAM role but does not have the specified capabilities. Therefore, it must be configured in the CodePipeline configuration for the CloudFormation deployment action.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-iam-template.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-iam-template.html)

Incorrect options:

Update the CodePipeline IAM role to have permissions to create all resources mentioned in the CloudFormation template - The given exception is not related to the permissions of the user or the CodePipeline IAM role running the CloudFormation template, so this option is incorrect.

Fix the CloudFormation template as a circular dependency exists and CloudFormation does not have that capability - A circular dependency, as the name implies, means that two resources depend on each other or that a resource depends on itself.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/handling-circular-dependency-errors-in-aws-cloudformation/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/handling-circular-dependency-errors-in-aws-cloudformation/)

This option is incorrect since a circular dependency would generate a different error.

Increase service limits for your S3 bucket since you have reached the limit - This option is a distraction since the exception has nothing to do with S3 service limits.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-iam-template.html#using-iam-capabilities](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-iam-template.html#using-iam-capabilities)

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/handling-circular-dependency-errors-in-aws-cloudformation/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/infrastructure-and-automation/handling-circular-dependency-errors-in-aws-cloudformation/)Theme

question:
An online programming platform wants to completely customize build tasks and run builds concurrently automatically to avoid the complexity of managing build environments. The company's DevOps team wants to use CodeBuild for all build tasks and wants artifacts created by CodeBuild to be named based on the branch being tested. The team wants this solution to be scalable to new branches with minimal additional effort.

As a DevOps engineer, how would you implement the simplest possible solution for this use case?

options.A: Create a single buildspec.yml file that will be the same for each branch and name the artifacts the same. When the artifact is uploaded to S3, create an S3 event that fires a Lambda function that will make an API call to CodeBuild, pull the branch name, and rename the file in S3
options.B: Create a buildspec.yml file that will look for the CODEBUILD_SOURCE_VERSION environment variable at runtime. Use the variable in the artifacts section of your buildspec.yml file
options.C: Create a buildspec.yml file that will be different for each branch. Create a new CodeBuild for each branch. When adding a new branch, make sure to edit the buildspec.yml file
options.D: Create a buildspec.yml file that will look for the BRANCH_NAME environment variable at runtime. For each existing and new branch, create a separate CodeBuild and set the BRANCH_NAME variable accordingly. Use the variable in the artifacts section of your buildspec.yml file

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a buildspec.yml file that will look for the CODEBUILD_SOURCE_VERSION environment variable at runtime. Use the variable in the artifacts section of your buildspec.yml file

AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service in the cloud. CodeBuild compiles source code, runs tests, and produces packages ready to deploy. CodeBuild eliminates the need to provision, manage and scale your own build servers.

A buildspec is a collection of build commands and related configurations, in YAML format, that CodeBuild uses to run a build. You can include a buildspec as part of the source code or define it when you create a build project.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html)

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html)

For the given use case, we need to use environment variables. The CODEBUILD_SOURCE_VERSION variable is exposed at runtime directly within CodeBuild and represents the name of the branch of the code being tested in CodeCommit. This is the best solution.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-env-ref-env-vars.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-env-ref-env-vars.html)

Incorrect options:

Create a buildspec.yml file that will look for the BRANCH_NAME environment variable at runtime. For each existing and new branch, create a separate CodeBuild and set the BRANCH_NAME variable accordingly. Use the variable in the artifacts section of your buildspec.yml file - Providing the branch name as BRANCH_NAME and creating separate CodeBuilds would be very tedious to maintain and error prone. This is definitely not the simplest solution.

Create a buildspec.yml file that will be different for each branch. Create a new CodeBuild for each branch. When adding a new branch, make sure to edit the buildspec.yml file - Maintaining a different buildspec.yml for each branch is inefficient and error-prone. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Create a single buildspec.yml file that will be the same for each branch and name the artifacts the same. When the artifact is uploaded to S3, create an S3 event that triggers a Lambda function that will make an API call to CodeBuild, pull the branch name, and rename the file in S3 - The option involving a Lambda function would work but is highly complex. This can be achieved directly using the CODEBUILD_SOURCE_VERSION environment variable.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-spec-ref.html)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-env-ref-env-vars.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codebuild/latest/userguide/build-env-ref-env-vars.html)

question:
A multinational retail company is planning for disaster recovery and needs data to be stored in Amazon S3 in two different regions that are on different continents. Data is written at a high rate of 10000 objects per second. For regulatory reasons, data must also be encrypted in transit and at rest. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

Which of the following solutions would you recommend?

options.A: Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "false". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-KMS. Configure Cross-Region Replication
options.B: Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "true". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-KMS. Configure Cross-Region Replication
options.C: Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "true". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-S3. Configure Cross-Region Replication
options.D: Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "false". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-S3. Configure Cross-Region Replication

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "false". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-S3. Configure Cross-Region Replication

By default, Amazon S3 allows both HTTP and HTTPS requests. To comply, you must confirm that your bucket policies explicitly deny access to HTTP requests. Bucket policies that allow HTTPS requests without explicitly denying HTTP may not comply with the rule.

To determine whether a request is HTTP or HTTPS in a bucket policy, use a condition that checks the "aws:SecureTransport" key. When this key is true, it means that the request is sent over HTTPS. Create a bucket policy that explicitly denies access when the request meets the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false." This policy explicitly denies HTTP requests.

Finally, if we encrypt using KMS, we can be throttled to 10000 objects per second. SSE-S3 is a better option in this case.

Incorrect options:

Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "true". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-S3. Configure Cross-Region Replication - As mentioned above, you need to set the condition "aws:SecureTransport": "false" for the solution to work.

Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "false". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-KMS. Configure Cross-Region Replication

Create a bucket policy to create a condition that denies any request that is "aws:SecureTransport": "true". Encrypt objects at rest using SSE-KMS. Configure Cross-Region Replication

If we use KMS to encrypt, we can be limited to 10000 objects per second. Therefore, both options are incorrect.

References:

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-use-bucket-policies-and-apply-defense-in-depth-to-help-secure-your-amazon-s3-data/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/security/how-to-use-bucket-policies-and-apply-defense-in-depth-to-help-secure-your-amazon-s3-data/)

question:
As part of the CI/CD pipeline, a DevOps engineer is performing a functional test using a CloudFormation template that will later be deployed to production. That CloudFormation template creates an S3 bucket and a Lambda function that transforms images uploaded to S3 into thumbnails. To test the Lambda function, some images are automatically uploaded and output thumbnails are expected from the Lambda function to the S3 bucket. As part of cleaning up these functional tests, the CloudFormation stack is removed, but at this point the removal fails.

What is the reason and how could this problem be solved?

options.A: The S3 bucket contains files and therefore cannot be deleted by CloudFormation. Add the Delete: Force property to your CloudFormation template so that the S3 bucket is emptied before being deleted
options.B: A StackPolicy prevents the CloudFormation template from being deleted. Clear the Stack Policy and try again
options.C: The S3 bucket contains files and therefore cannot be deleted by CloudFormation. Create an additional Custom Resource backed by a Lambda function that performs bucket cleanup
options.D: The Lambda function is still using the S3 bucket and CloudFormation cannot therefore delete the S3 bucket. Place a WaitCondition in the Lambda function to fix the problem

explanation:
Correct option:

The S3 bucket contains files and therefore cannot be deleted by CloudFormation. Create an additional Custom Resource backed by a Lambda function that performs bucket cleanup

In a CloudFormation template, you can use the AWS::CloudFormation::CustomResource or Custom::String resource type to specify custom resources. Custom resources provide a way to write custom provisioning logic in the CloudFormation template and have CloudFormation execute it during a stack operation, such as when you create, update, or delete a stack.

Some resources must be empty before they can be deleted. For example, you must delete all objects in an Amazon S3 bucket or remove all instances in an Amazon EC2 security group before you can delete the bucket or security group.

For this use case, the problem is that the S3 bucket is not empty before being deleted, so you need to implement a Lambda-backed Custom Resource that cleans up the bucket for you.

via - [https://docs.amazonaws.cn/en_us/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-cfn-customresource.html](https://docs.amazonaws.cn/en_us/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-cfn-customresource.html)

question:
An e-commerce company has deployed its main application in two Auto Scaling groups (ASG) and two Application Load Balancers (ALB). They have a Route 53 record that points to the ALB+ASG group where the application was most recently deployed. The deployments alternate between the two groups, and each time a deployment occurs it is done on the inactive ALB+ASG group. Finally, the Route 53 registry is updated. It turns out that some of your clients are not behaving correctly regarding DNS registration and are therefore making requests to the inactive ALB+ASG group.

The company wants to improve this behavior with minimal cost and also reduce the complexity of the solution. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement. Which of the following options would you suggest?

options.A: Delete one ALB and keep the two ASGs. When new deployments occur, deploy the previous ASG, and then swap the target group in the ALB rule. Keep the Route53 record pointing to the ALB
options.B: Deploy the application in Elastic Beanstalk under two environments. To do a deployment, deploy to the previous environment, then perform a CNAME swap
options.C: Deploy a set of NGINX proxies on each application instance so that if requests are made through the inactive ALB, they are forwarded to the correct ALB
options.D: Change the TTL of Route53 to 1 minute before doing a deployment. Do the deployment and then increase the TTL back to the previous value

explanation:
Correct option:

Delete one ALB and keep the two ASGs. When new deployments occur, deploy the previous ASG, and then swap the target group in the ALB rule. Keep the Route53 record pointing to the ALB

An ALB distributes incoming application traffic between multiple destinations, such as EC2 instances, in multiple Availability Zones. A listener verifies connection requests from clients using the protocol and port that you configure. The rules you define for a listener determine how the load balancer routes requests to their registered destinations. Each target group routes requests to one or more registered destinations, such as EC2 instances, using the protocol and port number that you specify. You can register a destination with multiple target groups.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html)

The problem occurs from using the second load balancer for the second application stack and then changing the DNS route to direct traffic to the other stack when necessary. The correct solution is to only replace the infrastructure behind the load balancer. In summary, we can migrate to a single ALB and then use only one target group at a time behind each ASG for correct routing. This also has the additional benefit that we will not need to pre-warm each ALB on each deployment.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-application-load-balancer-simplifies-deployment-with-weighted-target-groups/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/aws/new-application-load-balancer-simplifies-deployment-with-weighted-target-groups/)

Incorrect options:

Deploy a set of NGINX proxies on each application instance so that if requests are made through the inactive ALB, they are forwarded to the correct ALB - Deploying an NGINX proxy would work but would be tedious to manage and would complicate deployments.

Change the TTL of Route53 to 1 minute before doing a deployment. Do the deployment and then increase the TTL back to the previous value - Changing the TTL won't help because clients are already behaving incorrectly with how they handle DNS records.

Deploy the application in Elastic Beanstalk under two environments. To do a deployment, deploy to the old environment, then do a CNAME swap - Migrating to Elastic Beanstalk won't help either since a CNAME swap is a DNS record change and clients don't seem to respect DNS responses.

question:
A data analytics company wants to create an automated solution to be alerted if EC2 instances are underutilized for more than 24 hours in order to save costs. The solution must require manual intervention by an operator validating the evaluation before proceeding with the termination of the instance.

As a DevOps engineer, how would you implement a solution with the LEAST development effort?

options.A: Enable Trusted Advisor and ensure that underutilized EC2 instance checking is active. Connect Trusted Advisor to an SNS topic for that verification and use a Lambda function as a subscriber to the SNS topic. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 5 minutes and use a Lambda function as a target. The Lambda function should make API calls to CloudWatch metrics and store the information in DynamoDB. Use a DynamoDB stream to detect an underutilization event for 24 hours and fire a Lambda function. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance
options.C: Create a CloudWatch alarm that tracks the minimum CPU utilization across all your EC2 instances. Connect the alarm to an SNS topic and use the Lambda function as a subscriber of the SNS topic. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance
options.D: Enable Trusted Advisor and ensure that underutilized EC2 instance checking is active. Create a CloudWatch Event that tracks events generated by Trusted Advisor and use a Lambda function as a target for that event. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable Trusted Advisor and ensure that underutilized EC2 instance checking is active. Create a CloudWatch Event that tracks events generated by Trusted Advisor and use a Lambda function as a target for that event. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance

Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS infrastructure in all regions and presents a summary of verification results. Recommends stopping or terminating EC2 instances with low utilization. You can also choose to scale your instances using Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling.

Trusted Advisor's cost optimization check allows you to review EC2 instances that have been running at any time in the last 14 days and alerts if daily CPU utilization was 10% or less and network I/O was 5 MB or less for 4 or more days. Running instances incur hourly charges. Estimated monthly savings are calculated using the current rate of On-Demand instances and the estimated number of days the instance could be underutilized.

You can use Amazon CloudWatch Events to detect and react to changes in the status of Trusted Advisor verifications. Then, based on the rules you create, CloudWatch Events invokes one or more target actions when the check status changes to the value you specify. Depending on the type of status change, you can send notifications, capture information, take corrective actions, or initiate other events. Finally, SSM Automation can include a manual approval step and proceed with terminating instances.

Monitoring Trusted Advisor check results with Amazon CloudWatch Events: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/cloudwatch-events-ta.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awssupport/latest/user/cloudwatch-events-ta.html)

Incorrect options:

Enable Trusted Advisor and ensure that underutilized EC2 instance checking is active. Connect Trusted Advisor to an SNS topic for that verification and use a Lambda function as a subscriber to the SNS topic. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance - You should use CloudWatch Events to track Trusted Advisor events and not SNS directly.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 5 minutes and use a Lambda function as a target. The Lambda function should make API calls to CloudWatch metrics and store the information in DynamoDB. Use a DynamoDB stream to detect an underutilization event for 24 hours and fire a Lambda function. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance - This flow involves a lot of development effort and uses unnecessary resources like DynamoDB Streams.Create a CloudWatch alarm that tracks the minimum CPU utilization across all your EC2 instances. Connect the alarm to an SNS topic and use the Lambda function as a subscriber of the SNS topic. The Lambda function should trigger an SSM Automation document with a manual approval step. Upon approval, the SSM document proceeds with the termination of the instance - An aggregated alarm does not allow each individual instance to be properly evaluated and creating an alarm per instance would be costly.

question:
A multimedia streaming solutions company has deployed an application that allows its customers to watch movies in real time. The application connects to an Amazon Aurora database, and the entire stack is currently deployed in the United States. The company has plans to expand to Europe and Asia for its operations. You need the movies table to be globally accessible, but the users and movies_watched tables to be regional only.

As a DevOps engineer, how would you implement this with as little application refactoring as possible?

options.A: Use an Amazon Aurora Global Database for the movies table and use DynamoDB for the users and movies_watched tables
options.B: Use a DynamoDB Global Table for the movies table and use DynamoDB for the users and movies_watched tables
options.C: Use an Amazon Aurora Global Database for the movies table and use Amazon Aurora for the users and movies_watched tables
options.D: Use a DynamoDB Global Table for the movies table and use Amazon Aurora for the users and movies_watched tables

explanation:
Correct option:

Use an Amazon Aurora Global Database for the movies table and use Amazon Aurora for the users and movies_watched tables

Amazon Aurora is a MySQL- and PostgreSQL-compatible relational database built for the cloud, combining the performance and availability of traditional enterprise databases with the simplicity and cost-effectiveness of open source. Amazon Aurora has a distributed, fault-tolerant, self-healing storage system that automatically scales up to 64 TB per database instance. Aurora is not an in-memory database.

Amazon Aurora Global Database is designed for globally distributed applications, allowing a single Amazon Aurora database to span multiple AWS Regions. Replicate your data with no impact on database performance, enable fast local reads with low latency in each region, and provide disaster recovery from regional failures. Amazon Aurora Global Database is the right choice for this use case.

For this use case, therefore, we need to have two Aurora clusters, one for the global table (movies table) and another for the local tables (users and movies_watched).

Incorrect options:

Use an Amazon Aurora Global Database for the movies table and use DynamoDB for the users and movies_watched tables

Use a DynamoDB Global Table for the movies table and use Amazon Aurora for the users and movies_watched tables

Use a DynamoDB Global Table for the movies table and use DynamoDB for the users and movies_watched tables

Here we are looking for a minimal refactor of the application. DynamoDB and Aurora have completely different APIs, since Aurora is SQL and DynamoDB is NoSQL. Therefore, all three options are incorrect as they include DynamoDB as one of the components.

question:
An e-commerce company wants to automate the patching of its hybrid fleet and distribute a few patches through its internal patch repositories each week. As a DevOps engineer in the company, you have been tasked with implementing this as efficiently as possible.

Which of the following options represents the BEST solution to meet this requirement?

options.A: Using SSM, run a RunCommand to install the custom repositories into the operating system's internal configuration files. Use the Default Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule the maintenance window with weekly recurrence
options.B: Manage your instances with AWS OpsWorks. Define a maintenance window and define custom Chef cookbooks for the "configure" lifecycle hook that will apply patches to the instances from the internal patch repositories. Schedule the window with weekly recurrence
options.C: Using SSM Parameter Store, configure custom repositories in the operating system's internal configuration files. Use the Default Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule the maintenance window with weekly recurrence
options.D: Using SSM, implement a Custom Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule the maintenance window with weekly recurrence

explanation:
Correct option:

Using SSM, implement a Custom Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule the maintenance window with weekly recurrence

SSM Patch Manager automates the process of patching managed instances with security-related and other types of updates. You can use Patch Manager to apply patches to both operating systems and applications. Patch Manager uses patch baselines, which include rules for auto-approving patches within certain days of their release, as well as a list of approved and rejected patches.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-patch.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-patch.html)

Patch Manager provides predefined patch baselines for each of the operating systems supported by Patch Manager. You can use these baselines as they are currently configured (you cannot customize them) or you can create your own custom patch baselines. Custom patch baselines allow you to have greater control over which patches are approved or rejected in your environment.

When you use the default repositories configured on an instance for patching operations, Patch Manager scans or installs security-related patches. This is the default behavior of Patch Manager.

However, on Linux systems you can also use Patch Manager to install patches that are not security related, or that come from a source repository other than the one configured by default on the instance. You can specify alternative patch source repositories when you create a custom patch baseline. In each custom patch baseline, you can specify patch source configurations for up to 20 versions of a supported Linux operating system. You can then configure a weekly maintenance window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/sysman-patch-baselines.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/sysman-patch-baselines.html)

Incorrect options:

Using SSM Parameter Store, configure custom repositories in the operating system's internal configuration files. Use the Default Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule maintenance window with weekly recurrence - SSM Parameter Store is used to store parameter values, but cannot write configuration files to EC2 instances itself.

Manage your instances with AWS OpsWorks. Define a maintenance window and define custom Chef cookbooks for the "configure" lifecycle hook that will apply patches to the instances from the internal patch repositories. Schedule the window with weekly recurrence - Using Chef cookbooks through OpsWorks might work, but SSM's Patch Manager is a better way to achieve this.Using SSM, run a RunCommand to install the custom repositories into the operating system's internal configuration files. Use the Default Patch Baseline. Define a Maintenance Window and include the Run Command RunPatchBaseline. Schedule the maintenance window to recur weekly - Using SSM RunCommand might work, but SSM's Patch Manager is a better way to achieve this.

question:
The compliance department at a Wall Street trading firm has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to assist with several strategic DevOps initiatives. The department has asked you to generate a list of all software packages installed on EC2 instances. The solution should be able to extend to future instances in the AWS account and send notifications if the instances are not properly configured to track your software.

Which of the following options are the best solutions that require the least effort to meet the requirements? (Select two)

options.A: Use AWS Inspector to track the list of packages installed on your EC2 instances. View metadata directly in the AWS Inspector Insights console
options.B: Install the SSM agent on the instances. Run an SSM Automation during maintenance windows to get the list of all packages using yum list installed. Write output to Amazon S3
options.C: Install the SSM agent on the instances. Run SSM Inventory to collect metadata and send it to Amazon S3
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule to fire a Lambda function on an hourly basis. Make a comparison of instances running on EC2 and those tracked by SSM
options.E: Use an SSM Run Command to have the SSM service find which instances are not currently being crawled by SSM

explanation:
Correct options:

Install the SSM agent on the instances. Run SSM Inventory to collect metadata and send it to Amazon S3

SSM Agent is software from Amazon that can be installed and configured on an EC2 instance, on-premises server, or virtual machine. SSM Agent allows Systems Manager to update, manage, and configure these resources. The agent processes requests from the Systems Manager service in the AWS cloud and then executes them as specified. It then sends status and execution information back to the Systems Manager service using the Amazon Message Delivery Service (service prefix: ec2messages).

SSM Inventory provides visibility into your computing environment on Amazon EC2 and on-premises. You can use Inventory to collect metadata from your managed instances. You can store this metadata in a central Amazon S3 bucket and then use built-in tools to query the data and quickly determine which instances are running the required software and which need to be updated.

Sample Inventory Cards: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-inventory.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-inventory.html)

Create a CloudWatch Event rule to fire a Lambda function on an hourly basis. Make a comparison of instances running on EC2 and those tracked by SSM

Since SSM does not have a native ability to identify which instances are not being tracked, a custom Lambda function is needed to compare EC2 instances to SSM-managed instances and send notifications if there are differences. This function can be triggered using CloudWatch Events.

Incorrect options:

Use an SSM Run Command to have the SSM service find which instances are not currently being tracked by SSM - SSM does not have a native ability to identify untracked instances.

Install the SSM agent on the instances. Run an SSM Automation during maintenance windows to get the list of all packages using yum list installed. Write the output to Amazon S3 - Although this would work, it requires more manual effort compared to SSM Inventory.

Use AWS Inspector to track the list of packages installed on your EC2 instances. View metadata directly in the AWS Inspector Insights console - Inspector is designed to find security vulnerabilities, not to list installed package metadata.

question:
An analytics company is capturing metrics from its services and applications on AWS using CloudWatch metrics. You need to be able to go back up to 7 years in time to view these metrics due to regulatory requirements. As a DevOps engineer in the company, you have been tasked with designing a solution that helps the company comply with regulations.

Which of the following options requires the least development effort to meet the requirements?

options.A: Create a CloudWatch dashboard on CloudWatch metrics. Enable "Extended Retention" on CloudWatch metrics, and implement an AWS Config rule that verifies this setting. If AWS Config detects non-compliance, use Auto Remediation to enable it again
options.B: Create a CloudWatch metrics stream and direct it to a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream. Send all metrics data to S3 using Firehose, and create a QuickSight dashboard to visualize the metrics. Use Athena to query specific time ranges
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 15 minutes. The target must be a Lambda function that executes an API to export metrics and store them in S3. Create a CloudWatch dashboard on metrics in S3
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 15 minutes. The target must be a Lambda function that executes an API to export metrics and store them in Amazon ES. Create a dashboard in Kibana to view metrics

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch metrics stream and direct it to a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream. Send all metrics data to S3 using Firehose, and create a QuickSight dashboard to visualize the metrics. Use Athena to query specific time ranges

You can use metric streams to continuously stream CloudWatch metrics to a destination of your choice with near real-time delivery and low latency. Supported destinations include AWS services such as Amazon S3 and also third-party services.

You can create a metric stream and point it to an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream that delivers CloudWatch metrics to a data lake such as Amazon S3. You can then use tools like Amazon Athena to gain insights into cost, performance, and resource utilization optimization for specific time ranges. Additionally, you can use a QuickSight dashboard to view metrics.

The Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream must trust CloudWatch using an IAM role that has write permissions to the Firehose. These permissions can be limited to the specific delivery stream that uses the metric stream. The IAM role must trust the streams.metrics.cloudwatch.amazonaws.com service principal.

Incorrect options:

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 15 minutes. The target must be a Lambda function that executes an API to export metrics and store them in Amazon ES. Create a dashboard in Kibana to view metrics

A CloudWatch metric represents a set of time-ordered data points that are published to CloudWatch. Data points automatically expire after 15 months on a rolling schedule; As new data arrives, the oldest data is deleted.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch_concepts.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/monitoring/cloudwatch_concepts.html)

Since CloudWatch metrics are only retained for 15 months, we need to export them for long-term storage. Although this option would work, it requires developing a custom Lambda function, which requires more effort.

Create a CloudWatch dashboard on CloudWatch metrics. Enable "Extended Retention" on CloudWatch metrics, and implement an AWS Config rule that verifies this setting. If AWS Config detects non-compliance, use Auto Remediation to enable it again - CloudWatch does not have an "Extended Retention" functionality.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that fires every 15 minutes. The target must be a Lambda function that executes an API to export metrics and store them in S3. Create a CloudWatch dashboard on metrics in S3 - CloudWatch dashboards can only consume CloudWatch metrics, not data stored in S3.

question:
A multinational retail company is operating a multi-account strategy using AWS Organizations. Each account produces logs in CloudWatch Logs, and the company wants to aggregate these logs into a single centralized account for archiving purposes. You need the solution to be secure and centralized. The target destination for the logs should require little or no provisioning on the storage side.

As a DevOps engineer, how would you implement a solution to meet these requirements?

options.A: Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the log destination. Kinesis Firehose destination must be Amazon S3
options.B: Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Streams and subscribe it to the destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the Kinesis Stream. Firehose target must be Amazon Redshift
options.C: Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Streams and subscribe it to the destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the Kinesis Stream. Firehose destination should be Amazon ES
options.D: Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Lambda function on that log subscription, and implement a script to send the data to Amazon ES

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the log destination. Kinesis Firehose destination must be Amazon S3

You can use subscriptions to access a real-time stream of log events from CloudWatch Logs and send them to other services such as Amazon Kinesis, Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose, or AWS Lambda for processing, analysis, or uploading to other systems. When log events are sent to the receiving service, they are Base64 encoded and gzipped.

To share log data between accounts using subscriptions, you can collaborate with another AWS account and receive its log events on your own resources, such as a Kinesis stream or Kinesis Data Firehose (this is known as cross-account data sharing). For example, this data can be read from a centralized Kinesis or Firehose stream for processing or analysis. Therefore, we must subscribe the log destination to a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream, which in turn has S3 as its destination.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CrossAccountSubscriptions.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/logs/CrossAccountSubscriptions.html)

Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Streams and subscribe it to the destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the Kinesis Stream. Firehose target should be Amazon Redshift - The problem is that Amazon Redshift is not a serverless service and requires provisioning.

Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Kinesis Streams and subscribe it to the destination. Create a Kinesis Firehose delivery stream and subscribe it to the Kinesis Stream. Firehose target should be Amazon ES - The problem is that Amazon ES is not a serverless service and requires provisioning.

Create a log destination in the centralized account, and create a log subscription to that destination. Create a Lambda function on that log subscription, and implement a script to send the data to Amazon ES - Although this could work, Amazon ES requires provisioning and also adds unnecessary complexity.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional, which of the following options would you implement to meet this requirement?

options.A: Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-healing. Configure as target a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-scaling. Enable the Slack integration in CloudWatch Events to send notifications
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-scaling. Configure as target a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel
options.D: Subscribe OpsWorks auto-healing notifications to an SNS topic. Subscribe a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-healing. Configure as target a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel

AWS OpsWorks is a configuration management service that provides managed Chef and Puppet instances. These platforms allow you to automate server configurations using code. OpsWorks allows you to automate how servers are configured, deployed and managed in EC2 instances or on-premises environments.

A stack is the highest-level entity in OpsWorks Stacks. It represents a set of instances that are managed together. Each stack contains one or more layers, and each layer represents a component such as balancers or application servers. Each layer has associated lifecycle events that automatically run recipes when events occur.

OpsWorks Stacks allows you to send state changes, such as stopped instances or failed deployments, to CloudWatch Events. The initiated_by field is filled when the instance is in states such as requested, terminating, or stopping. This field can take values like:

user - when a user initiates the change

auto-scaling - when auto-scaling starts

auto-healing - when auto-healing starts

For this case, it is required to detect auto-healing events, so the value must be auto-healing. CloudWatch Events does not have a direct integration with Slack, so you need a Lambda function as a target to send the notification.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/how-to-set-up-aws-opsworks-stacks-auto-healing-notifications-in-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/how-to-set-up-aws-opsworks-stacks-auto-healing-notifications-in-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)

Incorrect options:

Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-scaling. Configure as target a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel - auto-scaling does not correspond to auto-healing events.

Subscribe OpsWorks auto-healing notifications to an SNS topic. Subscribe a Lambda function that will send notifications to the Slack channel - OpsWorks does not directly send auto-healing notifications to SNS.

Create a CloudWatch Events rule for aws.opsworks and set the initiated_by field to auto-scaling. Enable Slack integration in CloudWatch Events to send notifications - auto-scaling does not correspond to auto-healing and CloudWatch Events does not have direct integration with Slack.

References:

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/how-to-set-up-aws-opsworks-stacks-auto-healing-notifications-in-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/mt/how-to-set-up-aws-opsworks-stacks-auto-healing-notifications-in-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)

question:
As a Lead DevOps Engineer at an analytics company, you are deploying a global application using a CI/CD pipeline composed of AWS CodeCommit, CodeBuild, CodeDeploy and orchestrated by AWS CodePipeline. Your pipeline is currently in eu-west-1 and you want to extend it to deploy your application to us-east-2. This will require creating a multi-step CodePipeline in that region and invoking it.

How would you implement a solution for this use case?

options.A: At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodeCommit step to push changes to the master branch of another CodeCommit repository in us-east-2. Make the CodePipeline in us-east-2 source CodeCommit
options.B: At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodeDeploy step to deploy the application to the CodePipeline in us-east-2
options.C: At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodePipeline step to invoke the CodePipeline in us-east-2. Ensure that the CodePipeline on us-east-2 has IAM permissions to read artifacts in S3 on eu-west-1
options.D: At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include an S3 step to copy the artifacts used by CodeDeploy to an S3 bucket in us-east-2. Make the CodePipeline in us-east-2 source S3

explanation:
Correct option:

At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include an S3 step to copy the artifacts used by CodeDeploy to an S3 bucket in us-east-2. Make the CodePipeline in us-east-2 source S3

AWS CodePipeline is a continuous delivery service that you can use to model, visualize, and automate the steps required to release your software. You can easily configure the different stages of a software release process. CodePipeline automates the steps required to continuously release software changes.

CodePipeline Overview: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/welcome-introducing.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/welcome-introducing.html)

CodePipeline Key Concepts:

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/concepts.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/concepts.html)

For this use case, you can use a deploy to S3 step to copy the artifacts to another bucket in another region. Then, the CodePipeline in the target region will react to the event and grab the files from that bucket to start the deployment.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/integrations-action-type.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/latest/userguide/integrations-action-type.html)

Incorrect options:

At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodeDeploy step to deploy the application to the CodePipeline in us-east-2 - CodeDeploy cannot deploy to the CodePipeline. Only deploy to EC2, on-premise, Lambda or ECS.

At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodeCommit step to push changes to the master branch of another CodeCommit repository in us-east-2. Make the CodePipeline in us-east-2 source CodeCommit - CodePipeline can source CodeCommit, but cannot push to repositories.

At the end of the pipeline in eu-west-1, include a CodePipeline step to invoke the CodePipeline in us-east-2. Ensure that the CodePipeline on us-east-2 has IAM permissions to read artifacts in S3 on eu-west-1 - CodePipeline cannot directly invoke another CodePipeline.

question:
The DevOps team at a business travel solutions company wants to use CodeDeploy to ensure zero downtime during deployments through rolling updates. The team wants to deploy the company's core web application to a set of EC2 instances running behind an Application Load Balancer. The team wants the deployment to be gradual and to automatically rollback in case of a failed deployment, which is determined if the application cannot pass health checks.

As a DevOps engineer, which of the following would you recommend for this use case?

options.A: In the AfterInstall hook in appspec.yml, verify that the service is working correctly. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures. In case the hook fails, CodeDeploy will rollback
options.B: Integrate CodeDeploy with the Application Load Balancer. In case the Application Load Balancer fails the health checks on the instances where the new version was deployed, it will notify CodeDeploy. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures
options.C: In the ValidateService hook in appspec.yml, verify that the service is working correctly. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures. In case the hook fails, CodeDeploy will rollback
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule on CodeDeploy to invoke a Lambda function on each per-instance deployment. The Lambda function will try the health check and if it fails, it will stop the deployment using StopDeployment API and then start a new deployment of the previous version using CreateDeployment API

explanation:
Correct option:

In the ValidateService hook in appspec.yml, verify that the service is working correctly. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures. In case the hook fails, CodeDeploy will rollback

CodeDeploy is a fully managed service that automates software deployments to services such as Amazon EC2, AWS Fargate, AWS Lambda, and on-premises servers. It makes it easier to release new versions, avoids downtime and manages the complexity of updating applications.

The AppSpec file is used to manage each deployment as a series of lifecycle hooks. During deployment, the CodeDeploy agent executes the defined hooks. If a hook fails, the deployment fails.

The ValidateService hook is the last event in the deployment lifecycle and allows you to verify that the application is working correctly after startup. You can configure CodeDeploy to do automatic rollback if this hook fails.

Sample appspec file: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file.html)

List of Lifecycle Event hooks for EC2 deployment: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html)

Lifecycle Event hooks availability for EC2 deployment and rollback scenarios: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html)

Incorrect options:

Integrate CodeDeploy with the Application Load Balancer. In case the Application Load Balancer fails the health checks on the instances where the new version was deployed, it will notify CodeDeploy. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures - ALB does not directly trigger rollback on CodeDeploy based on health checks.

In the AfterInstall hook in appspec.yml, verify that the service is working correctly. Configure CodeDeploy to rollback on deployment failures. In case the hook fails, CodeDeploy will rollback - AfterInstall occurs before the application is fully running, so it does not properly validate health checks.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule on CodeDeploy to invoke a Lambda function on each per-instance deployment. The Lambda function will try the health check and if it fails, it will stop the deployment using StopDeployment API and then start a new deployment of the previous version using CreateDeployment API - This adds unnecessary complexity, since CodeDeploy already supports automatic rollback.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file.html)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html)

question:
The DevOps team at a leading travel booking services company is using a CloudFormation template to deploy a Lambda function. The Lambda function code is uploaded to S3 in a file named s3://my-bucket/my-lambda-code.zip by CodePipeline after passing all required build checks. CodePipeline invokes the CloudFormation template to deploy the new code. The team has found that although the CloudFormation template runs successfully, the Lambda function is not updated.

As a DevOps engineer, what can you do to quickly fix this problem? (Select three)

options.A: Upload the code each time to a new S3 bucket
options.B: Add a 3 second pause before starting the CloudFormation job. This is an eventual consistency issue due to overwriting PUT
options.C: Enable the SAM Framework option
options.D: Upload the code each time with a different file name in the same bucket
options.E: Clear the Lambda cache with a Custom Job in CodePipeline before the CloudFormation step
options.F: Enable versioning on S3 and provide an S3ObjectVersion key

explanation:
Correct options:

Upload the code each time to a new S3 bucket

Upload the code each time with a different file name in the same bucket

Enable versioning on S3 and provide an S3ObjectVersion key

You can use CloudFormation to deploy and update compute, database, and many other resources in a declarative style that abstracts the complexity of specific APIs. CloudFormation is designed to enable resource lifecycles to be managed in a repeatable, predictable, and secure manner, with automatic rollbacks, state management, and administration across accounts and regions.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/)

The problem here is that CloudFormation does not detect that a new file has been uploaded to S3 unless you change one of these parameters: S3Bucket, S3Key or S3ObjectVersion.

Changes to a deployment package on S3 are not automatically detected during stack updates. To update the function code, you need to change the object key or its version in the template.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-lambda-function-code.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-lambda-function-code.html)

Incorrect options:

Clear the Lambda cache with a Custom Job in CodePipeline before the CloudFormation step - There is no such thing as a Lambda cache.

Add a 3 second pause before starting the CloudFormation job. This is an eventual consistency issue due to overwriting PUT - It is not an eventual consistency issue in this context.

Enable the SAM Framework option - AWS SAM is a framework for building serverless applications, but it would involve rewriting the template, which is not a quick fix.

References:

[https://aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudformation/)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-lambda-function-code.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-lambda-function-code.html)

question:
As a DevOps engineer at an IT company, you have deployed a web application with a health check that currently verifies whether the application is actively running. The application is running on an ASG and the ALB health check integration is enabled. Recently your application has had problems connecting to a backend database and as a result users have experienced problems accessing the site through the faulty instances.

How can you improve the user experience with the least effort?

options.A: Improve the health check so that the return status code corresponds to the connectivity with the database
options.B: Improve the Health Check so that it reports a JSON document that contains the health status of the connectivity to the database. Adjust the ALB health check to search for a specific string in the result using a regular expression
options.C: Migrate the application to Elastic Beanstalk and enable advanced health monitoring
options.D: Include the health check in a Route 53 record so that users passing through the ALB are not routed to unhealthy instances

explanation:
Correct option:

Improve the health check so that the return status code corresponds to the connectivity with the database

Configuring health checks in an Application Load Balancer is key to ensuring that an application works correctly. The ALB considers an instance healthy if it responds with an HTTP code 200. If the instance returns a code outside the 2XX range or does not respond, it is marked unhealthy and stops receiving traffic.

The current problem is that the health check only validates that the application is active, but does not validate critical dependencies such as the database. Therefore, the health check endpoint should be enhanced to fail (for example, return a code other than 2XX) when there is no connectivity to the database. This will allow the ALB to stop sending traffic to faulty instances.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)

Incorrect options:

Migrate the application to Elastic Beanstalk and enable advanced health monitoring - Requires a lot of effort and does not directly solve the problem.

Improve the Health Check so that it reports a JSON document that contains the health status of the connectivity to the database. Adjust the ALB health check to look for a specific string in the result using a regular expression - The ALB does not evaluate body content, only HTTP status codes.

Include the health check in a Route 53 record so that users passing through the ALB are not routed to unhealthy instances - Route 53 does not route at the instance level behind an ALB.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/target-group-health-checks.html)

[https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/implementing-health-checks.pdf](https://d1.awsstatic.com/builderslibrary/pdfs/implementing-health-checks.pdf)

question:
As a Lead DevOps Engineer at an e-commerce company, you want to upgrade the major version of your MySQL database, which is managed by CloudFormation with AWS::RDS::DBInstance and configured in Multi-AZ.

You have a requirement to minimize downtime as much as possible, what steps should you take to achieve this?

options.A: Update the RDS database by changing DBEngineVersion to the next higher version, then run an UpdateStack operation
options.B: Update the RDS database by changing EngineVersion to the next higher version, then run an UpdateStack operation
options.C: Create an RDS Read Replica in a CloudFormation template by specifying SourceDBInstanceIdentifier and wait for it to be created. Then update the EngineVersion of the Read Replica to the next higher version. Then promote the Read Replica and use it as the new main database
options.D: Create an RDS Read Replica in a CloudFormation template by specifying SourceDBInstanceIdentifier and wait for it to be created. Then update DBEngineVersion of the Read Replica to the next higher version. Then promote the Read Replica and use it as the new main database

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an RDS Read Replica in a CloudFormation template by specifying SourceDBInstanceIdentifier and wait for it to be created. Then update the EngineVersion of the Read Replica to the next higher version. Then promote the Read Replica and use it as the new main database

You can minimize downtime during an upgrade by using a rolling upgrade strategy with read replicas. Amazon RDS does not fully automate this process, but you can achieve this by creating a read replica, updating its EngineVersion, promoting it, and redirecting traffic to it.

If you want to create a Read Replica, you must specify the SourceDBInstanceIdentifier property, which indicates that the instance is a replica.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-rds-database-instance.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-properties-rds-database-instance.html)

You should consider that Multi-AZ does not eliminate downtime during a major version upgrade. Multi-AZ is designed for high availability, not to avoid downtime in upgrades, since operations like mysql_upgrade require interruption.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/best-practices-for-upgrading-amazon-rds-for-mysql-and-amazon-rds-for-mariadb/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/database/best-practices-for-upgrading-amazon-rds-for-mysql-and-amazon-rds-for-mariadb/)

Incorrect options:

Create an RDS Read Replica in a CloudFormation template by specifying SourceDBInstanceIdentifier and wait for it to be created. Then update DBEngineVersion of the Read Replica to the next higher version. Then promote the Read Replica and use it as the new primary database - The correct property is EngineVersion, not DBEngineVersion.

Update the RDS database by changing EngineVersion to the next higher version, then run an UpdateStack operation - Changing EngineVersion in CloudFormation creates a new resource replacing the existing one, which involves downtime.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-update-behaviors.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/using-cfn-updating-stacks-update-behaviors.html)

Update the RDS database by changing DBEngineVersion to the next higher version, then running an UpdateStack operation - The DBEngineVersion property does not exist, so it is incorrect.
