question:
The DevOps team at your company is using CodeDeploy to deploy new versions of a Lambda function after it has passed CodeBuild via CodePipeline. Before deploying, CodePipeline has a step that optionally initiates a file restructure to an S3 bucket that is backward compatible. This restructuring is done using a Step Function execution that invokes a task in Fargate. The new Lambda function cannot function until the restructuring task has been completely completed.

As a DevOps engineer, how can you ensure that no traffic is sent to the new Lambda function until the task is complete?

options.A: Enable Canary Deployment in CodeDeploy so that only a fraction of the service is served by the new Lambda function while the restructure occurs
options.B: In your appspec.yml file, include an AfterAllowTraffic hook that verifies the completion of the Step Function execution
options.C: In your appspec.yml file, include a BeforeAllowTraffic hook that verifies the completion of the Step Function execution
options.D: Include an extra step in the Step Function to notify CodeDeploy of the completion of the restructure and begin sending traffic to the new Lambda function

explanation:
Correct option:

In your appspec.yml file, include a BeforeAllowTraffic hook that verifies the completion of the Step Function execution

The AppSpec file is used to manage each deployment as a series of lifecycle hooks. In Lambda deployments, CodeDeploy uses these hooks to decide when to switch traffic to the new version.

The BeforeAllowTraffic hook is executed before traffic is routed to the new version of the Lambda function. This allows external conditions to be validated before exposing the new version.

For this case, this hook should be used to verify that the Step Functions execution (restructure to S3) has completely finished before allowing traffic.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-example.html#appspec-file-example-lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-example.html#appspec-file-example-lambda)

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html#appspec-hooks-lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html#appspec-hooks-lambda)

Incorrect options:

In your appspec.yml file, include an AfterAllowTraffic hook that verifies the completion of the Step Function execution - At this point the traffic has already been redirected, so it does not meet the requirement.

Enable Canary Deployment in CodeDeploy so that only a fraction of the service is served by the new Lambda function while the restructure occurs - This would send traffic before the process finishes.

Include an extra step in the Step Function to notify CodeDeploy of the completion of the restructure and begin sending traffic to the new Lambda function - There is no direct mechanism for Step Functions to control traffic switching in CodeDeploy.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-example.html#appspec-file-example-lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-example.html#appspec-file-example-lambda)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html#appspec-hooks-lambda](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/reference-appspec-file-structure-hooks.html#appspec-hooks-lambda)

question:
An IT company is deploying a Python Flask-based application and wants to ensure that it has a base AMI that contains the necessary runtime as well as operating system patches. That AMI will be referenced programmatically from all regions in your account in a scalable manner. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

Which of the following options would you recommend for this use case? (Select two)

options.A: Store the AMI ID in the SSM Parameter Store in one region, and have a Lambda function that copies the AMI to all other regions, and stores the corresponding ID in SSM. Use the same parameter name to reuse between regions
options.B: Create an SSM Automation document to create the AMI in a repeatable manner
options.C: Use AWS Inspector to create a patched AMI using the latest working AMI
options.D: Use AWS Lambda to create a patched AMI using the latest working AMI
options.E: Store the AMI ID in the SSM Parameter Store in a region, and create a Step Function that copies the AMI ID value to other regions. Use the same parameter name to reuse between regions

explanation:
Correct options:

Create an SSM Automation document to create the AMI in a repeatable manner

An SSM Automation document defines the actions that Systems Manager performs on managed instances and other AWS resources when an automation is run. It contains sequential steps that allow you to build repeatable workflows.

You can use Systems Manager along with maintenance windows to automate the creation of AMIs periodically and consistently for both Windows and Linux.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/ec2-systems-manager-ami-automation/](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/ec2-systems-manager-ami-automation/)

Store the AMI ID in the SSM Parameter Store in one region, and have a Lambda function that copies the AMI to all other regions, and stores the corresponding ID in SSM. Use the same parameter name to reuse between regions

The ID of an AMI is region-specific, so the AMI must be copied between regions. Each region will have a different ID, but you can use the same parameter name in the SSM Parameter Store for easy programmatic consumption.

Incorrect options:

Store the AMI ID in the SSM Parameter Store in a region, and create a Step Function that copies the AMI ID value to other regions. Use the same parameter name to reuse between regions - This only copies the ID, but not the AMI. The AMI would continue to exist in a single region.

Use AWS Inspector to create a patched AMI using the latest working AMI - Inspector is used for vulnerability scanning, not creating AMIs.

Use AWS Lambda to create a patched AMI using the latest working AMI - Lambda is not used to create AMIs in this way.

References:

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/automation-documents.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/automation-documents.html)

[https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/ec2-systems-manager-ami-automation/](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/ec2-systems-manager-ami-automation/)

question:
A retail company is finalizing its migration to AWS and realizes that while some employees have passed the AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional certification and are familiar with AWS, others are still getting started and haven't even earned Associate-level certifications. The company has established specific architectural and tagging rules for internal resources and wants to minimize the risk of entry-level employees creating non-compliant resources.

As a DevOps engineer, how would you implement this requirement while allowing employees to create the resources they need?

options.A: Place entry-level IAM users in a group and create an IAM policy that requires conditional approvals from senior DevOps engineers when creating resources. Connect an SNS topic to the IAM approval channel
options.B: Define common architectures as CloudFormation templates. Place IAM users in a beginner group and only allow them to launch stacks from those CloudFormation templates, restricting any write access to other services
options.C: Define common architectures as CloudFormation templates. Create Service Catalog stacks from these templates and ensure tagging is correctly configured. Place IAM users in a beginner group and only allow them to launch stacks from Service Catalog, restricting any write access to other services
options.D: Create custom AWS Config rules that verify compliance for company resources using a Lambda function. Update the Lambda function over time as the company improves its rules. Give IAM users full access to AWS

explanation:
Correct option:

Define common architectures as CloudFormation templates. Create Service Catalog stacks from these templates and ensure tagging is correctly configured. Place IAM users in a beginner group and only allow them to launch stacks from Service Catalog, restricting any write access to other services

AWS Service Catalog allows administrators to create, manage, and distribute catalogs of approved products to end users. These users can launch resources in a controlled manner using predefined templates that comply with organizational policies.

A product in Service Catalog is an application or service typically defined using CloudFormation templates. Administrators control which users can launch these products, ensuring compliance with architecture and labeling standards.

For this case, Service Catalog is the right solution because it allows you to restrict novice users to launching only approved configurations without giving them direct access to create arbitrary resources.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicecatalog/latest/adminguide/introduction.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/servicecatalog/latest/adminguide/introduction.html)

Incorrect options:

Define common architectures as CloudFormation templates. Place IAM users in a beginner group and only allow them to launch stacks from those CloudFormation templates, restricting any write access to other services - CloudFormation does not allow you to restrict which templates users can use via IAM.

Create custom AWS Config rules that verify compliance for company resources using a Lambda function. Update the Lambda function over time as the company improves its rules. Give IAM users full access to AWS - AWS Config only detects non-compliance, it does not prevent it.

Place entry-level IAM users in a group and create an IAM policy that requires conditional approvals from senior DevOps engineers when creating resources. Connect an SNS topic to the IAM approval channel - IAM does not support conditional approval flows.

question:
A gaming company wants to be able to receive near real-time notifications when the DeleteTable API call is invoked in DynamoDB.

As a DevOps engineer in the company, how would you implement this at the lowest possible cost?

options.A: Send CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs and use a Lambda function that is triggered by a CloudWatch Logs metrics filter. Use the Lambda function to send an SNS notification
options.B: Enable CloudTrail. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to trace an AWS API call via CloudTrail and use SNS as a target
options.C: Create a CloudTrail event filter and connect it to a Lambda function. Use the Lambda function to send an SNS notification
options.D: Enable DynamoDB Streams and use a Lambda function consuming the stream. Send alerts to SNS when a record is deleted

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable CloudTrail. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to trace an AWS API call via CloudTrail and use SNS as a target

CloudTrail provides visibility into the activity in your AWS account by recording actions taken. It includes information such as who made the request, what service was used, what action was executed, and its parameters.

To detect specific API calls like DeleteTable, you can use CloudWatch Events (EventBridge) with the "AWS API Call via CloudTrail" pattern. This allows you to react in near real time to events recorded by CloudTrail and send notifications directly to SNS.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)

Incorrect options:

Enable DynamoDB Streams and use a Lambda function consuming the stream. Send alerts to SNS when a record is deleted - DynamoDB Streams only captures item-level changes, not API calls like DeleteTable.

Send CloudTrail logs to CloudWatch Logs and use a Lambda function that is triggered by a CloudWatch Logs metrics filter. Use the Lambda function to send an SNS notification - It works but involves greater cost and complexity when processing all the logs.

Create a CloudTrail event filter and connect it to a Lambda function. Use the Lambda function to send an SNS notification - CloudTrail does not allow you to directly connect filtered events to Lambda.

References:

[https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/Create-CloudWatch-Events-CloudTrail-Rule.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/Create-CloudWatch-Events-CloudTrail-Rule.html)

question:
A retail company uses open-source Jenkins in its on-premise infrastructure to perform CI/CD. You have decided to migrate to AWS and take advantage of the elasticity properties of the cloud for more efficient workloads. You need to ensure that your Jenkins configuration is highly available, fault tolerant, and also elastic to run builds. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build the most cost-effective solution for this requirement.

Which of the following solutions would you recommend?

options.A: Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in multiple AZs. Enable the CodeBuild plugin for Jenkins so that builds run as CodeBuild builds
options.B: Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in a single AZ, managed by an Auto Scaling Group. Enable the CodeBuild plugin for Jenkins so that builds run as CodeBuild builds
options.C: Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in multiple AZs. Create an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances that act as Jenkins slaves. Configure Jenkins to run builds on these slaves
options.D: Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in a single AZ, managed by an Auto Scaling Group. Configure Jenkins to run builds on these slaves

explanation:
Correct option:

Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in multiple AZs. Enable the CodeBuild plugin for Jenkins so that builds run as CodeBuild builds

On AWS, an application like Jenkins must be designed for high availability by distributing instances across multiple AZs and using a load balancer. This ensures fault tolerance.

Using the AWS CodeBuild plugin allows Jenkins jobs to run on CodeBuild instead of their own nodes. This eliminates the need to manage infrastructure for builds, providing full elasticity and optimizing costs, since you only pay for the execution time.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/setting-up-a-ci-cd-pipeline-by-integrating-jenkins-with-aws-codebuild-and-aws-codedeploy/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/setting-up-a-ci-cd-pipeline-by-integrating-jenkins-with-aws-codebuild-and-aws-codedeploy/)

Incorrect options:

Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in a single AZ, managed by an Auto Scaling Group. Enable the CodeBuild plugin for Jenkins so that builds run as CodeBuild builds - Does not comply with high availability as it is in a single AZ.

Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in multiple AZs. Create an Auto Scaling Group of EC2 instances that act as Jenkins slaves. Configure Jenkins to run builds on these slaves - This requires managing build infrastructure, increasing costs and complexity.

Deploy Jenkins as a multi-master configuration in a single AZ, managed by an Auto Scaling Group. Configure Jenkins to run builds on these slaves - It is not highly available and also involves managing build infrastructure.

question:
A Big Data analytics company has deployed a streaming processing application using KCL to read records from Kinesis Data Streams configured with multiple shards. The application is running on an EC2 instance. It seems that the consuming application is lagging under a large load and therefore the logs are not processed in time and are eventually lost from the stream.

As a DevOps engineer, you have been tasked with improving the reliability of this application with minimal changes, what would you do? (Select two)

options.A: Increase the number of shards in Kinesis to increase throughput
options.B: Run the application in an Auto Scaling Group and scale based on the CloudWatch MillisBehindLatest metric
options.C: Reduce the number of shards in Kinesis to reduce the load
options.D: Increase stream data retention period
options.E: Migrate the application to AWS Lambda

explanation:
Correct options:

Run the application in an Auto Scaling Group and scale based on the CloudWatch MillisBehindLatest metric

In a typical Kinesis Data Streams architecture, you have producers that continuously send data to Kinesis Data Streams, and consumers process the data in real time. Consumers (such as a custom application running on Amazon EC2 or an Amazon Kinesis Data Firehose delivery stream) can store their results using an AWS service such as Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon Redshift, or Amazon S3.

via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/key-concepts.html

The Kinesis Client Library (KCL) ensures that for each shard there is a log processor running and processing that shard. The library also simplifies reading data from the stream. The Kinesis Client Library uses an Amazon DynamoDB table to store control data.

For the given case, you need to run KCL on multiple EC2 instances behind an Auto Scaling Group. Running more KCL processes is the key here, and for this we need an Auto Scaling Group based on the MillisBehindLatest metric, which represents the time that the current iterator is behind the most recent record in the shard. The Kinesis Client Library publishes custom metrics to Amazon CloudWatch on your behalf, using your KCL application name as the namespace.

via - https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/monitoring-with-kcl.html

Increase stream data retention period

The retention period is the time during which data records remain accessible after being added to the stream. The default retention period is 24 hours. To prevent records from being lost, it is advisable to increase the retention time and allow more margin for processing them.

Incorrect options:

Migrate the application to AWS Lambda - It will not help with processing time, since the same processing code would run on either EC2 or Lambda.

Increasing the number of shards in Kinesis to increase throughput - It can increase the total throughput of the stream, but does not directly impact processing performance if there is currently only one KCL process running.

Decrease the number of shards in Kinesis to reduce load - It would reduce throughput and would not improve the performance of the consuming application.

References:

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/key-concepts.html

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/streams/latest/dev/monitoring-with-kcl.html

question:
A multinational company has defined labeling guidelines and standards for all of its resources in AWS and wants to create a dashboard to visualize the compliance of all resources with the ability to find non-compliant resources. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to develop a solution for this requirement.

Which of the following options would you suggest to solve this use case?

options.A: Use SSM to track resource groups without tags. Export that data using SSM Inventory to S3 and build a dashboard in QuickSight
options.B: Use AWS Service Catalog to get an inventory of all the resources in your account. Use the integrated dashboard to track compliance
options.C: Use AWS Config to track resources in your account. Use SNS to send changes to a Lambda function that writes to S3. Create a QuickSight dashboard on that data
options.D: Trace all resources with AWS CloudTrail. Export data to S3 and create a dashboard in QuickSight

explanation:
Correct option:

Use AWS Config to track resources in your account. Use SNS to send changes to a Lambda function that writes to S3. Create a QuickSight dashboard on that data

AWS Config is a fully managed service that provides resource inventory, configuration history, and change notifications. Allows you to evaluate compliance using rules, including tagging validations.

You can use managed rules like required-tags to validate tags. Configuration changes can be sent to SNS and processed with Lambda to be stored in S3 and then displayed in QuickSight.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/config/](https://aws.amazon.com/config/)

Incorrect options:

Use AWS Service Catalog to get an inventory of all the resources in your account. Use the integrated dashboard to track compliance - Service Catalog does not provide complete resource inventory.

Use SSM to track resource groups without tags. Export that data using SSM Inventory to S3 and build a dashboard in QuickSight - SSM Inventory is focused on instances and not all resources.

Trace all resources with AWS CloudTrail. Export data to S3 and create a dashboard in QuickSight - CloudTrail records API calls, not resource inventory.

question:
A social media company has multiple EC2 instances that are behind an Auto Scaling group (ASG) and you would like to recover all log files within these instances before they are terminated. You would also like to build a metadata index of all the log files so that you can efficiently find them by instance id and date range.

As a DevOps Engineer, which of the following options would you recommend to address the given requirements? (Select three)

options.A: Create a termination hook for your ASG and create a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function must invoke an SSM Run Command to send the log files from the EC2 instance to CloudWatch Logs. Create a log subscription to send to Firehose and then to S3
options.B: Create a DynamoDB table with a primary key of instance-id and a sort key of datetime
options.C: Create a termination hook for your ASG and create a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function must invoke an SSM Run Command to send the log files from the EC2 instance to S3
options.D: Create a Lambda function that is triggered by S3 events for PUT operations. Write to DynamoDB table
options.E: Create a Lambda function that is triggered by CloudWatch Events for PUT operations. Write to DynamoDB table
options.F: Create a DynamoDB table with a primary key of datetime and a sort key of instance-id

explanation:
Correct options:

Create a termination hook for your ASG and create a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function must invoke an SSM Run Command to send the log files from the EC2 instance to S3

Lifecycle hooks allow you to perform custom actions by pausing instances while an ASG launches or terminates them. For example, when a scale-in event occurs, the instance that is to be terminated first is unregistered from the load balancer (if the Auto Scaling group is being used with Elastic Load Balancing). Then, a lifecycle hook pauses the instance before it is terminated. While the instance is in a standby state, you can, for example, connect to the instance and download logs or other data before the instance is completely terminated.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

You can use a CloudWatch Events rule to invoke a Lambda function when a lifecycle action occurs. The Lambda function is invoked when Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling sends an event for a lifecycle action to CloudWatch Events. The event contains information about the instance being launched or terminated and a token that you can use to control the lifecycle action. Finally, the Lambda function can invoke an SSM Run Command to send the log files from the EC2 instance to S3. SSM Run Command allows you to remotely and securely manage the configuration of your managed instances.

Create a Lambda function that is triggered by S3 events for PUT operations. Write to DynamoDB table

You can use Lambda to process event notifications from Amazon Simple Storage Service. Amazon S3 can send an event to a Lambda function when an object is created or deleted. Amazon S3 invokes your function asynchronously with an event that contains details about the object. The Lambda will subsequently write the event information to the DynamoDB table.

Create a DynamoDB table with a primary key of instance-id and a sort key of datetime

When you create a DynamoDB table, in addition to the table name, you must specify the primary key. The primary key uniquely identifies each item in the table, so no two items can have the same key. For the given use case, you need to set the primary key as a combination of instance-id partition key and datetime sort key, since we are looking for a specific instance id and date range.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.CoreComponents.html#HowItWorks.CoreComponents.PrimaryKey](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.CoreComponents.html#HowItWorks.CoreComponents.PrimaryKey)

Incorrect options:Create a termination hook for your ASG and create a CloudWatch Events rule to trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function must invoke an SSM Run Command to send the log files from the EC2 instance to CloudWatch Logs. Create a log subscription to send to Firehose and then to S3 - We should send the log files to S3 directly from the EC2 instance instead of through CloudWatch, since we are doing a one-time export of them. CloudWatch Logs is a good solution for streaming logs as they are generated.

Create a Lambda function that is triggered by CloudWatch Events for PUT operations. Write to DynamoDB table - We need the Lambda function to be triggered by S3 events instead of CloudWatch Events, since for CloudWatch Events we would also need to have a CloudTrail trail recording actions in the specific S3 bucket.

Create a DynamoDB table with a primary key of datetime and a sort key of instance-id - As mentioned above, since the use case requires searching by a specific instance id and a date range, you should use instance-id as the Partition Key and datetime as the Sort Key. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/autoscaling/ec2/userguide/lifecycle-hooks.html?utm_source=chatgpt.com)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.CoreComponents.html#HowItWorks.CoreComponents.PrimaryKey](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/HowItWorks.CoreComponents.html#HowItWorks.CoreComponents.PrimaryKey)

question:
A Big Data analytics company is operating a distributed Cassandra cluster on EC2. Each instance in the cluster must have a list of the IPs of all other instances to function correctly, stored in a configuration file. As a DevOps Engineer in the company, you would like the solution to adapt automatically when new EC2 instances join the cluster, or when some EC2 instances are terminated.

Which of the following solutions would you recommend for the given requirement?

options.A: Manage EC2 instances using an Auto Scaling Group. Include a lifecycle hook for the pending and termination status of the instance that will trigger a user-data script on the EC2 instance. The script executes a call to the EC2 DescribeInstances API and updates the configuration file locally
options.B: Manage EC2 instances using OpsWorks. Include a Chef cookbook in the configure lifecycle event which will update the configuration file accordingly
options.C: Manage EC2 instances using an Auto Scaling Group. Include a lifecycle hook for the pending and termination status of the instance that will trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function will issue a call to the EC2 DescribeInstances API and update the configuration file over SSH
options.D: Manage EC2 instances using OpsWorks. Include a Chef cookbook in the lifecycle setup event which will update the configuration file accordingly

explanation:
Correct option:

Manage EC2 instances using OpsWorks. Include a Chef cookbook in the configure lifecycle event which will update the configuration file accordingly

AWS OpsWorks is a configuration management service that provides managed Chef and Puppet instances. Chef and Puppet are automation platforms that allow you to use code to automate your server configurations. OpsWorks allows you to use Chef and Puppet to automate how servers are configured, deployed, and managed across your Amazon EC2 instances or on-premises computing environments.

A stack is the highest-level entity in AWS OpsWorks Stacks. Represents a set of instances that you want to manage collectively, typically because they have a common purpose such as serving PHP applications. In addition to serving as a container, a stack handles tasks that apply to the group of instances as a whole, such as managing applications and cookbooks.

Each stack contains one or more layers, each of which represents a component of the stack, such as a load balancer or a set of application servers. Each layer has a set of five lifecycle events, each with an associated set of layer-specific recipes. When an event occurs on an instance of the layer, AWS OpsWorks Stacks automatically runs the appropriate set of recipes.

The lifecycle hook that runs on ALL instances, every time one instance wakes up or another goes down, is the configure hook. Therefore, this option is the best for the given use case.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opsworks/latest/userguide/workingcookbook-events.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/opsworks/latest/userguide/workingcookbook-events.html)

Incorrect options:

Manage EC2 instances using OpsWorks. Include a Chef cookbook in the lifecycle setup event that will update the configuration file accordingly - As mentioned earlier in the explanation, the setup hook is only used when an instance is created for the first time, so this option is incorrect.

Manage EC2 instances using an Auto Scaling Group. Include a lifecycle hook for the pending and termination status of the instance that will trigger an AWS Lambda function. The Lambda function will issue a call to the EC2 DescribeInstances API and update the configuration file over SSH - Lifecycle hooks in Auto Scaling Groups may seem like a good idea at first, but using AWS Lambda for this solution is not practical, as SSHing to the instance from Lambda will not work.

Manage EC2 instances using an Auto Scaling Group. Include a lifecycle hook for instance pending and termination status that will trigger a user-data script on EC2 instances. The script executes a call to the EC2 DescribeInstances API and updates the configuration file locally - User-data scripts in EC2 only run on the first boot of the instance, so this option acts only as a distractor.

question:
The development team at a social media company is using AWS CodeCommit to store code. As a Lead DevOps Engineer in the company, you have defined a company-level rule that the team should not be able to push to the master branch. You've added all developers in an IAM developers group and attached the AWS managed policy arn:aws:iam::aws:policy/AWSCodeCommitPowerUser to the group. This policy provides full access to AWS CodeCommit repositories but does not allow deletion of repositories, however your developers can still push to the master branch.

How should you prevent developers from pushing to the master branch?

options.A: Modify the AWS Managed IAM policy attached to the group to Deny codecommit:GitPush with a condition on the master branch
options.B: Add a new IAM policy attached to the group for Deny codecommit:GitPush with a condition on the master branch
options.C: Include a git commit pre-hook that invokes a Lambda function and checks if the push is made to master
options.D: Include a CodeCommit repository policy in each repository with an explicit Deny for codecommit:GitPush

explanation:
Correct option:

Add a new IAM policy attached to the group for Deny codecommit:GitPush with a condition on the master branch

Any user of a CodeCommit repository who has sufficient permissions to push to the repository can contribute to any branch in that repository. You can configure a branch so that only some users of the repository can push or merge code to that branch. For example, you might want to configure a branch used for production code so that only a subset of senior developers can push or merge changes to that branch. Other developers can still pull from the branch, create their own branches, and create pull requests, but they cannot push or merge changes to that branch. You can configure this access by creating a conditional policy that uses a context key for one or more branches in IAM.

For the given use case, you need to add an additional policy with an explicit Deny. Note that an Explicit Deny always takes priority over anything else.

Limit pushes and merges to branches in AWS CodeCommit: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html)

Incorrect options:

Include a CodeCommit repository policy in each repository with an explicit Deny for codecommit:GitPush - This option has been added as a distractor since CodeCommit repository policies do not exist.

Modify the AWS Managed IAM policy attached to the group for Deny codecommit:GitPush with a condition on the master branch - You cannot modify an AWS Managed IAM policy, so this option is incorrect.

Include a git commit pre-hook that invokes a Lambda function and checks if the push is made to master - Although it would be interesting, CodeCommit does not yet have a pre-hook functionality to integrate with Lambda.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codecommit/latest/userguide/how-to-conditional-branch.html)

question:
As a DevOps Engineer at a social media company, you've implemented a CI/CD pipeline that takes code from a CodeCommit repository, builds it using CodeBuild using instructions in a local Dockerfile, and then pushes it to ECR at 123456789.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-web-app. The last step in your CI/CD pipeline is to deploy the application to your ECS cluster. It seems that while you do this, the application is only partially updated on some ECS instances that are running an older version of your image. You've found that terminating the instance or clearing the local Docker cache fixes the problem, but you'd like to implement something more robust that provides visibility and identification to track where container images are deployed.

How should you implement a solution to address this problem?

options.A: When creating a new task definition for your ECS service, make sure to add the latest tag to the full image name so that ECS gets the correct image every time
options.B: When creating a new task definition for your ECS service, make sure to add the sha256 hash to the full image name so that ECS gets the correct image every time
options.C: After the deployment step in CodePipeline finishes, include a Custom Step using a Lambda function that triggers an SSM Run Command. That command will clear the local Docker cache and stop the task
options.D: After the deployment step in CodePipeline finishes, include a Custom Step using a Lambda function that triggers an AWS Lambda function. That function will SSH to your ECS instances and clear the local Docker cache and stop the task

explanation:
Correct option:

When creating a new task definition for your ECS service, make sure to add the sha256 hash to the full image name so that ECS gets the correct image every time

Amazon ECS SHA Tracking provides visibility and identification to track where container images are deployed using task state change events broadcast to CloudWatch Events. SHA Tracking is integrated with Amazon ECR, ECS, Fargate, and CloudWatch Events to support application lifecycle operations. You can use the IMAGEID property, which is the SHA digest for the Docker image used to start the container.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/container-metadata.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/container-metadata.html)

The problem here is that the ECS instances do not detect that a newer version of the image is available, because the name 123456789.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-web-app is reused. Therefore, by specifying the sha256 for example: aws_account_id.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-web-app@sha256:94afd1f2e64d908bc90dbca0035a5b567EXAMPLE, we are assured that newer versions of the Docker image will have a different hash value and therefore the ECS cluster you will always get the newest image at the end of our CI/CD pipeline.

Incorrect options:

After the deployment step in CodePipeline finishes, include a Custom Step using a Lambda function that triggers an SSM Run Command. That command will clear the local Docker cache and stop the task - SSM Run Command allows you to remotely and securely manage the configuration of your managed instances. A managed instance is any EC2 instance or on-premises machine in your hybrid environment that has been configured for Systems Manager. SSM Run Command might work, but it's not an elegant solution.

After the deployment step in CodePipeline finishes, include a Custom Step using a Lambda function that triggers an AWS Lambda function. That function will SSH to your ECS instances and clear the local Docker cache and stop the task - Lambda functions cannot SSH to EC2 instances, so this option is incorrect.

When creating a new task definition for your ECS service, make sure to add the latest tag to the full name of the image so that ECS gets the correct image every time - Adding the latest tag won't help because 123456789.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-web-app is the same as 123456789.dkr.ecr.region.amazonaws.com/my-web-app:latest. The latest tag cannot provide visibility and identification to track where container images are deployed.

REFERENCES

[https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2019/10/amazon-ecs-now-supports-ecs-image-sha-tracking/](https://aws.amazon.com/about-aws/whats-new/2019/10/amazon-ecs-now-supports-ecs-image-sha-tracking/)

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/container-metadata.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonECS/latest/developerguide/container-metadata.html)

question:
A financial services company has a solution in place to track all API calls made by users, applications, and within the AWS account. Recently, you experienced a hack and were able to find among the logs that some compromised API calls were made. The company wants to know with 100% certainty that the log files represent the correct sequence of events and that they have not been altered. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

Which of the following options would you suggest as the most effective solution?

options.A: Enable AWS account configuration tracking using AWS Config. Deliver the logs to an S3 bucket and choose a lifecycle policy that immediately archives the files to Glacier. Implement a Glacier Vault Lock policy
options.B: Enable API call logging using AWS CloudTrail. Deliver the logs to an S3 bucket and choose a lifecycle policy that immediately archives the files to Glacier. Implement a Glacier Vault Lock policy
options.C: Enable API call logging using AWS CloudTrail. Deliver the logs to an S3 bucket, and use the log integrity check API call to verify the log file
options.D: Enable AWS account configuration tracking using AWS Config. Deliver configuration logs to S3 and use the Log Integrity Check API to verify the log files

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable API call logging using AWS CloudTrail. Deliver the logs to an S3 bucket, and use the log integrity check API call to verify the log file

CloudTrail provides visibility into user activity by recording actions taken in your account. CloudTrail records important information about each action, including who made the request, the services used, the actions executed, the parameters of the actions, and the response elements returned by the AWS service. This information helps you track changes to your AWS resources and troubleshoot operational issues.

How CloudTrail Works: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)

To determine whether a log file was modified, deleted, or remains unchanged after CloudTrail delivered it, you can use CloudTrail log file integrity validation. This functionality is built using industry standard algorithms: SHA-256 for hashing and SHA-256 with RSA for digital signing.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-intro.html)

For the given use case, to track API calls made within your account, you need to use AWS CloudTrail. Then, the correct way to verify the integrity of the logs is to use the CloudTrail validate-logs command.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-cli.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/awscloudtrail/latest/userguide/cloudtrail-log-file-validation-cli.html)

Incorrect options:

Enable API call logging using AWS CloudTrail. Deliver the logs to an S3 bucket and choose a lifecycle policy that immediately archives the files to Glacier. Implement a Glacier Vault Lock Policy - S3 Glacier Vault Lock allows you to implement and enforce compliance controls for individual S3 Glacier vaults using a vault lock policy. You can specify controls such as “write once read many” (WORM) in a vault lock policy and lock the policy against future edits. Once locked, the policy can no longer be modified. Please note that while having a Glacier Vault Lock policy can help ensure that files cannot be altered, it does not provide us with end-to-end assurance that CloudTrail actually produced those files nor does it allow us to compare them against a hash to ensure that they remain unchanged.

Enable AWS account configuration tracking using AWS Config. Deliver configuration logs to S3 and use the Log Integrity Check API to verify the log files - AWS Config is used to track resource configuration over time. Although Config has integration with CloudTrail to show who made API calls, Config alone will not give us the information about who made the API calls.Enable AWS account configuration tracking using AWS Config. Implement a Glacier Vault Lock Policy - AWS Config is used to track resource configuration over time. Although Config has integration with CloudTrail to show who made API calls, Config alone will not give us the information of who made the API calls. Note that while having a Glacier Vault Lock policy can help ensure that files cannot be altered, it does not provide end-to-end assurance that CloudTrail actually produced those files nor does it allow you to check them against a hash to ensure they remain unchanged.

question:
A multinational retail company is in the process of capturing its entire infrastructure as code using CloudFormation. The infrastructure inventory is large and will contain a network stack, an application stack, a data stack, and so on. Some teams are ready to move forward with the process while others are lagging, and there is a desire to keep the entire infrastructure version controlled.

The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this use case. How would you implement it?

options.A: Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Create a master stack that contains all other stacks as a nested template. Deploy the master template using CloudFormation every time a nested stack template is updated in version control
options.B: Create a master template that contains all the stacks in your infrastructure. Collaborate on that template using pull requests and merges to the master branch in your code repository. Deploy the master template every time it is updated
options.C: Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Deploy them using CloudFormation as they are ready. Use outputs and exports to reference values ​​in the stacks. Keep each file separately in a version-controlled repository
options.D: Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Create a master stack that contains all other stacks as nested templates. Deploy the master template once using CloudFormation and then update the individually nested stacks as new CloudFormation code is created

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Deploy them using CloudFormation as they are ready. Use outputs and exports to reference values ​​in the stacks. Keep each file separately in a version-controlled repository

When using CloudFormation, you work with templates and stacks. You create templates to describe your AWS resources and their properties. When you use AWS CloudFormation, you manage related resources as a single unit called a stack. You create, update, and delete a collection of resources by creating, updating, and deleting stacks. All resources in a stack are defined by the stack's CloudFormation template.

In CloudFormation, the best practice is to separate stacks into individual, separate logical components that have dependencies on each other. To link these dependencies, it is best to use Exports and Imports. Each individual CloudFormation template must be a separate file.

CloudFormation best practices: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#cross-stack](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#cross-stack)

Incorrect options:

Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Create a master stack that contains all other stacks as a nested template. Deploy the master template using CloudFormation every time a nested stack template is updated in version control

Create a template per logical element of your infrastructure. Create a master stack that contains all other stacks as a nested template. Deploy the master template once using CloudFormation and then update the individually nested stacks as new CloudFormation code is created

The problem with both options is that different teams are working on different parts of the infrastructure with their own timelines, so it is difficult to combine all elements of the infrastructure into a single master template. It is much better to have one template per logical infrastructure element that is owned by the corresponding team and then use outputs and exports to reference values ​​in the stacks. Nested Stacks can be useful if a component configuration (such as a Load Balancer) can be reused across many stacks.

Create a master template that contains all the stacks in your infrastructure. Collaborate on that template using pull requests and merges to the master branch in your code repository. Deploy the master template every time it is updated - Using outputs and exports for individual templates is much better than collaborating through pull requests at the code repository level. Using individual templates gives ownership to the contributing team to ensure that CloudFormation templates are always functional and ready to be referenced in other stacks.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/cfn-whatis-concepts.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/cfn-whatis-concepts.html)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#cross-stack](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html#cross-stack)

question:
A cybersecurity company has detected a possible exposure of its own AWS account credentials being published in public GitHub repositories. The company wants to implement a workflow to be alerted if credentials are leaked, generate a report of all API calls recently made using those credentials, and disable the credentials. The entire workflow execution must be auditable.

The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a robust solution for this requirement. Which of the following options would you implement?

options.A: Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED in the Health service. Trigger a Lambda function that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail and SNS to achieve the desired requirements
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED on the CloudTrail service. Trigger a Step Function workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED in the Health service. Trigger a Step Function workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED on the CloudTrail service. Trigger a Lambda workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED in the Health service. Trigger a Step Function workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements

Step Functions is a fully managed service that makes it easy to coordinate distributed application components and microservices using visual workflows.

How Step Functions Work: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/)

AWS monitors popular code repository sites for IAM access keys that have been publicly exposed. AWS Health raises an AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED event when an IAM access key has been publicly exposed on GitHub. A CloudWatch Events rule detects this event and invokes a Step Function that orchestrates the automated workflow to remove the exposed IAM access key and summarize recent API activity for that key. The workflow will also issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS. The AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED event is exposed by the Personal Health Dashboard service.

Mitigating security events using AWS Health and CloudTrail: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automate-your-it-operations-using-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automate-your-it-operations-using-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)

Incorrect options:

Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED in the Health service. Trigger a Lambda function that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements - Since how to react to this event is complex and may require retries, and you want to have a complete audit trail of each workflow, you should use Step Functions instead of a Lambda function. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED on the CloudTrail service. Trigger a Lambda workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements - How to react to this event is complex and may require retries, and you want a full audit trail of each workflow, so you should use Step Functions instead of Lambda. Additionally, the AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED event is generated by AWS Health and not CloudTrail, so this option is incorrect.

Create a CloudWatch Event that checks AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED on the CloudTrail service. Trigger a Step Function workflow that will issue API calls to IAM, CloudTrail, and SNS to achieve the desired requirements - The AWS_RISK_CREDENTIALS_EXPOSED event is raised by the AWS Health service and NOT by CloudTrail, therefore this option is incorrect.

REFERENCES

[https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automate-your-it-operations-using-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automate-your-it-operations-using-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/health/latest/ug/getting-started-phd.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/health/latest/ug/getting-started-phd.html)

question:
The DevOps team at a presentation software company is deploying their core application using Elastic Beanstalk. The application is deployed using a Deploy stage in a CodePipeline pipeline. Technical requirements require changing the configuration of the Application Load Balancer associated with Elastic Beanstalk by adding an HTTP to HTTPS redirection rule.

As a DevOps Engineer, you do not have permissions to directly edit the Elastic Beanstalk environment, how can you proceed?

options.A: Create a file called .ebextensions/alb.config in your code repository and add a container_commands block in which you will specify a command to be executed in leader_only mode. The EC2 instance will issue an API call to the Load Balancer to add the redirect rule
options.B: Using the EB CLI, create a file .elasticbeanstalk/saved_configs/config.yml, and specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Run a deploy using the EB CLI from your computer to the Elastic Beanstalk environment
options.C: Using the EB CLI, create a file .elasticbeanstalk/saved_configs/config.yml, and specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Configure CodePipeline to deploy to Elastic Beanstalk using the EB CLI and push the code
options.D: Create a file called .ebextensions/alb.config in your code repository and add an option_settings block in which you will specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Push your code and let CodePipeline run

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a file called .ebextensions/alb.config in your code repository and add an option_settings block in which you will specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Push your code and let CodePipeline run

You can use Elastic Beanstalk configuration files (.ebextensions) along with your web application source code to configure your environment and customize the AWS resources it contains. Configuration files are documents in YAML or JSON format with a .config extension that you place in a folder called .ebextensions and deploy in your application bundle. You can use the option_settings key to modify the environment settings. You can choose between general options for all environments and platform-specific options.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/ebextensions.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/ebextensions.html)

Note: The recommended values apply when you create or update an environment in the Elastic Beanstalk API using a client. For example, the client can be the AWS Management Console, Elastic Beanstalk Command Line Interface (EB CLI), AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or SDKs. Recommended values ​​are set directly at the API level and have the highest precedence. Settings applied at the API level cannot be changed using option_settings, as the API has the highest precedence.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/command-options.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/command-options.html)

Configuration changes made directly to the Elastic Beanstalk environment will not persist if you use the following methods:

Configure an Elastic Beanstalk resource directly from the console of a specific AWS service.

Install a package, create a file, or run a command directly from your EC2 instance.

For the given use case, using a .ebextensions file and configuring the rules in the option_settings block is the correct option.

Incorrect options:

Using the EB CLI, create a file .elasticbeanstalk/saved_configs/config.yml, and specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Configure CodePipeline to deploy to Elastic Beanstalk using the EB CLI and push code - This option has been added as a distractor since you cannot configure CodePipeline to deploy using the EB CLI.

Using the EB CLI, create a file .elasticbeanstalk/saved_configs/config.yml, and specify the rules for the aws:elbv2:listener:default key. Run a deploy using the EB CLI from your computer to the Elastic Beanstalk environment - Using the EB CLI from your computer would normally work, but the question specifies that you do not have the necessary permissions to make direct changes to the Beanstalk environment. Therefore, we must use CodePipeline.Create a file called .ebextensions/alb.config in your code repository and add a container_commands block in which you will specify a command to be executed in leader_only mode. The EC2 instance will issue an API call to the Load Balancer to add the redirect rule - Using container_commands might work, but it is not a good practice as the EC2 instance would issue a command towards the ALB and therefore the configuration would be different than the one specified by Beanstalk, and the EC2 instance may not have sufficient permissions through its IAM role to execute that command. Therefore, this option is incorrect.

question:
The DevOps team at a retail company has deployed its main application on EC2 instances using CodeDeploy and an RDS PostgreSQL database to store the data, while using DynamoDB to store the user sessions. As a Lead DevOps Engineer in the company, you would like the application to securely access RDS and DynamoDB.

How can you do this in the safest way?

options.A: Store RDS credentials and DynamoDB credentials in Secrets Manager and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager
options.B: Store RDS credentials in a DynamoDB table and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access DynamoDB
options.C: Store IAM user credentials and RDS credentials in Secrets Manager and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager
options.D: Store RDS credentials in Secrets Manager and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager and DynamoDB

explanation:
Correct option:

Store RDS credentials in Secrets Manager and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager and DynamoDB

AWS Secrets Manager is a secrets management service that helps you protect access to your applications, services, and IT resources. This service allows you to easily rotate, manage, and recover database credentials, API keys, and other secrets throughout their lifecycle.

You can use Secrets Manager to natively rotate credentials for Amazon Relational Database Service (RDS), Amazon DocumentDB, and Amazon Redshift. You can extend Secrets Manager to rotate other secrets, such as credentials for Oracle databases hosted on EC2 or OAuth refresh tokens, by modifying example Lambda functions available in the Secrets Manager documentation.

To access PostgreSQL, you can use database credentials and it is best to store them in Secrets Manager from a security best practices perspective. Access to Secrets Manager is regulated by an IAM role with the corresponding policy. You must write this IAM policy allowing your application on EC2 instances to access specific secrets. Then, in your application code, you can replace plaintext secrets with code that retrieves these secrets programmatically using the Secrets Manager APIs. To access the DynamoDB table, you must also add the appropriate policy to this IAM role.

Incorrect options:

Store RDS credentials and DynamoDB credentials in Secrets Manager and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager - As mentioned in the explanation above, Secrets Manager does NOT support DynamoDB, therefore this option is incorrect.

Store RDS credentials in a DynamoDB table and create an instance IAM role for EC2 to access DynamoDB - It is not recommended to store RDS credentials in DynamoDB as it can be accessed by anyone who has access to the underlying table. This constitutes a serious security threat.

Storing IAM user credentials and RDS credentials in Secrets Manager and creating an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager - Storing IAM user credentials in Secrets Manager is a distraction, as no IAM user credentials are required to build a solution for this use case. You can directly use an instance IAM role for EC2 to access Secrets Manager.

REFERENCES

[https://aws.amazon.com/secrets-manager/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/secrets-manager/faqs/)

question:
As part of the CI/CD pipeline, the DevOps team at a retail company wants to deploy the latest application code to a staging environment and the team also wants to run an automated set of functional tests before deploying to production. The code is managed via CodeCommit. Usually, the functional test suite runs for more than two hours. The company has hired you as an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer Professional to build a solution for this requirement.

How would you create the CI/CD pipeline to run the test suite most efficiently?

options.A: Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and as a first stage run a CodeBuild build that will run the test suite against the staging environment. Upon passing, deploy to staging using CodeDeploy and if successful, deploy to production
options.B: Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a CodeBuild build that will run the test suite. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production
options.C: Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a custom stage using a Lambda function that will run the test suite. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production
options.D: Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a custom stage using a Lambda function that will invoke a Step Function execution. The Step Function will run the test suite. Create a CloudWatch Event rule upon completion of your Step Function execution to invoke a Lambda function and signal CodePipeline on success or failure. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a CodeBuild build that will run the test suite. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production

CodeCommit is a secure, highly scalable, and managed source code control service that makes it easy for teams to collaborate on code. A CI/CD pipeline helps you automate steps in your software delivery process, such as initiating automatic builds and then deploying to Amazon EC2 instances. You can use AWS CodePipeline, a service that builds, tests, and deploys your code every time there is a change, based on the release process models you define to orchestrate each step in your release process.

Sample AWS CodePipeline pipeline architecture:

Highly recommend reading this excellent reference AWS DevOps blog on using CodePipeline with CodeBuild to automate testing - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/automating-your-api-testing-with-aws-codebuild-aws-codepipeline-and-postman/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/automating-your-api-testing-with-aws-codebuild-aws-codepipeline-and-postman/)

AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service in the cloud. CodeBuild compiles source code, runs tests, and produces packages ready to deploy. CodeBuild eliminates the need to provision, manage, and scale your own build servers. CodeBuild automatically scales up and down and processes multiple builds concurrently, so your builds don't have to wait in a queue. CodeBuild recently announced the release of a new feature called Reports. This functionality allows you to view reports generated by functional or integration tests. Reports can be in JUnit XML or Cucumber JSON format. You can see metrics like success rate, test execution duration, and number of successful vs. failed/error cases in one place.

AWS CodeBuild Test Reports: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/test-reports-with-aws-codebuild/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/test-reports-with-aws-codebuild/)

For the given use case, you need to use a CodeBuild build to run the test suite, but you must first deploy to staging before running CodeBuild. It is common on the exam to show the same steps in a different order, so be careful.

Incorrect options:

Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and as a first stage run a CodeBuild build that will run the test suite against the staging environment. When passing, deploy to staging using CodeDeploy and if successful, deploy to production - As mentioned earlier in the explanation, you cannot have the CodeBuild testing stage before deploying to the staging environment, therefore this option is incorrect.Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a custom stage using a Lambda function that will run the test suite. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production - Lambda must be dropped to run the test suite as the maximum execution time of a Lambda function is 15 minutes, so it will not support this use case as the functional test suite runs for more than two hours.

Create a CodePipeline pointing to the master branch of your CodeCommit repository and automatically deploy to a staging environment using CodeDeploy. After that stage, invoke a custom stage using a Lambda function that will invoke a Step Function execution. The Step Function will run the test suite. Create a CloudWatch Event rule upon completion of your Step Function execution to invoke a Lambda function and signal CodePipeline on success or failure. If the stage does not fail, the last stage will deploy the application to production - AWS Step Functions is a fully managed service that makes it easy to coordinate distributed application components and microservices using visual workflows. Although the Step Functions solution would work, it is extremely complex and not the most efficient solution.

How Step Functions Work: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/)

question:
A financial planning company runs a tax optimization app that allows people to enter their personal financial information and get recommendations. The company is committed to maximum security for personally identifiable information (PII) stored in S3 buckets, and as part of compliance requirements, needs to implement a solution to be alerted in the event of new PII and its access in S3.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer, what solution would you recommend that requires MINIMAL development effort?

options.A: Enable Amazon Macie on the selected S3 buckets. Configure alerts using CloudWatch Events
options.B: Create an Amazon Lambda function that is integrated with Amazon SageMaker to detect PII data. Integrate Lambda function with S3 events for PUT requests
options.C: Configure an S3 bucket policy that filters requests that contain PII data using a conditional statement
options.D: Enable Amazon GuardDuty on selected S3 buckets. Set up alerts using CloudWatch Alarms

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable Amazon Macie on the selected S3 buckets. Configure alerts using CloudWatch Events

Amazon Macie is a security service that uses machine learning to automatically discover, classify, and protect sensitive data in AWS. Macie automatically detects a large and growing list of sensitive data types, including personally identifiable information (PII) such as names, addresses, and credit card numbers. It also provides continuous visibility into the security and privacy of data stored in Amazon S3.

How Macie Works: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/macie/](https://aws.amazon.com/macie/)

For the given use case, you can enable Macie on specific S3 buckets and then configure SNS notifications using CloudWatch events for Macie alerts.

For a more in-depth look at how to query PII data using Macie, check out this excellent blog:

Incorrect options:

Enable Amazon GuardDuty on selected S3 buckets. Configure alerts using CloudWatch Alarms - Amazon GuardDuty is a threat detection service that continuously monitors malicious activity and unauthorized behavior to protect your accounts and workloads on AWS.

How GuardDuty Works: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/](https://aws.amazon.com/guardduty/)

Create an Amazon Lambda function that is integrated with Amazon SageMaker to detect PII data. Integrating Lambda function with S3 events for PUT requests - Amazon Lambda + SageMaker might work but requires significant development effort and probably won't deliver optimal results.

Configure an S3 bucket policy that filters requests that contain PII data using a conditional statement - S3 bucket policies cannot parse the data content in a request. This option has been added as a distractor.

question:
An IT company is creating an online reservation system for hotels. The booking flow that the company has implemented can take more than 3 hours to complete as a manual verification step by a third-party provider is required to ensure that the transactions are not fraudulent.

As a DevOps Engineer, you need to expose this as a secure API to end customers. The website must be able to support 5000 requests at the same time. How should you implement this as simply as possible?

options.A: Create the reservation flow in Step Functions. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with Step Functions. Secure your API using Cognito
options.B: Create the reservation flow in AWS Lambda. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with AWS Lambda. The Lambda function will wait for the response from the service provider and then return the status to API Gateway. Secure your API using Cognito
options.C: Create the reservation flow in AWS Lambda. Enable public invocations of Lambda functions so that customers can initiate the reservation process. The Lambda function will wait for the response from the service provider and then return the status to the client. Secure calls using IAM
options.D: Create the reservation flow in Step Functions. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with AWS Lambda, which will in turn invoke the Step Functions workflow. Secure your API using Cognito

explanation:
Correct option:

Create the reservation flow in Step Functions. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with Step Functions. Secure your API using Cognito

API Gateway APIs can directly invoke an AWS service and pass a payload to it. It is a common way to provide a public and secure API for selected AWS services.

Amazon API Gateway integrates with AWS Step Functions, allowing you to call Step Functions using APIs you create to simplify and customize interfaces to your applications. Step Functions make it easy to coordinate distributed application components and microservices as a series of steps in a visual workflow. You can create state machines in the Step Functions console or using the Step Functions API to specify and run your app's steps at scale. API Gateway is a fully managed service that makes it easy for developers to publish, maintain, monitor, and secure APIs at any scale.

How API Gateway Works: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/](https://aws.amazon.com/api-gateway/)

How Step Functions Work: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/)

For the given use case, you need to implement the booking flow using Step Functions. A key reason is that AWS Lambda has a maximum execution time of 15 minutes, while flow requires more than 3 hours. Additionally, API Gateway can handle thousands of concurrent requests and by integrating it directly with Step Functions you avoid Lambda concurrency limitations.

Incorrect options:

Create the reservation flow in Step Functions. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with AWS Lambda, which will in turn invoke the Step Functions workflow. Securing your API using Cognito - AWS Lambda has an execution and concurrency limit, and using it as an intermediary is not necessary when API Gateway can integrate directly with Step Functions.

Create the reservation flow in AWS Lambda. Create an API Gateway stage using a service integration with AWS Lambda. The Lambda function will wait for the response from the service provider and then return the status to API Gateway. Secure your API using Cognito

Create the reservation flow in AWS Lambda. Enable public invocations of Lambda functions so that customers can initiate the reservation process. The Lambda function will wait for the response from the service provider and then return the status to the client. Secure calls using IAM

Lambda functions cannot handle this flow because it can take more than 3 hours, which exceeds the maximum execution limit of 15 minutes.

question:
The technology team at a healthcare solutions company has developed a REST API that is deployed in an Auto Scaling Group behind an Application Load Balancer. The API stores the data payload in DynamoDB and the static content is served over S3. By performing some analysis, it has been found that 85% of read requests are shared among users.

As a DevOps Engineer, how can you improve application performance while reducing cost?

options.A: Enable ElastiCache Redis for DynamoDB and ElastiCache Memcached for S3
options.B: Enable DAX for DynamoDB and ElastiCache Memcached for S3
options.C: Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3
options.D: Enable ElastiCache Redis for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3

explanation:
Correct option:

Enable DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3

DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) is a highly available, fully managed in-memory cache for Amazon DynamoDB that delivers up to 10x performance improvement—from milliseconds to microseconds—even with millions of requests per second.

DAX is tightly integrated with DynamoDB—you simply provision a DAX cluster, use the DAX Client SDK to point your existing DynamoDB API calls to the DAX cluster, and let DAX handle the rest. Because DAX is API-level compatible with DynamoDB, you don't have to make functional changes to your application code. DAX is used to natively cache DynamoDB reads.

CloudFront is a CDN (Content Delivery Network) service that delivers static and dynamic web content, video streams and APIs around the world, securely and at scale. By design, delivering data from CloudFront can be more cost-effective than delivering it directly from S3 to users.

When a user requests content served with CloudFront, the request is routed to a nearby Edge Location. If CloudFront has a cached copy of the requested file, it delivers it to the user providing a fast response (low latency). If the file is not cached, CloudFront fetches it from the source, for example the S3 bucket where the content is stored.

Therefore, you can use CloudFront to improve application performance by serving static content from S3.

Incorrect options:

Enable ElastiCache Redis for DynamoDB and CloudFront for S3

Amazon ElastiCache for Redis is an extremely fast in-memory data store that provides sub-millisecond latency for real-time, internet-scale applications. It is an excellent option for cases such as caching, messaging, gaming, leaderboards, geospatial, machine learning, media streaming, queues and real-time analytics.

ElastiCache for Redis Overview: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/redis/](https://aws.amazon.com/elasticache/redis/)

Although you can integrate Redis with DynamoDB, it is much more complex than using DAX, which is a better option in this case.

Enable DAX for DynamoDB and ElastiCache Memcached for S3

Enable ElastiCache Redis for DynamoDB and ElastiCache Memcached for S3

Amazon ElastiCache for Memcached is a Memcached-compatible in-memory key-value storage service that can be used as a cache or datastore. It is useful to reduce latency, increase throughput and relieve database load.

ElastiCache cannot be used to cache static content coming from S3, so these options are incorrect.
