question:
As a DevOps Engineer in an IT company, you are looking to create a daily EBS backup workflow. That workflow should take an EBS volume and create a snapshot from it. When the snapshot is created, it must be copied to another region. In the event that the other region is unavailable due to a disaster, that backup must be copied to a third region. An email address must be notified of the final result. There is a requirement to maintain an audit trail of all executions as well.

How can you implement this efficiently and in a fault-tolerant manner?

options.A: Create an AWS Step Function. Implement each step as a Lambda function and add failure logic between steps to handle conditional cases
options.B: Create an EC2 instance in the region where the EBS volume is. Create a CRON script that invokes a Python script that performs all the steps and logic described above. For each step completed, write metadata to a DynamoDB table
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that runs daily. This triggers a Lambda function written in Python that performs all the steps and logic described above. Analyze run history using AWS Config
options.D: Create an SSM automation that will perform each action. Add failure logic between steps to handle conditional cases

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an AWS Step Function. Implement each step as a Lambda function and add failure logic between steps to handle conditional cases

Step Functions is a fully managed service that makes it easy to coordinate distributed application components and microservices using visual workflows.

How Step Functions Work: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/](https://aws.amazon.com/step-functions/)

For the given use case, you need to combine Step Functions, Lambda, and CloudWatch Events into a coherent solution. You can use Step Functions to coordinate business logic to automate the snapshot management flow with error handling, retry logic, and execution flow defined within the Step Functions definition. CloudWatch Events integrates with Step Functions and Lambda to allow you to run custom code when relevant events occur.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automating-amazon-ebs-snapshot-management-with-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automating-amazon-ebs-snapshot-management-with-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)

For a more in-depth analysis of this solution, it is recommended to review the following reference material: [https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automating-amazon-ebs-snapshot-management-with-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/compute/automating-amazon-ebs-snapshot-management-with-aws-step-functions-and-amazon-cloudwatch-events/)

Incorrect options:

Create an EC2 instance in the region where the EBS volume is. Create a CRON script that invokes a Python script that performs all the steps and logic described above. For each step completed, writing metadata to a DynamoDB table - Create an EC2 instance might work, but if it finishes you would have to recreate it. Failure scenarios would be difficult to analyze and maintaining an audit trail in DynamoDB would probably not be user-friendly.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that runs daily. This triggers a Lambda function written in Python that performs all the steps and logic described above. Analyze execution history using AWS Config - Creating a CloudWatch Event + Lambda rule might work, but the Lambda function may have timeout issues if the backup takes more than 15 minutes, and AWS Config cannot store execution history. AWS Config only provides a detailed view of the resources associated with your AWS account, including how they are configured, how they relate to each other, and how those configurations have changed over time.

Create an SSM automation that will perform each action. Add failure logic between steps to handle conditional cases - An SSM automation cannot contain complex logic to handle failures, although it would provide an execution history.An SSM automation document defines the actions that Systems Manager performs on your managed instances and other AWS resources when an automation runs. A document contains one or more steps that are executed in sequential order. Each step is built around a single action. The output of one step can be used as input in a later step. The process of executing these actions and their steps is called automation flow.

question:
The DevOps team at an e-commerce company is working with the internal security team to improve the security flow of the code release process. The DevOps team wants to start a third-party code vulnerability scanning tool every time code is uploaded to their CodeCommit repository. The code must be sent via an external API.

As an AWS Certified DevOps Engineer, how would you implement this most efficiently?

options.A: Create a CodeCommit hook on an EC2 instance that transmits changes from CodeCommit to the local file system. A cron job on the EC2 instance will compress the code and send it to the third party API when changes are detected
options.B: Create a CloudWatch Event rule with a 5-minute cron that triggers a Lambda function that will check for new commits in your CodeCommit repository. If new commits are detected, download and compress the code and then send it to the third party's API
options.C: Create a CloudWatch Event rule in your CodeCommit repository that reacts to pushes. As a target, choose an AWS Lambda function that will request the code from CodeCommit, compress it, and send it to the third party's API
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule in your CodeCommit repository that reacts to pushes. As a target, choose an S3 bucket so that the code is automatically compressed in S3. Create an S3 event rule to fire a Lambda function that will retrieve the compressed code from S3 and send it to the third party's API

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CloudWatch Event rule in your CodeCommit repository that reacts to pushes. As a target, choose an AWS Lambda function that will request the code from CodeCommit, compress it, and send it to the third party's API

Amazon CloudWatch Events delivers a near real-time stream of system events that describe changes to AWS resources. Using simple rules that you can quickly configure, you can match events and route those events to one or more destination functions or streams. You can generate custom events at the application level and publish them to CloudWatch Events. You can also set up scheduled events that are generated periodically. A rule matches incoming events and routes them to targets for processing.

CloudWatch Events Overview: via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html)

For the given use case, you can configure a CloudWatch Event rule for each push to the CodeCommit repository that triggers the configured target Lambda function. The Lambda function will, in turn, request the code from CodeCommit, compress it, and send it to the third party's API.

Incorrect options:

Create a CloudWatch Event rule in your CodeCommit repository that reacts to pushes. As a target, choose an S3 bucket so that the code is automatically compressed in S3. Create an S3 event rule to trigger a Lambda function that will retrieve the compressed code from S3 and send it to the third party API - CloudWatch Event rules cannot target S3 buckets. Although you can use an S3 trigger, you would eventually need to invoke Lambda to process the code via the API. Therefore, it is more efficient to directly invoke the Lambda function from the CloudWatch Event rule.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule with a 5-minute cron that triggers a Lambda function that will check for new commits in your CodeCommit repository. If new commits are detected, download and compress the code and then send it to the third party's API - Scheduled rules would introduce latency and be inefficient.

Create a CodeCommit hook on an EC2 instance that transmits changes from CodeCommit to the local file system. A cron job on the EC2 instance will compress the code and send it to the third party API when changes are detected - The CodeCommit hook on EC2 is a distractor and does not exist.

REFERENCES

[https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonCloudWatch/latest/events/WhatIsCloudWatchEvents.html)

question:
A cyber forensics company wants to ensure that CloudTrail is always enabled in their AWS account. You also need to have an audit trail of the CloudTrail state. In case of compliance breaches, the company would want to resolve them automatically.

As a DevOps Engineer, how can you implement a solution for this requirement?

options.A: Place all your AWS IAM users under an IAM group called 'everyone'. Create a deny IAM policy on that group to prevent users from using the DeleteTrail API. Create an AWS Config rule that tracks whether each user is in that IAM group. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to be alerted in case of breaches, and fire a Lambda function that will add users to the 'everyone' group automatically
options.B: Create an AWS Config rule to track whether CloudTrail is enabled. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to be alerted in case of breaches, and fire a Lambda function that will re-enable CloudTrail
options.C: Place all your AWS IAM users under an IAM group called 'everyone'. Create a deny IAM policy on that group to prevent users from using the DeleteTrail API. Create a CloudWatch Event rule that will fire a Lambda function every 5 minutes. That Lambda function will check if CloudTrail is enabled using an API call and re-enable it if necessary
options.D: Create a CloudWatch Event rule that will fire a Lambda function every 5 minutes. That Lambda function will check if CloudTrail is enabled using an API call and re-enable it if necessary

explanation:
Correct option:

Create an AWS Config rule to track whether CloudTrail is enabled. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to be alerted in case of breaches, and fire a Lambda function that will re-enable CloudTrail

CloudTrail provides visibility into user activity by recording actions taken in your account. CloudTrail records important information about each action, including who made the request, the services used, the actions performed, the parameters of the actions, and the response elements returned by the AWS service. This information helps track changes made to your AWS resources and troubleshoot operational issues.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/](https://aws.amazon.com/cloudtrail/)

AWS Config is a fully managed service that provides you with an inventory of AWS resources, configuration history, and notifications of configuration changes to enable security and governance. With AWS Config you can discover existing AWS resources, export a complete inventory of your AWS resources with all configuration details, and determine how a resource was configured at any given time.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/config/](https://aws.amazon.com/config/)

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/config/faq/](https://aws.amazon.com/config/faq/)

You need to have an AWS Config rule to maintain auditability and track compliance over time. You can use the Config cloudtrail-enabled managed rule to check if AWS CloudTrail is enabled in your AWS account. You can use the Config cloudtrail-security-trail-enabled managed rules to verify that at least one AWS CloudTrail trail defined with security best practices exists. To be alerted of compliance issues, use a CloudWatch Event rule and then connect it to a Lambda function that will automatically re-enable CloudTrail.

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudtrail-enabled.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudtrail-enabled.html)

via - [https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudtrail-security-trail-enabled.html](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/config/latest/developerguide/cloudtrail-security-trail-enabled.html)

Incorrect options:

Place all your AWS IAM users under an IAM group called 'everyone'. Create a deny IAM policy on that group to prevent users from using the DeleteTrail API. Create an AWS Config rule that tracks whether each user is in that IAM group. Create a CloudWatch Event rule to be alerted in case of breaches, and fire a Lambda function that will add users to the 'everyone' group automaticallyPlace all your AWS IAM users under an IAM group called 'everyone'. Create a deny IAM policy on that group to prevent users from using the DeleteTrail API. Create a CloudWatch Event rule that will fire a Lambda function every 5 minutes. That Lambda function will check if CloudTrail is enabled using an API call and re-enable it if necessary

IAM users within a group with a deny policy sounds like a great idea at first, but you have to remember that you can create IAM roles, and they won't have that restriction, and so you can assume those roles and then issue API calls over CloudTrail to disable it. This solution will not work and therefore both options are incorrect.

Create a CloudWatch Event rule that will fire a Lambda function every 5 minutes. That Lambda function will check if CloudTrail is enabled using an API call and re-enable it if necessary - You need to have an AWS Config rule to maintain auditability and track compliance over time, since using a Lambda function to trigger an API call would only tell you the state of CloudTrail at that point in time.

question:
Your company has adopted a git repository technology to store and version control your application code. Your company wants to ensure that the production branch of the code is deployed to the production environment, but would also like to enable other versions of the code to be deployed to the development and staging environments to perform various kinds of user acceptance testing.

As a DevOps Engineer, what solution would you implement for the given requirement?

options.A: Create a CodeCommit repository for the development code and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodeCommit repository and CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes from the production branch to the production environment after a manual approval has occurred on the first CodePipeline
options.B: Create a CodeCommit repository and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes to the production branch to the production environment after the code is merged via a pull request
options.C: Create a CodeCommit repository for the development code and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodeCommit repository and CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes from the production branch to the production environment after the code is merged via a pull request
options.D: Create a CodeCommit repository and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a manual approval step after deployment to staging to ensure that the application is reviewed before being deployed to production in the last stage of the pipeline

explanation:
Correct option:

Create a CodeCommit repository and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes to the production branch to the production environment after the code is merged via a pull request

CodeCommit is a secure, highly scalable, and managed source code control service that makes it easy for teams to collaborate on code. A CI/CD pipeline helps you automate steps in your software delivery process, such as initiating automatic builds and then deploying to Amazon EC2 instances. You can use AWS CodePipeline, a service that builds, tests, and deploys your code whenever there is a code change, based on the release process models you define to orchestrate each step in your release process.

via - [https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/projects/set-up-ci-cd-pipeline/](https://aws.amazon.com/getting-started/projects/set-up-ci-cd-pipeline/)

Here you only need a git repository and create a production branch for deployments to production. The other key requirement of the given use case is that two versions of the code need to be deployed to different environments. As such, you will need two CodePipelines. If you had one with a manual approval step at the end, then the code deployed to production would come from the master branch instead of the production branch. Here, we specifically need the code in the production branch to be deployed to production, therefore we need a second CodePipeline and merge code from master to production using Pull Requests.

Code Pipeline Overview: via - [https://aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/faqs/](https://aws.amazon.com/codepipeline/faqs/)

Incorrect options:

Create a CodeCommit repository and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a manual approval step after deployment to staging to ensure that the application is reviewed before being deployed to production in the last stage of the pipeline - As mentioned in the previous explanation, a key requirement is that two versions of the code need to be deployed to different environments. If you use a manual approval step after deploying to staging, then the same version of code from the master branch would also be deployed to the production environment. Instead, you need to maintain a production branch of the code that can be deployed to the production environment.Create a CodeCommit repository for the development code and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodeCommit repository and CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes from the production branch to the production environment after the code is merged via a pull request - It is a best practice to work with branches in your git repository to create features, since that is the intended use of branches. Don't create separate repositories for features. You should not maintain separate repositories to manage two versions of code that need to be deployed to different environments. The reference to merging via a pull request has been added as a distractor.

Create a CodeCommit repository for the development code and create a CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy any changes in the master branch to the development and staging environments. Create a second CodeCommit repository and CodePipeline pipeline that will deploy changes from the production branch to the production environment after a manual approval step has occurred in the first CodePipeline - It is a best practice to work with branches in your git repository to create features, since that is the intended use of branches.
